This study presents a theoretical analysis of intermodal forward Brillouin scattering within solid-core photonic crystal fibers. The proposed model incorporates the impact of fiber imperfections on mode coupling, specifically examining how hexagonal lattice defects influence coupling between the fundamental quasi-TE mode and higher-order quasi-TM modes. Utilizing a perturbation method, the research identifies critical speeds for these higher-order modes and predicts the maximum coupling coefficient. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that fiber imperfections can be engineered to adjust the hexagonal lattice to achieve degenerate propagation of the fundamental and higher-order modes. This capability offers a means to broaden the interaction bandwidth for high-sensitivity distributed sensing applications. Additionally, the study confirms that the derived formulas remain valid for fibers with small pitch values, ensuring applicability across a wide range of operating wavelengths. Finally, the potential for sensing various physical parameters is illustrated by calculating the relative sensitivity of the fundamental mode to external pressure and the higher-order mode to temperature. These findings are supported by numerical simulations conducted in COMSOL Multiphysics. The research was conducted within the framework of the French National Research Agency's "ANR-19-CE05-0009" program. Keywords: Intermodal, Brillouin, Photonic crystal fiber, Solid core, Perturbation, Sensing.

This paper establishes a broad extension of the geometric foundation theorem regarding spherical subgroups within the B-type Coxeter groups $GL(n,R)$ and $O(n,R)$. Furthermore, this theorem facilitates the computation of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic for arbitrary spherical subgroups in $O(n,R)$. Specifically, the Euler-Poincaré characteristic of $GL(n,R)$ is determined as $n+1$, whereas for any spherical subgroup $H$ of $O(n,R)$, it is given by $\chi(H)=\frac{n}{2}+1$. Additionally, the theorem enables the calculation of the Poincaré polynomials and Hilbert-Poincaré series for spherical subgroups $H$ in $O(3,R)$ and $O(4,R)$. The Set-Union Knapsack problem involves selecting a subset of items to maximize the coverage of unique item types, ensuring the total weight does not exceed a specified capacity. This challenge has applications in fields such as diet planning, portfolio management, and resource allocation. This paper introduces a new metaheuristic designed to identify high-quality solutions for this problem. We also examine the Productive and Efficacious Local search (PEL) method, which is grounded in the concept of productive directions within combinatorial optimization. We adapt PEL to address the Set-Union Knapsack challenge and evaluate its performance against other metaheuristics, including Variable Neighbourhood Descent, Iterated Local Search, and a Genetic Algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate that PEL is both productive and effective, consistently outperforming the compared methods. Furthermore, we apply PEL to the Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem, a variant where item weights are replaced by costs, and the objective becomes maximizing coverage within a fixed budget. Our findings indicate that PEL remains highly effective in this context as well. The study concludes that PEL is a potent and versatile tool for solving multiple combinatorial optimization problems. Online gaming operators face significant challenges in predicting player attrition, a process that is both costly and time-intensive. This article introduces a novel approach to attrition forecasting by leveraging betting patterns within an online environment. Our proposed method utilizes a supervised learning algorithm to identify patterns that indicate future player churn. We validate the efficacy of this method through case studies conducted across various betting domains. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves performance comparable to that of the operator's existing solution. Furthermore, our method offers the distinct advantage of being rapid, low-cost, and scalable. The two-dimensional Ising model serves as a paradigm for the conventional, second-order, and universal phase transition that occurs when a symmetry-breaking field is removed at the critical temperature. In contrast, Ising field theory, which describes the associated conformal field theory, remains valid in the presence of this symmetry-breaking field. We demonstrate that, within the framework of Ising field theory, the free energy of a thin film exhibits a nonanalytic Yang-Lee edge singularity as a function of the symmetry-breaking field. This finding aligns with the broader principle that quantum or statistical field theories, even those not at a critical point, can display nonanalyticities when symmetry-breaking fields are present. This principle extends beyond the Ising model to encompass other nonabelian field theories, including those governing superfluids and quantum chromodynamics. Furthermore, we show that the quantum field theory of a Bose gas, which exhibits supersymmetry in the limit of zero interaction strength, also features a Yang-Lee singularity in its free energy when a supersymmetry-breaking field is applied. Finally, we discuss the physical implications of these findings for the magnetic free energy of a superfluid and for the bosonic Yang-Lee singularity observed in the magnetic free energy of a ferromagnet. Our findings suggest that this singularity may persist in the clean limit and could be observable in experiments involving granular or disordered thin films. Additionally, we examine the implications of these results for the recently proposed concept of a ferromagnetic Yang-Lee singularity, which would represent the first observation of a nonabelian singularity in a non-SU(N) field theory. This would provide the first experimental evidence of a nonabelian singularity in a field theory that is not at a critical point. The proposed experiment involves measuring the magnetic free energy of an ultra-pure ferromagnetic thin film as a function of the applied magnetic field, specifically in the temperature range slightly below the Curie temperature. Such measurements would enable the observation of the previously predicted ferromagnetic Yang-Lee singularity. This represents the first instance of a nonabelian singularity being observed in a field theory that is not at a critical point. The study of such singularities in non-critical field theories is expected to yield new insights into the fundamental nature of these theories. For instance, the nonabelian singularity could be interpreted as a manifestation of a hidden conformal symmetry within the field theory. Cycling is a popular mode of transport that offers both environmental and personal health advantages. However, the mobility benefits often come at the cost of increased exposure to road traffic accidents. To address this, there is a growing need for intelligent systems capable of predicting crashes and assessing risks for cyclists. This paper introduces a novel risk descriptor designed to predict incidents based on the dynamic context of cycling. This descriptor integrates dynamic and static elements, including the cyclist's behavior, traffic volume, road characteristics, and weather conditions. The context variables are derived from a video-driven approach, utilizing computer vision to extract dynamic data and a knowledge graph to organize static information. The study validates the proposed descriptor using a dataset comprising 1,000 cyclists, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting crashes with an area under the ROC curve exceeding 0.85. Additionally, the paper explores the potential for this descriptor to support intelligent systems in predicting and preventing cyclist accidents. This paper introduces a new approach to motion planning for dynamic robots subject to safety-critical constraints, utilizing control barrier functions (CBF). The proposed method ensures secure pathfinding by integrating CBFs into the graph search algorithm A*, resulting in a more resilient system capable of safely navigating unstructured, hazardous environments. Furthermore, the technique incorporates CBF-Nash equilibrium constraints to address adversarial attacks, thereby guaranteeing safe trajectory planning even when adversaries attempt to compromise the system. We present a novel framework that embeds CBF-Nash equilibrium into the A* cost function, allowing the algorithm to generate CBF-Nash safe trajectories. The study concludes with a simulation study of a 2D robot navigating a hazardous zone. Results demonstrate that embedding CBF-Nash equilibrium into A* enables the robot to identify a safe trajectory through the dangerous area, even in the presence of adversarial attacks. Additionally, the proposed algorithm successfully plans a safe path in real-time, outperforming existing methods. Finally, we implemented the method on a real-time hardware platform, showcasing its practical viability. The simulation outcomes confirm the method's ability to plan safe trajectories for dynamic robots within hazardous regions, even under adversarial conditions. Furthermore, the experimental results validate the proposed approach's suitability for real-time applications. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/raja-agarwal/CBF-A-Star. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial examples, which are intentionally perturbed inputs designed to deceive them. This study explores the relationship between adversarial robustness and model memorization, positing that memorization serves as the underlying cause for vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We introduce a novel defense mechanism that reduces memorization by applying a mean filter to the neural representations of training data. Our findings demonstrate that robustness and memorization are inversely related: as memorization decreases, robustness improves. Furthermore, we propose an alternative hypothesis for adversarial susceptibility, suggesting that the network's tendency to fit training data too closely is the primary factor. Finally, we examine the influence of data augmentation and dropout on adversarial robustness, with experimental results confirming that both techniques enhance resilience by lowering memorization. We demonstrate that every dilation surface possesses a closed geodesic whose monodromy ensures all its iterates remain geometrically distinct. This finding is achieved by proving that horizon saddle links for dilation surfaces constitute exactly the aperiodic closed horizon Sierpinski sets, thereby establishing the Morse-Smale nature of these links. Additionally, we provide a partial resolution to a conjecture by Avila and Kodytek regarding dilation surfaces that lack a Lyapunov spectrum, showing that such surfaces must contain a nontrivial invariant sub-dilation surface. Furthermore, we establish that every dilation surface contains a closed horizon Sierpinski set, thereby extending the work of Avila and Kodytek. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential future research directions in this area. This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing functional connectivity that integrates both positive and negative correlations. We demonstrate that this "total association" effectively captures the functional connectivity of the human mind and significantly enhances the accuracy of individual personality trait prediction. We also validate the robustness of the total association metric through simulations. Furthermore, we illustrate how functional connectomes derived via total association facilitate a more precise identification of brain regions involved in social cognition. These findings underscore the critical role of negative correlations in functional connectivity analysis. Classical Segal-Bargmann theory offers a unitary equivalence between $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n, dx)$ and the space of square-integrable holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}^n$ with respect to the measure $d\mu(z) = \pi^{-n} e^{-|z|^2} d^2z$. This equivalence is realized through an integral Segal-Bargmann map $S$, which maps a function $f(x)$ to $F(z) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K(z,x) f(x) dx$, where the kernel is defined as $K(z,x) = (\pi^{-1/2})^n e^{-\frac{1}{2}(z+\bar{z}-x)^2} e^{\frac{1}{2}(z+\bar{z})x}$. This study extends that theory into the framework of Clifford algebra-valued functions. By defining a generalized Segal-Bargmann map $S_{\mathbb{R}^n\oplus\mathbb{R}^n\oplus\mathbb{R}^{n-1}}$ and a Taylor series isomorphism $T_{\mathbb{R}^{n-1}}$, we demonstrate their respective isomorphisms. Furthermore, the algebraic structure of the tensor product space $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n, dx) \otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}^n, dx) \otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}^{n-1}, dx)$ is mapped isomorphically to the space of square-integrable Clifford analytic functions on $\mathbb{C}^n \oplus \mathbb{C}^{n-1}$. Additionally, we establish the corresponding relationships for Taylor series isomorphisms. Finally, the study confirms the invariance of the Segal-Bargmann map under rotations within $\mathbb{R}^n \oplus \mathbb{R}^n \oplus \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. These findings provide a foundation for the algebraic analysis of Clifford-valued functions and hold significant potential for applications in theoretical physics. This work investigates Gaussian processes conditioned on a specific functional of their sample paths. We establish non-trivial existence results by imposing mild conditions on the target process and its boundary values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Gaussian fields can be conditioned on nondegenerate closed sets in a non-trivial manner, provided the set is bounded and has a non-zero minimum distance from the support of the unconditioned field. Additionally, we explore Gaussian processes conditioned on linear subspaces of their sample paths, deriving key properties such as stationarity and Markovian behavior. In particular, we identify a family of non-trivial examples involving Gaussian fields conditioned on constant functions, which includes the free boundary Schramm-Loewner evolution ($SLE$) measure as a special case. Our approach relies on novel integral representations of Gaussian measures conditioned on functionals of their paths, utilizing the novel concept of conditional characteristic functional. These findings are supported by illustrative examples and computational simulations. The paper concludes with several open questions. Notably, we address the conditioning of Gaussian fields on non-compact closed sets, such as half-spaces, and provide a detailed analysis of the Gaussian measure conditioned on a half-space. Finally, we examine the relationship between our findings and the concept of Gaussian measures with line conditioning, as well as the recently proposed notion of Gaussian measures conditioned on geometric objects. These latter concepts are currently under review in a related paper. The present study also draws inspiration from recent research on Gaussian fields conditioned on closed sets. This paper investigates the performance of a wireless sensor network (WSN) by examining the relationship between a ground-based sensor grid and an expanding coverage area. As the region grows, we analyze the link between the number of sensors within that area and the size of that size. We introduce a coverage metric that accounts for sensor distribution across both ground and aerial-sky dimensions. Utilizing a Poisson point process, we model the random placement of sensors on the ground and apply a Poisson process to represent sensors in the sky. The sky sensors are assumed to possess sufficient mobility to cover vacant ground sensor zones. We demonstrate that the counts of ground and sky sensors in any finite region are independent Poisson random variables. Furthermore, we show that the Poisson process remains invariant when augmented by the points of a finite set. We also establish that the Poisson process is closed under the superposition of independent processes. Leveraging these properties, we derive a closed-form expression for the probability that no ground sensors exist within a given region. Additionally, we provide an expression for a coverage function that quantifies the probability that all ground sensors within a region are observed by at least one sky sensor. Finally, we examine the asymptotic behavior of this coverage function as the region size increases. We demonstrate that as the region becomes very large, the probability that a sky sensor covers a ground sensor within that region approaches zero. However, the probability that at least one sky sensor covers a ground sensor in the region approaches one as the number of sky sensors grows large. We also analyze the rate of convergence for this coverage function and find that it is inversely proportional to the number of sky sensors. We further illustrate that the coverage function approaches its limit as the number of sky sensors tends to infinity. Finally, we show that the coverage function is monotonically increasing with respect to both the number of sky sensors and the region size. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The results indicate that increasing the number of sky sensors significantly improves coverage, whereas enlarging the region size has a negligible impact. This suggests that achieving full coverage of a large region requires a substantial number of sky sensors. We also observe that the coverage function is not linear with respect to the number of sky sensors. This nonlinearity implies that adding more sky sensors yields diminishing returns, meaning each additional sensor contributes less to overall coverage than the previous one did. These insights are valuable for WSN design, resource allocation, and optimization. They can guide decisions on how many sky sensors are needed to achieve a desired level of coverage

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is designed to investigate fundamental properties of neutrinos, including their absolute mass scale, CP-violation phase, and the hierarchy of their mass states. As a next-generation neutrino experiment, DUNE will utilize a 1.356 MW proton beam from the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) to generate a high-statistics neutrino beam. These particles will travel 1,300 km through the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota before interacting with a large liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC). This extensive baseline and detector volume are essential for observing the oscillation of all three neutrino flavors. The experiment aims to measure the CP-violating phase with an uncertainty of approximately 15 degrees, thereby establishing a new era of precision in neutrino physics. This paper outlines the anticipated performance of the Far Detector at DUNE. Additionally, we examine the impact of the Near Detector, which will help constrain the initial neutrino beam flux and reduce uncertainties in the interaction cross-section. Furthermore, we explore the potential of combining DUNE data with other neutrino experiments to further refine measurements of the CP-violating phase and the absolute neutrino mass scale. Our findings indicate that the Far Detector alone can determine the CP-violating phase with an uncertainty of about 15 degrees, while the absolute mass scale can be measured with 10% precision using a 300 kton argon detector. When augmented by the Near Detector and complementary experiments, the uncertainty in the CP-violating phase could be reduced to roughly 10 degrees, and the uncertainty in the absolute mass scale might reach as low as 5%. These results demonstrate that DUNE will usher in a new age of accuracy within neutrino physics. This document serves as a white paper for the 2021 SPS Accelerator Study (ASSP). The ASSP is a strategic initiative by the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) to evaluate the scientific potential of the SPS for the DUNE far and near detectors, as well as for a potential European Muon Collider. The full paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01001. We introduce a machine learning-enhanced top tagger designed for the CMS experiment, specifically for the analysis of associated-top production at the LHC. Utilizing a graph neural network, the tagger processes the jet's constituent particles to generate a classification of the object. To interpret this model, we apply the Shapley value method, which quantifies the contribution of each input feature to a specific prediction. This approach offers a transparent and mathematically rigorous framework for feature importance, enabling the investigation of potential correlations within the data. Our results demonstrate that the tagger achieves a 10% improvement in performance compared to current top-tagging methods. Furthermore, the feature importance analysis reveals that substructures such as diffuse radiation and three-pronged subjets are critical to the tagger's decision-making process. These findings indicate that the enhanced capabilities stem from the tagger's ability to resolve complex substructures within jets, thereby improving its discrimination power. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/CMSTopGroup/topTagger_2022. Semantic enhancement of Value Added Services (VOs) is crucial for facilitating a more integrated and seamless user experience. This paper introduces a method to improve VOs by formally defining the meanings of semantic annotations within a Voucher Enhancement Language (VEL). VEL is a novel language designed to extend VOs with semantic information, utilizing a subset of the RDF data model. The proposed approach enables a more user-centric VO structure by integrating additional VEL-based data. Furthermore, VEL can be formally translated into RDF, thereby enriching both the VO and existing semantic knowledge bases. This work represents the foundation of the VEL4VO project, which aims to provide a formal and extensible framework for semantic enhancement of value-added services. The project's primary goal is to establish a formal basis for VEL and its application to VOs, ensuring compatibility with semantic knowledge bases and supporting various access methods. This document details the formalization of VEL and VOs, along with their respective semantics. VEL is defined as a syntactic and semantic language based on XML, while VOs are formalized using an existing language definition. The paper also outlines the formalization of VEL's semantics and describes how VEL can be translated into RDF. Finally, the work addresses the formalization of semantic access to VEL and its interaction with semantic knowledge bases. Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential in addressing complex decision-making tasks. However, the variance inherent in RL's update mechanism often hinders agent performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a variance reduction-based experience replay (VRER) module designed to enhance the stability of policy updates. VRER achieves this by mitigating the impact of high-variance gradients through two key strategies: first, it mitigates the effects of biased and high-variance function approximations by storing a sufficient number of samples; second, it minimizes the influence of high-variance gradients during each policy update by selecting a subset of samples with the lowest variance for training. We evaluated VRER across three distinct RL algorithms using various function approximators on the Atari benchmark. The results indicate that VRER effectively stabilizes policy updates, leading to improved performance. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that VRER is particularly beneficial when training with a limited number of samples. The source code for VRER is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/Var-Exp-Rep.

Spatiotemporal learning is a fundamental challenge in various real-world applications, including weather forecasting, traffic prediction, and anomaly detection. Current approaches typically model the spatiotemporal distribution by integrating temporal feature learning with spatial correlation analysis. However, existing methods often overlook the spatiotemporal evolution of motion features, such as wind velocity and pedestrian flow speed, which are critical for understanding dynamic changes. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called MoDeRNN (Motion features driven Recurrent Neural Network), designed to incorporate motion features into predictive learning. MoDeRNN comprises two primary components: a Motion Feature Extractor (MFE) and a Motion-driven RNN (MD-RNN). The MFE captures motion features from input data, while the MD-RNN utilizes these features to enhance predictive performance. We evaluated MoDeRNN across three datasets—two weather datasets and one pedestrian trajectory dataset—covering tasks like temperature prediction, precipitation nowcasting, and trajectory prediction. The results demonstrate that including motion features significantly improves prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies and case analyses to provide deeper insights into the characteristics of motion features. Overall, MoDeRNN serves as a general-purpose framework for leveraging motion features in spatiotemporal learning. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/MoDeRNN.

This paper introduces Josephine, a new type system designed to bridge the advantages of both Rust and Python. While Python offers a straightforward and secure approach to memory management, it lacks the expressive capabilities needed for high-performance applications. Conversely, Rust provides fine-grained control over memory layout and operations but demands more effort to write correct code. By integrating the simplicity and security of Python with the expressiveness of Rust, Josephine enables programmers to define the lifetimes of Rust references using JavaScript. The study demonstrates that this hybrid language is effective, safe, and performant. Furthermore, it outlines the design and implementation of Josephine, proving that the proposed language constructs are expressible, its semantics are decidable, and that the necessary type checking can be realized. The paper concludes by discussing potential future enhancements. Josephine is accessible at https://github.com/brandon-rust/josephine. When two astronomical images are combined, the resulting point spread function (PSF) is often approximated by convolving the individual PSFs. This study examines the discrepancies between the PSF of the true combined image and the approximate PSF derived from the summation of individual contributions. We establish that these differences are governed by the second moments of the individual PSFs and the square of their flux ratio. Consequently, the relative difference in flux between the broadened and broadening stars must be less than 0.01 to ensure the deconvolution process remains unaffected. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the root mean square error of the deconvolution is directly proportional to the second moments of the broadened star and inversely proportional to the second moments of the broadening star. These findings are applicable to both analytical and numerical deconvolution methods. Additionally, we illustrate how these differences influence the accuracy of photometry and astrometry in the combined images. Our results indicate that astrometry is more sensitive to these discrepancies than photometry. Finally, we present a practical example of how these differences impact the measurement of the flux and position of a quasar in a Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3/IR) image. This case study confirms that the derived differences are significant enough to necessitate the use of the PSF from the actual combined image for both photometric and astrometric measurements. We conclude that the PSF of a true combined image should be employed whenever feasible. This is particularly critical when measuring the flux of a source in a deep image using a shallow image as a reference, or when measuring the position of a source in a high-resolution image using a low-resolution image as a reference. In such scenarios, the relative flux difference between the deep and shallow images should remain below 0.01, and the difference in resolution between the high- and low-resolution images should be minimal. Otherwise, the derived flux and position will be inaccurate. We also note that these conclusions are independent of the specific deconvolution method utilized. Finally, we provide a Python package, named \texttt{psf\_diff}, which calculates these differences for any pair of input PSFs. This tool is available at \url{https://github.com/rajanishkumar/psf_diff}. The code is written in Python and is compatible with both Windows and Linux operating systems. This study investigates the fracture resilience of crystalline materials through a computational framework that integrates atomistic modeling with machine learning. We developed a machine learning potential grounded in the physics of brittle fracture, designed to accurately represent the brittle-to-ductile transition. Utilizing this potential, we conducted molecular dynamics simulations to calculate fracture toughness across various orientations in single crystals of silicon and aluminum oxide. Furthermore, we employed machine learning to rapidly and precisely predict fracture toughness for the entire space group of silicon and aluminum oxide. Our results indicate that fracture toughness is highly sensitive to orientation and exhibits periodicity, which can be explained by the underlying crystallographic structure. This methodology offers a powerful approach for efficiently and precisely characterizing the fracture resilience of crystalline materials. Additionally, the capability to predict material properties for all 230 space groups in crystalline materials holds significant potential for high-throughput materials discovery. This study offers a novel a priori estimate regarding the maximum norm for solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations under periodic initial conditions. By employing a new resolution based on the fractional part of the equation, the proof remains independent of the maximum norm, thereby establishing a new proof for the global existence of smooth solutions. This approach utilizes a specific time discretization that avoids reliance on Gronwall's inequality. The methodology can be readily extended to other partial differential equations. The findings are available as an arXiv preprint at [arXiv:2101.01007v1 [math.AP]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01007). The corresponding video demonstration can be found at [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222).

We introduce a novel protocol that leverages quantum computers to efficiently validate the correctness of quantum computations. This method relies on minimal quantum resources, specifically demanding only a single qubit of working memory and a sparse oracle. Crucially, our approach achieves linear runtime, thereby overcoming the superlinear complexity barrier established by Beame, Childs, and Kuperberg (STOC 2017). Furthermore, we demonstrate that any rejection instance identified by our protocol can be transformed into an accepting input in constant time with high probability, a capability that distinguishes our method from prior research. Finally, we extend this verification framework to the broader context of interactive proofs, yielding new findings within that domain. Notably, our primary protocol remains robust against a constant fraction of malicious gates, provided the error correction code possesses a constant distance. Additionally, we demonstrate that traditional verification can be accomplished in linear time with high probability when a constant number of gates are faulty. These findings are anticipated to advance the fields of quantum verification and classical verification. The implementation of our protocol is available on GitHub. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to facilitate the deployment of blockchain solutions within the Internet of Things (IoT). The framework enables the exchange of data and services among IoT devices, IoT applications, and blockchain nodes. It supports three specific communication modes: IoT-to-IOT, IoT-to-Blockchain, IoT-to-Application, and reciprocally, Blockchain-to-IOT, Blockchain-to-IOT, and Application-to-IOT. To address the challenges inherent in these interactions, the study proposes a framework that leverages the complementary strengths of both technologies. This solution utilizes smart contracts to manage transactions between IoT devices and nodes, while incorporating oracles to ensure reliable data exchange between the IoT ecosystem and the blockchain network. The proposed approach was validated through a food supply chain use case, demonstrating its practical applicability. The paper concludes by discussing potential future enhancements. Keywords: Internet of Things (IoT), Blockchain, Oracle, Smart Contracts.

This study introduces a new approach to generating realistic cell shapes using implicit neural representations. By employing a neural network to encode the cell boundary as an implicit function, the method enables creative and practical 3D shape modeling of cell forms. We demonstrate that this technique surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in modeling cell forms, particularly for those with complex morphologies. Furthermore, the approach supports a wide range of creative shape designs, including those that are biologically implausible, and facilitates manipulation of generated cells through gradient-based optimization. Finally, the method is shown to be effective for inverse design applications, such as engineering cells with specified surface or volume properties. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb2000/icmr2022.

Document accessibility is essential for individuals who rely on assistive technologies to access digital content. However, access to documents created with proprietary software often remains restricted due to compatibility and cost barriers. This paper introduces a novel, cost-effective approach to enhancing document accessibility by converting PDF files into formats compatible with assistive technology using open-source tools. The proposed method employs Tesseract OCR to extract text from PDF documents and subsequently converts them into JAWS-friendly HTML files. To improve the accuracy of the OCR conversion, the system integrates a GPT-3-based Large Language Model (LLM) that analyzes the extracted text and generates a refined version. This system was evaluated using a dataset of 100 documents, including invoices, bank statements, and resumes. The results demonstrate that the system significantly boosts the performance of assistive technologies in reading and interpreting the converted documents. Furthermore, the integration of the LLM ensures that the system can handle various document types with greater precision. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta123456789/Document-Accessibility. This system is particularly beneficial for users facing challenges with proprietary software, such as Microsoft Word, while offering a more affordable and accessible solution for assistive technology practitioners. Future work will focus on expanding the document types supported by the system and further refining the accuracy of the text extraction process. We introduce XLNet, a generalized autoregressive pre-training method designed for language understanding. Unlike BERT, which relies on masking, our approach maximizes the expected performance of downstream tasks by employing an autoregressive pre-training objective. To ensure robustness and capture diverse linguistic phenomena, we utilize position-biased, word-biased, and word-shuffled masking strategies. Additionally, we implement an expected mask pre-training objective to enhance the model's resilience against the varying probabilities of mask tokens. Pre-trained on the GLUE benchmark, XLNet achieves state-of-the-art results across eight tasks, surpassing BERT by 2.5 to 4.1 points. Furthermore, when applied to the recently introduced Natural Language Inference (nli) dataset, XLNet outperforms BERT by 10.4 points and establishes a new state-of-the-art. Notably, XLNet successfully addresses the contradiction and neutral labels while maintaining high accuracy in the entailment category, thereby fulfilling the three-way classification requirement of the nli dataset. Stellar activity significantly influences the interpretation of exoplanet atmospheres, yet its effects are typically examined at low-resolution wavelengths (R ~ 100) where numerous activity-induced spectral features complicate transmission spectrum analysis. This study presents a high-resolution characterization of the K2-18 system, a small, active M-dwarf hosting a sub-Neptune, utilizing data from the Keck/HIRES and Keck/NIRSPEC instruments. We identified numerous emission lines from the host star, which were subsequently modeled to determine the distribution of high-energy radiation. Our analysis reveals that the high-energy radiation flux from K2-18 is comparable to that of TRAPPIST-1, a star known to host planets in the Earth-to-Super-Earth mass range. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the host star's X-ray flux and the planet's atmospheric scale height, suggesting that high-resolution spectroscopy can effectively mitigate the impact of stellar activity on exoplanet atmospheric characterization. These findings are supported by a detailed analysis of the K2-18 system's high-resolution spectra. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy serves as a powerful tool for characterizing small exoplanets around active stars, offering a pathway to better understand their atmospheric properties. This approach is particularly valuable for the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope, which is expected to observe numerous small planets around active stars. Our findings suggest that high-resolution spectroscopy can substantially aid in the atmospheric characterization of these systems. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive list of emission lines from the K2-18 host star, which can be utilized to model the distribution of high-energy radiation. This study presents the first experimental characterization of the swimming mechanics of *Hydrachna centripeda*, a species of water centipede. We demonstrate that these creatures employ a novel locomotion strategy, utilizing elastic leg movements to propel themselves across the water surface. Furthermore, we quantify the relationship between the centipedes' body mass and their swimming velocity, revealing that their size enables them to overcome water surface tension effects, thereby achieving speeds comparable to those of larger species. Finally, we analyze the centipedes' response to external forces, such as wind, and illustrate how their body shape and size facilitate rapid directional changes. These findings are supported by a simple mathematical model of the centipede as a chain of rigid segments connected by elastic joints. The model indicates that the centipedes' swimming behavior is governed by the interplay between their body geometry and the water surface's surface tension. Additionally, we show that the swimming dynamics of both the centipede and a simplified model can be described using a single dimensionless parameter, which represents the ratio of the centipede's weight to the water surface tension force. This study presents a new numerical approach designed to model the global propagation of tsunamis generated by asteroid impacts. The method employs a sequence of nested computational domains, each utilizing a finite volume scheme on an unstructured mesh of triangular cells. To accurately capture the transition between near-field and far-field dynamics, the algorithm relies on a specific set of assumptions and a critical parameter: the free surface elevation. This parameter is determined through a matching procedure that ensures the continuity of the solution across adjacent nested domains. The algorithm's efficacy is assessed through a series of tests examining key issues, including the selection of an appropriate domain, the alignment of collision energy with observed craters, and the impact of mesh resolution on the resulting solutions. These examinations are essential for accurately simulating the complex dynamics of the near-field-to-far-field transition. Ultimately, the algorithm is applied to simulate the far-field propagation of tsunamis resulting from the collision of a 10 km asteroid with Earth. The simulation reveals a significant amplification of wave height as the near-field transitions to the far-field, with the maximum wave height reaching approximately 100 meters. This substantial amplification is attributed to the interaction between the incoming wave and the surrounding bathymetry. The research concludes that this methodology offers a robust framework for simulating the transmission of dispersive waves from an asteroid impact, with potential extensions to other celestial bodies. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable for modeling other phenomena, such as seismic wave transmission from earthquakes, where energy release is more gradual than in an instantaneous impact. This capability is particularly valuable for analyzing the transmission of dispersive waves from large-scale events, such as the 2011 Tohoku earthquake. The algorithm is implemented in C++ and is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/abraham-fernando/TSUNAMI. We present early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of a unique class of galaxies characterized by being optically faint yet infrared (IR) luminous. These objects are defined by their extremely high IR-to-optical flux ratios, with $f_{\rm IR}/f_{\rm 1.6\mu m}$ values reaching up to $10^5$ and $f_{\rm IR}/f_{\rm 0.6\mu m}$ exceeding $10^6$. Our analysis of 1000 galaxies from the Early Release Science Early Data (ERS-ED) program demonstrates that this population is not merely a selection artifact. Instead, they represent a distinct group of low-redshift ($z<1$) galaxies that are optically too dim to be detected in Hubble Space Telescope (HST) imaging but are readily observable in the mid-infrared (MIR) bands of JWST/NIRCam. These galaxies are predominantly dusty star-forming systems with star formation rates (SFR) ranging from 0.1 to 100 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, where the majority of their optical light is reprocessed by dust. Our findings indicate that these galaxies are primarily composed of young stars with ages less than 100 Myr, exhibiting a top-heavy stellar mass function and a significant fraction of massive stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the IR-to-optical ratio serves as a robust indicator of stellar age, with younger galaxies displaying higher ratios. This population is likely a significant contributor to the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) at $z<1$, and their presence suggests that a substantial fraction of galaxies may be missed in HST surveys due to their optical faintness. We conclude that JWST's MIR capabilities are essential for a more complete understanding of galaxy evolution. Finally, we discuss the potential for these galaxies to be progenitors of the bright galaxies observed at higher redshifts. We introduce a gravitation theory that extends Einstein's general relativity by incorporating the Gauss-Bonnet term found in five-dimensional Riemannian geometry. This framework maintains a direct geometric interpretation and admits solutions that offer new insights into the nature of black holes. Specifically, we examine a class of static, spherically symmetric black hole spacetimes, where the black hole mass exhibits a non-linear relationship with its horizon radius. Furthermore, these spacetimes possess small black holes that bypass the usual nucleation barrier characteristic of their large black hole counterparts; consequently, these small black holes can arise through the standard gravitational collapse of matter. The thermodynamics of these black holes are analyzed, revealing phase transition phenomena analogous to those observed in four-dimensional Einstein gravity. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological structure of the event horizon surface significantly influences black hole properties. In particular, black holes surrounding anti-de Sitter space demonstrate enhanced stability compared to those in asymptotically flat environments. Finally, we derive an exact solution to the gravitational equations describing a rotating black hole with a non-linear mass-radius relation. This solution generalizes the C. Myers and J. Perry black hole and shares similar thermodynamic characteristics with its static counterpart. We also provide the explicit form of this rotating solution in the context of asymptotically anti-de Sitter space. These findings suggest that the topological aspect of the black hole's event horizon surface plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of black holes in our universe. These results may offer valuable insights for understanding the black holes observed in our universe. This paper is the first of a series; in the subsequent work, we will explore the physical properties of these black holes in greater detail. The series will conclude with a third paper titled: "Small Black Holes and the Topological Structure of the Event Horizon Surface." We examine the self-organization of hard spheres and mass points in the two-dimensional limit, as well as self-organizing mass points in a channel, when subjected to a slow, random input sequence. We demonstrate that random disks naturally segregate into layers based on their size, whereas a specific class of random sequences—alternating sequences—can induce the formation of non-trivial layered structures even among objects with identical sizes. This phenomenon is driven by a specific kind of jamming that occurs in the channel disk system. We also present a simple model for mass points that successfully predicts the layering of random spheres and the layer formations generated by alternating sequences. Furthermore, we find that the layer structure emerging from an alternating sequence is contingent upon the specific sequence itself, even when the individual elements are drawn from the same size distribution. Finally, we illustrate that the layer structure produced by an alternating sequence can be precisely anticipated by examining the alternating sequence's properties. These findings are supported by computer simulations. Our results indicate that the layering of randomly mixing disks is an inherent property of the system, while the layering of size-sorted disks within an alternating sequence is an emergent property arising from the specific characteristics of that sequence. This size-sorted layering is not universal across all alternating sequences but is instead tied to the specific features of the sequence and the initial state of the system. Our study of the mass point model offers a straightforward explanation for these phenomena. We anticipate that these results will prove valuable for the design of new sorting and separation methods. Additionally, our findings may offer insights into the self-organization of granular materials in space and the formation of planetary systems. This study examines the spatial and temporal patterns of very low and high seasonal precipitation across the globe, analyzing how these patterns shift under different El Niño types. The methodology involves identifying the 30-year period with the highest precipitation rate for each season between 1951 and 2020, followed by a comparison with the corresponding period of lowest precipitation. These contrasts are then overlaid with maps depicting the global spatial footprint of the three primary El Niño types. The results reveal that the three El Niño types exhibit distinct spatial signatures of extremely low and high precipitation, with these signatures varying by season. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the three El Niño types display different temporal behaviors regarding very low and high precipitation. These findings suggest that the three El Niño types leave unique global imprints on seasonal precipitation extremes, a conclusion supported by the observed differential responses of precipitation to the three types. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of monitoring all three El Niño types to accurately predict the potential impacts of global precipitation extremes. We examine the connection between structural and mechanical non-affinity in amorphous solids by conducting computer simulations of two-dimensional repulsive disks near their jamming threshold. While measuring mechanical non-affinity is straightforward, quantifying structural non-affinity is more complex; we address this by analyzing the pair distribution function and applying anisotropic scattering. Our findings indicate that structural and mechanical non-affine displacements exhibit a strongly correlated, linear relationship, a result that is significant for understanding shear transformation zones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the correlation between the mean square mechanical and structural non-affine displacements remains independent of the radius used to calculate structural non-affinity. Finally, we confirm that the relationship between the two types of non-affinity is consistent across various preparation protocols, including compression from the liquid phase, compression from the Gaussian ensemble, and unjamming. These insights are derived from extensive simulations involving on the order of $10^5$ particles. The methodology for measuring structural non-affinity is also applicable to experimental techniques such as four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and small-angle scattering. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package to facilitate the calculation of structural non-affinity. This paper serves as a tutorial for researchers interested in applying these concepts to their own systems. Our results suggest that the physical mechanisms driving non-affine growth are universal across different preparation methods, a conclusion supported by the fact that the ratio of mechanical to structural non-affinity is independent of the specific protocol employed. This universality extends to the relationship between the two non-affinities, which is governed by the system's excess volume. The implications of these results for understanding the physics of non-affine growth are discussed. Finally, we explore the relationship between non-affinity and non-uniformity in the pair distribution function. Our analysis reveals that the primary contribution to non-uniform scattering arises from the anisotropy of the $g(r)$ function, which is directly linked to non-uniform scattering. We also examine the link between non-uniform scattering and the pair distribution function's Fourier transform, showing that the non-uniform scattering component is proportional to the imaginary part of the Fourier transform of the anisotropic component. This relationship is verified by comparing our theoretical predictions with numerical simulations. The study concludes by discussing the potential for future research in this area. We establish conditions ensuring the existence of positive solutions and analyze the dynamics of the corresponding zero solution. Furthermore, we derive sufficient criteria for the global asymptotic stability of the zero solution and the positive solution. Finally, we validate these theoretical findings through numerical simulations. The study concludes by outlining potential extensions of the proposed model. Additionally, we provide an appendix containing the proofs for the stability theorems. This paper introduces a new method for assessing the robustness of cyber-physical systems. We define a robust control strategy as one that maintains a specific formal property, described by an STL formula, despite disturbances within a defined set. Our approach enables the calculation of disturbance bounds for given strategies, property formulas, and disturbance sets, or conversely, the synthesis of strategies that guarantee property satisfaction under potential disturbances. Central to this work is a novel concept called "robustness," derived from Signal Temporal Logic, which quantifies how closely a system's trajectory adheres to a temporal property. This metric facilitates the optimization of control strategies to either maximize robustness or ensure robustness remains above a specific threshold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework is sound and complete regarding the robust satisfaction of STL formulas. Finally, we introduce an algorithm to compute the robustness of STL formulas and illustrate the practical utility of our robustness definition through a case study on a wheeled robot. This paper investigates a nonlinear diffusion equation defined on a complete Riemannian manifold $M$ with non-negative Ricci curvature. We introduce two nonlinear operators, $T_1$ and $T_2$, which serve as gradient approximations for the diffusion equation's right-hand side. We demonstrate that $T_1$ and $T_2$ adhere to the principles of causality, stability, and spatial and temporal translation invariance. Furthermore, we establish that $T_1$ fulfills the principle of locality. Additionally, we prove that $T_1$ exhibits data dependence within a region determined by the manifold's manifold distance and the solution's norm. The $L^p$-stability of $T_1$ is guaranteed under conditions involving the manifold's manifold diameter, the solution's norm, and the eigenvalues of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Finally, we show that $T_2$ maintains $L^p$-stability provided the eigenvalues of the Laplace-Beltrami operator are bounded from below. These findings are applicable to sub-Riemannian manifolds. All results are supported by numerical experiments. The manuscript includes a Python implementation of $T_1$ and $T_2$ for Euclidean space, available at https://github.com/SebastianSchmid1992/NonlinearDiffusion. Keywords: nonlinear diffusion, manifold, gradient approximation, data dependence.

The nature of compact radio sources, particularly those with angular sizes under 1 arcsecond, remains poorly understood. This study investigates their properties by stacking images of approximately 100,000 sources from the NVSS catalog that meet the criteria of being compact, radio-emitting, and having a redshift greater than 0.01. The analysis examines their spectral indices, source counts, and spectral energy distributions (SEDs). The resulting stacked image reveals a bright, double-lobed structure oriented along a position angle of roughly 100 degrees, with a central component exhibiting a Gaussian profile of about 10 kpc (1 arcsec) and a half-power width of approximately 2 kpc (0.2 arcsec). The spectral index of the central region is measured at $\alpha = -0.7 \pm 0.1$, while the lobes have an index of $\alpha = -0.2 \pm 0.1$. The total flux density is estimated at $1.1 \pm 0.1$ mJy, with the lobes contributing about 0.2 mJy each. The source count distribution aligns with NVSS predictions for sources with flux densities between 0.5 and 1.5 mJy, and the SED indicates a peak flux density of approximately 1.5 mJy at 1.4 GHz. These findings suggest that the stacked image represents a typical radio galaxy, characterized by a central region likely containing an active galactic nucleus (AGN) and two large-scale jets feeding the lobes. The study concludes that the majority of compact radio sources are likely radio galaxies. Furthermore, the observed source counts and SEDs are consistent with a black hole mass of approximately $10^8 M_{\odot}$, which is typical for AGNs in massive galaxies. Finally, the research demonstrates that the NVSS is a valuable resource for investigating the properties of compact radio sources. (Abridged)

We present a framework for analyzing the statistical nonlocality of dynamical patterns, defined as the correlation length of their temporal fluctuations. This approach is applied to a two-component reaction-diffusion system exhibiting a dynamically coherent statistical state, where the local concentration of one species fluctuates in time with a finite correlation length relative to the concentration of the other species. We demonstrate that this statistical nonlocality emerges from the competition between the intrinsic relaxation rates of the two species and their cross-diffusion coefficients. Furthermore, we show that the system's relaxation dynamics can be accurately modeled using a single effective linear relaxation rate, which is derived from the system parameters and the coherence length of the dynamical pattern. This work extends our previous study on the emergence of dynamically coherent statistical states in the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction [Phys. Rev. E 103, 062203 (2021)]. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of this framework in both natural and engineered systems. Specifically, we illustrate how it can be utilized to control the relaxation dynamics of such systems by adjusting the statistical nonlocality. Finally, we highlight the relevance of this framework to various other systems, including those in ecology, biology, and chemistry. Our findings suggest that these systems may exhibit dynamically coherent statistical states, thereby offering new insights into their behavior and opening avenues for future research. We introduce a phenomenological framework designed to investigate flexible scattering amplitudes across any dimension. This approach relies on a basis of functions derived from physical considerations, specifically crossing symmetry and unitarity. By computing the complete unitary cutting structure for two-loop form factors within any dimension, we demonstrate how this method can be applied to construct general scattering amplitudes and form factors. Furthermore, we utilize this technique to derive new analytic expressions for planar $N=4$ super Yang-Mills two-loop form factors, covering both the crossing-symmetric and non-crossing-symmetric components. Finally, we present numerical tests that validate our results against Monte-Carlo integrations. Our methodology is broadly applicable to any process where a scattering amplitude decomposes into building blocks, such as form factors. Additionally, our findings can be incorporated into the recent open-source software package \texttt{xfscatt}, which is available at \url{https://github.com/xfscatt/xfscatt}. This study examines how a conducting plate affects blackbody radiation within a cavity and subsequently investigates blackbody thermodynamics under the influence of the Casimir effect. The cavity's volume is defined by a cube of side length $L$, where the specific mode $(L,L,L)$ is selected to maximize the Casimir force. The analysis demonstrates that the system's temperature is no longer uniform throughout the volume. Furthermore, the total energy of the system is not directly proportional to the temperature, and the heat capacity becomes negative in certain regions. These findings indicate that the system's behavior diverges significantly from standard blackbody radiation thermodynamics. Finally, the entropy of the system is calculated, and the second law of thermodynamics is examined. The results confirm that entropy is not distributed uniformly, and the second law remains valid only when the conducting plate is removed from the cavity. Additionally, the study explores the possibility of extracting work from the system and analyzes the associated efficiency. Ultimately, the efficiency exceeds that of a Carnot engine only when the conducting plate is withdrawn. These conclusions suggest that the second law of thermodynamics is violated in the presence of the conducting plate. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings. This paper introduces a novel privacy metric for location tracking, defined by an entropy-based formula that measures the uncertainty regarding a data subject's specific positions within a sequence. Unlike most existing privacy metrics, which assume a posterior distribution over possible positions, our measure utilizes a conditional prior. This approach enables a more realistic assessment of privacy in tracking data releases, as it accounts for data subject-specific factors that influence the probability of occupying specific positions. We propose a novel privacy metric and its corresponding disclosure risk, demonstrating that releasing tracking data under this framework results in lower disclosure risk compared to traditional metrics. Furthermore, we develop a new differential privacy mechanism for location tracking that ensures privacy according to our proposed measure. Finally, we evaluate the trade-off between privacy and utility for this mechanism against other established location privacy mechanisms. Experimental results indicate that our mechanism achieves both higher privacy levels and superior utility relative to other methods. This paper introduces NDT-Transformer, a new neural network architecture designed for 3D point cloud localization. Unlike many recent approaches that rely on 3D keypoints or utilize NDT solely as a final refinement step, NDT-Transformer directly models the NDT description. It employs a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework to learn the mapping from 3D points to Gaussian parameters, enabling end-to-end localization. The model is trained on a large-scale dataset featuring 3D point clouds and pre-computed NDT descriptions. Experimental results demonstrate that NDT-Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D localization, particularly within challenging environments. Furthermore, the approach exhibits strong robustness against sensor noise and variations in point density. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is widely employed to investigate brain networks and their alterations in both healthy and diseased states. However, the reliability of connectivity metrics derived from rs-fMRI data remains uncertain. This study aimed to assess the precision of functional connectivity estimation and its dependence on key experimental parameters, including sample size, spatial resolution, and temporal resolution. We utilized a realistic head phantom to generate synthetic rs-fMRI data, incorporating realistic head motion and physiological noise. Functional connectivity was quantified using Pearson's correlation, and estimation precision was evaluated via the coefficient of variation (CV). Our results indicate that achieving a 10% CV requires a sample size of approximately 100 scans (roughly 10 hours of scanning) at 3 mm resolution, or only 20 scans at 6 mm resolution. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the precision of rs-fMRI connectivity measurements is independent of temporal resolution. These insights offer a quantitative basis for optimizing experimental designs in rs-fMRI research. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package, `reliability-fmri`, which enables users to replicate these results and explore the impact of other experimental parameters on connectivity reliability. This paper investigates a beeping network consisting of $n$ nodes, where each node operates in one of two modes: beep (transmitting silence) or listen (receiving silence). The objective is to execute a naming protocol that assigns a unique ID from the set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ to every node. We introduce a novel energy-efficient naming algorithm where nodes in beep mode conserve energy by activating only a single antenna, whereas nodes in listen mode spend no energy as they rely on pre-existing radio signals. Our approach guarantees a deterministic, distributed, and asynchronous naming solution with a worst-case running time of $O(n^2 \log^2 n)$ rounds. This represents an improvement over the established lower bound of $\Omega(n^2 \log n)$ for energy-efficient naming algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm is optimal by proving that any deterministic, distributed, and asynchronous naming algorithm must require at least $\Omega(n^2 \log n)$ rounds. Additionally, we establish that any randomized, distributed, and asynchronous naming algorithm necessitates a minimum of $\Omega(n^2)$ rounds. Finally, we extend our method to address the leader election problem. Our resulting energy-efficient, deterministic, distributed, and asynchronous leader election algorithm completes in $O(n^2 \log^2 n)$ rounds, surpassing the $O(n^2 \log n)$ lower bound applicable to all distributed (non-energy-efficient) leader election algorithms. This solution is also provably optimal, as we show that any deterministic, distributed, and asynchronous leader election algorithm cannot succeed in fewer than $\Omega(n^2 \log n)$ rounds. We also prove that any randomized, distributed, and asynchronous leader election algorithm requires at least $\Omega(n^2)$ rounds. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first provably optimal solutions for both naming and leader election problems within the beeping network model. Our findings are supported by extensive experimental validation. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ehsan123456789/Beeping-Naming}. Pre-trained language models have driven significant advancements in Natural Language Processing, yet their application to code-mixed languages remains constrained. This limitation stems from the assumption that code-mixed text exhibits a uniform distribution of languages within sentences, a notion that fails to capture the diverse patterns of mixing. To address this, we introduce PESTO, a novel encoder designed to account for the varied mixing patterns found in code-mixed data. We developed a straightforward metric to quantify the degree of code-mixing at both sentence and word levels. Leveraging this measure, we created a new encoding technique that dynamically adjusts positional encodings based on mixing patterns and reduces the scale of embeddings for word-level metrics. We evaluated this encoding on two prominent code-mixed datasets, focusing on the GLUE benchmark. PESTO consistently outperforms baseline models, demonstrating an average relative improvement of 2.5% across all GLUE tasks. Additionally, our experiments indicate that this enhanced encoding effectively generalizes to other language pairs beyond those in the GLUE benchmark. This study investigates the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) in H$_3$S, utilizing a pressure-variable Debye temperature within the Allen-Dynes modification of McMillan's equation. The analysis reveals that at 160 GPa, the isotope coefficient $T_{c0}/T_{c\delta}$ reaches 1.2, aligning with experimental findings. Furthermore, the study identifies a pressure threshold of 160 GPa, beyond which the isotope effect diminishes. This reduction is attributed to the van Hove singularity, which causes a shift in the pressure-dependent phonon density of states from a peak to a plateau. Consequently, the pressure-dependent Debye temperature changes from a peak to a nearly constant value, thereby suppressing the isotope effect. These theoretical predictions offer valuable insights for future experimental research. Additionally, the findings suggest that the van Hove singularity phenomenon may be applicable to other hydrogen-rich high-temperature superconductors. Finally, the pressure-independent McMillan equation is shown to be inadequate for describing the isotope effect in H$_3$S. The proposed theoretical framework is expected to advance the understanding of the superconducting mechanism in H$_3$S. This paper presents a new visual relocalization approach that utilizes an offline-built surfel map to estimate 3D-2D matches, thereby reducing the search space for keypoint matching. To further enhance the accuracy of visual relocalization, we employ learned features that surpass the efficacy of handcrafted ones. Our method's performance is evaluated against two primary baselines: (1) a handcrafted feature baseline that integrates visual relocalization with surfel map assistance, and (2) an online global relocalization baseline utilizing learned features without leveraging the surfel map. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms both baselines, achieving a 10.5% improvement over the surfel-assisted baseline and a 13.5% gain over the global relocalization baseline. Additionally, the method exhibits superior robustness, exhibiting a 2.5x and 1.5x reduction in failure rates compared to the surfel-assisted and online global relocalization baselines, respectively. This finding provides a significant simplification of the description of rational functions on tropical curves and extends naturally to higher dimensions. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this result for the study of rational functions on tropical abelian varieties and their connections to Jacobians and theta divisors. The paper also includes an appendix by David Jensen, which establishes a finiteness theorem for the semiring of effective divisors on tropical arcs over a tropical moduli space. This work generalizes and refines the primary theorem from our earlier study in *Advances in Mathematics*, specifically regarding tropical curves. Additionally, our methods offer a straightforward proof of a key result by Maclagan and Rullgård concerning rational functions on tropical curves. The techniques developed here are also applicable to other areas of tropical geometry, such as the study of rational functions on tropical abelian varieties. To facilitate this application, we have included a detailed discussion on rational functions within an abelian variety. Our results confirm a conjecture by Maclagan and Rullgård regarding rational functions on tropical curves and provide a finite presentation of these functions on tropical abelian varieties, thereby validating a conjecture by Jensen and Rullgård. This paper examines the consistent convergence of empirical semigroups toward the (weak) Q-process within the framework of sub-Markovian transition semigroups. We establish two distinct empirical processes: one derived from a sample of forward trajectories and the other from a sample of backward trajectories. We analyze the consistent convergence of each, noting that the empirical semigroup based on forward trajectories converges to the minimal Q-process, whereas the one based on backward trajectories converges to the (weak) Q-process. Additionally, we demonstrate that the empirical process generated from forward trajectories may fail to converge to the (weak) Q-process. Finally, we illustrate an application of this methodology for estimating the (weak) Q-process in a specific context. Notably, the proposed approach is applicable to any Markov process, including those defined on general state spaces. Furthermore, the methodology can be adapted to estimate the (weak) Q-process using data from both forward and backward trajectories. However, in this combined scenario, the resulting empirical process targets the (weak) Q-process only if the forward empirical process does not converge to the minimal Q-process. In such instances, the number of forward trajectories must be carefully calibrated relative to the number of backward trajectories. This balance is determined by the respective rates of convergence to the (weak) Q-process for both the forward and backward empirical processes. We provide a practical guideline for selecting the appropriate number of trajectories in this context. These results are supported by numerical experiments. The discovery of superconductivity in FeSe at 1 K sparked significant interest in FeSe-based superconductors, as their experimental phase diagrams indicate that non-uniform spin fluctuations drive a nematic instability. To investigate this, we employed a variational cluster approximation (VCA) to analyze the phase diagram of LiFeAs, a FeSe-based compound situated at the extreme edge of the phase diagram. Our results demonstrate that the system is most stable in a superconducting state, with no evidence of a nematic phase. This finding underscores the necessity for a more sophisticated model to accurately describe FeSe. Furthermore, we show that incorporating a moderate electron-phonon coupling of $\lambda=0.5$ into LiFeAs elevates the superconducting transition temperature to $T_c=10$ K. This outcome aligns with the experimentally observed $T_c$ of LiFeAs and suggests that electron-phonon interactions play a crucial role in its superconductivity. Additionally, we observe that the superconducting state is predominantly $s$-wave, with a minor $d$-wave component. These findings provide a foundation for future research into FeSe-based superconductors. Finally, we compare our VCA predictions with results from the functional renormalization group (fRG) method, demonstrating that VCA offers a more efficient approach for studying multiorbital systems. This is because VCA avoids the uncontrolled approximations inherent in fRG, which relies on a perturbative expansion of the self-energy. Instead, VCA employs a non-perturbative self-energy, ensuring that the method remains valid across a broader range of interaction strengths. Consequently, VCA is particularly well-suited for investigating high-temperature superconductivity. Our analysis reveals that the $p$-orbital makes a substantial contribution to the superconducting gap, a factor that must be accounted for in FeSe-based compounds. Two-Higgs-Doublet Models (2HDM) are a popular extension of the Standard Model (SM) that naturally incorporate flavor conservation and CP invariance. This study presents a new method for utilizing particle frameworks in self-assembly, where neural networks are trained to generate force fields that drive particles toward target structures. The framework's versatility is demonstrated across multiple systems, ranging from simple to complex, and the approach is extended to include flexible molecules capable of conformational changes. Furthermore, the method successfully produces functional supramolecular architectures, such as light-harvesting systems and molecular machines. These findings suggest that the proposed strategy can facilitate the computational design of advanced materials and devices. We investigate robustness conditions for anomalies and chirality within chiral gauge theories, demonstrating that these conditions are intrinsically linked. Specifically, we establish that robustness is guaranteed whenever the theory's phase diagram features multiple phases separated by gapless phases that cannot be shifted away. Furthermore, we present a method to identify the phases of any chiral gauge theory by analyzing the phases of its duals, which are defined as theories obtained by gauging a one-form symmetry. This approach enables us to construct phase diagrams for various chiral gauge theories, such as those involving fermions in the fundamental and adjoint representations. Additionally, we examine a potential conflict between robustness and the recent conjecture that all phases in chiral gauge theories are either gapped or described by quantum field theories. To resolve this tension, we propose that certain theories possess gapless phases that are not captured by quantum field theories. Finally, we explore the relationship between robustness and emergent supersymmetry in chiral gauge theories. Our findings suggest that supersymmetric extensions of these theories exhibit robustness whenever they display emergent supersymmetry. Consequently, we can determine which theories possess gapless phases fixed by a conformal manifold and which require a more fundamental description beyond quantum field theory. This paper establishes a novel ill-posedness result regarding the existence of solutions to the steady Navier-Stokes equations within critical Besov spaces. Specifically, for any given data $a \in B^{1+\frac{n}{p}}_{p,1}$ where $1<p<\infty$ and $n$ denotes the spatial dimension, and for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a perturbation $b$ satisfying $\|b\|_{B^{1+\frac{n}{p}}_{p,1}}<\varepsilon$ such that the Navier-Stokes equation $(1.1)$ admits no solution of the form $u=Qa+Qb$. Furthermore, this finding resolves a question posed by Fabes and Jones regarding the solvability of the steady Navier-Stokes equations in critical homogeneous Besov spaces. Additionally, we demonstrate an analogous ill-posedness result for the Cauchy problem of the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations within critical homogeneous Besov spaces. These results extend our prior work \cite{LLW1} concerning the ill-posedness of the steady Navier-Stokes equations in $L^{\infty}$. Finally, we note that the ill-posedness result for the time-dependent case can be derived from the framework established by Koch and Tataru \cite{KT}. However, our approach offers a significant advantage by accommodating a broader range of spatial dimensions and parameters. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents preliminary results and introduces critical Besov spaces; Section 3 proves the ill-posedness result for the steady Navier-Stokes equations, followed by the corresponding result for the time-dependent case in Section 4. This study experimentally examines the thermal pressure exerted by a magnon beam on an antiferromagnetic insulator, achieving the highest sensitivity to thermal magnon pressure to date. By employing a thin layer of the same ferromagnetic insulator, we detect minute shifts in the spectrum of a propagating thermal magnon beam within a yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) waveguide, originating from a room-temperature source heated by a few milliwatts. This magnon beam thermal pressure is further compared against the spectral displacement caused by a co-propagating microwave field. Both phenomena are analyzed through a combination of thermal and hydrodynamic models alongside finite element simulations. The observed thermal spectral displacement scales linearly with the microwave power delivered to the source heater, confirming that the microwave beam is entirely converted into a thermal magnon beam. This finding validates the thermal nature of the displacement and establishes a method for quantifying the pressure of a thermal magnon beam. Additionally, the results demonstrate that thermal magnons exert a non-negligible pressure on magnetic insulators, a factor that must be accounted for in future magnonic devices. Finally, the study confirms the existence of a thermal force acting on magnetic sublattices, a critical component for the development of future magnonic technologies. These findings are achieved using a straightforward experimental configuration that enables the precise characterization of a thermal magnon beam. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to other ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic insulators, offering a pathway to investigate the thermal properties of magnons in these systems. Ultimately, this work represents a significant advancement in the field of thermal magnonics. The accompanying data can be utilized to validate and refine theoretical models of thermal magnon behavior.
