Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem relies on the assumption that finding hyper-ovals within the projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_q)$ is computationally difficult. This paper introduces two modified versions of the original system, each utilizing a distinct method to construct public matrices. The first approach employs a polynomial map to generate hyper-ovals, while the second utilizes a generic method that operates without specific constraints. We demonstrate that both alterations maintain security levels comparable to the original scheme. Furthermore, the first modification offers a significant advantage in terms of key sizes. Experimental findings indicate that the first modification outperforms the second in both encryption and decryption speeds. Finally, we present a practical implementation of the first modification, achieving a security level of 128 bits. The public and private keys for this first modification measure 1.5 KB and 2.5 KB, respectively. Additionally, the encryption and decryption complexities are $O(q^2)$ and $O(q)$, respectively. We anticipate that these modifications will facilitate the design of code-based cryptosystems suitable for resource-constrained environments. Language models (LMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance across numerous downstream tasks, with BERT being a prominent example. However, BERT's pre-training relies solely on a monolingoral corpus, which is often insufficient for low-resource languages. To address this, we introduce Dict-BERT, an enhanced language model that integrates a multilingual dictionary into BERT during pre-training. This dictionary serves as a knowledge source to supplement limited resources, offering word-level information such as part-of-speech tags, lemmatized forms, and morphological features. By leveraging this word-level data, Dict-BERT can be effectively applied to low-resource languages. We evaluated Dict-BERT on English and Swahili, comparing it against BERT and other state-of-the-art models. The results indicate that Dict-BERT outperforms BERT in both datasets and achieves competitive performance on the English dataset relative to existing models. Furthermore, we plan to release the pre-trained Dict-BERT models to the community. The implementation code and pre-trained models will be available at https://github.com/taehyungkim/DictBERT. Our paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07025.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties collaborate to train machine learning models by contributing distinct feature sets. This paper introduces two novel pragmatic privacy attacks targeting VFL, utilizing real-world data to demonstrate that VFL models can be effectively reverse-engineered. The first attack targets a specific party's vertical slice, while the second is more general, capable of compromising any vertical slice. Our experimental findings indicate that both attacks achieve high precision and recall rates, even when the target slice contains a limited number of features. Furthermore, we observe that these attacks can successfully recover the target slice independently of the performance metrics of the other parties' slices. These results suggest that VFL is vulnerable to such reverse engineering, thereby challenging the assumption that the framework inherently safeguards participant privacy. This approach incorporates both the proton's light-cone distribution amplitude and the dark antibaryon's form factor. Utilizing this model, we compute the form factors and tensor coefficients for the $B\to p\bar{p}_D$ transition, where $p_D$ denotes the dark antibaryon. Furthermore, we investigate the $B$-meson decay $B^+\to p\bar{p}_D$, deriving the corresponding decay width and lifetime. Our findings indicate that the decay width for $B^+\to p\bar{p}_D$ is many orders of magnitude smaller than that of the standard process $B^+\to p\bar{p}$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ratio of the $B^+$ lifetime to the $B^+$ production cross section is independent of the dark antibaryon's mass. These results suggest that the $B^+\to p\bar{p}_D$ channel is experimentally unobservable at the LHC. Finally, our study confirms that the $B^+\to p\bar{p}_D$ contribution to the $B^+$ lifetime does not impose any constraints on the dark antibaryon mass. These conclusions are consistent with existing experimental data. Our findings further imply that the $B^+\to p\bar{p}_D$ process could be investigated at the Belle II facility, where the primary challenge lies in identifying the dark antibaryon. This paper introduces a new intelligent city defense framework designed to counter cyber-physical attacks on critical infrastructure. The system's core component is a game-theoretic tactical resource management (TRM) model, which utilizes a two-player, two-state game to determine the optimal allocation of defensive assets for both defenders and attackers. By modeling the interaction between a city operator and an adversary, the model evaluates the attacker's options to either strike a specific target or reveal their presence, forcing the operator to distribute resources between active monitoring and physical defense. We developed a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to calculate the expected costs for the operator under each scenario, enabling the derivation of a Nash equilibrium through a closed-form solution. This optimal strategy is subsequently integrated into a broader city protection system, which incorporates strategic planning and operational policies to deliver a comprehensive defense solution. This study examines the thermodynamics of charged black holes within a chamber, focusing on the influence of the "box effect" (the inverse square law) on charged anti-de Sitter (CAdS) black holes. We demonstrate that all black hole types within this system exhibit a Hawking--Page phase transition. Furthermore, we establish that charged AdS black holes in a box display an extremal limit, whereas charged AdS$_3$ black holes do not. Finally, we analyze the impact of charge on extremality and determine that both the extremality of charged AdS black holes in a box and the charge of extremal AdS$_3$ black holes in a box are non-monotonic functions of the horizon radius. These findings offer valuable insights into the behavior of black holes within a box framework. Additionally, we note that our results align with those obtained in the AdS$_2$ context. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in semi-supervised learning for graph-based tasks, such as node classification. However, their performance often deteriorates when trained on highly imbalanced, limited labeled datasets. To address this, we introduce a novel pseudo-labeling framework designed to enhance GNNs under label scarcity. Our approach employs a graph partitioning strategy to isolate subgraphs containing a high proportion of in-degree labels, thereby mitigating the adverse effects of out-degree labeled nodes. Finally, we develop a dynamic graph construction mechanism that generates a new graph representation for each training iteration, facilitating the selection of high-quality pseudo-labels. This study examines the generation of betatron radiation during the proton-electron beam interaction at the AWAKE facility. We present a comprehensive analysis of the spectral and angular characteristics of this radiation, which holds significant promise for novel applications in quantum electrodynamics research. The analysis incorporates an exact treatment of space charge forces, enabling the simulation of high-intensity electron beams. Our findings indicate that the beam dynamics and the resulting space charge forces are highly sensitive to the transverse position of the interaction point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the radiation spectrum can be substantially amplified through the use of strong focusing. These results are illustrated through detailed simulations of the AWAKE interaction point. Additionally, we explore potential methods for detecting this betatron radiation. Our simulations suggest that the photon yield could be considerable, potentially allowing for detection via a beamline spectrometer. This capability could serve as a valuable tool for characterising the electron beam within the interaction region. Ultimately, the observed radiation effects are found to be negligible, ensuring they do not compromise the proton-electron interaction physics. These conclusions are based on a specific set of parameters, which we outline in this paper. We also discuss the potential impact of these findings on future AWAKE Run 2 experiments. Ultimately, our results highlight the importance of understanding the dynamics of the electron beam generated by the proton beam in the AWAKE interaction point. This is crucial for optimizing the beam for the intended $p-\gamma$- $e$ interaction physics. Furthermore, the study underscores the need for advanced simulation tools capable of accurately modeling the complex interaction between a relativistic proton bunch and a high-intensity electron beam. Such tools are essential for investigating the novel physics phenomena that may arise from this interaction. This study introduces a suite of algorithms for distributed decision tree learning that adhere to differential privacy (DP). These methods enable the creation of highly accurate and robust distributed DP decision trees from horizontal data held in local silos. Our proposed model, $\textsc{PrivSplit}$, employs a novel mechanism for estimating the optimal split point at each node, achieving a sample complexity that is provably superior to any alternative mechanism. We also present $\textsc{PrivGrow}$, a distributed decision tree growth algorithm that utilizes $\textsc{PrivSplit}$ to construct the tree. Furthermore, we develop a novel method for generating DP samples from the resulting tree structure. We evaluate the performance of our algorithms against state-of-the-art centralized baselines across multiple datasets, demonstrating that our approach achieves accuracy within 1% of centralized methods. Additionally, we show that our algorithms surpass existing distributed privacy-preserving machine learning techniques, such as secure multiparty computation, in both accuracy and scalability. Chain Event Graphs (CEGs) extend the capabilities of Discrete Event Models (DEMs) by offering a more detailed representation of stochastic processes. While previous research has established methods for estimating CEG parameters and determining the graph's structure, this study introduces a novel Bayesian framework that simultaneously infers both the CEG structure and its parameters. This approach is grounded in a specific prior distribution that integrates a penalty term into the posterior probability. The penalty term comprises two distinct components: one that counts the number of parameters and another that counts the number of states within event nodes. This proposed framework is demonstrated using a dataset of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The analysis reveals that, compared to a standard Bayesian approach, the penalty-based method tends to select sparser CEG structures, resulting in a lower count of parameters. Furthermore, the Bayesian framework successfully infers a CEG that captures the disease progression of COPD. Finally, the paper discusses the potential for extending this methodology to other structured graphical models. The code required to replicate the analysis is accessible at https://github.com/maartensl/CEGBayes. Keywords: Chain event graphs, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Discrete event models, Markov models, Model selection, Model selection, Parameter estimation, Penalty, Posterior, Prior.

We introduce a new dynamical model rooted in generalized heavy ball methods, designed to ensure the strong convergence of iterates toward the Tikhonov-regularized minimizer with the smallest norm for a convex and differentiable function. This system features a Tikhonov regularization term that diminishes over time at a rate of $t^{-1}$ and a damping force that decreases at a rate of $t^{-1-\alpha}$, where $\alpha \in [0,1/2)$. We demonstrate that trajectories of this generalized heavy ball system converge strongly to the Tikhonov-regularized solution of minimal norm for the limiting argument at infinity. Furthermore, we establish that the objective function values converge at a rate of $O(t^{-1-2(1-2\alpha)})$. These findings extend our prior research (arXiv:2006.01000) by accommodating an additional inertia term in the system's energy and a broader range of $\alpha$ values. Additionally, we prove that these results apply to a generalized forward-backward operator splitting scheme, advancing the work of Bauschke et al. (2017) by allowing the step-size to vary and approaching the target operator more closely as time progresses. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that our proposed model achieves superior convergence rates compared to existing methods. This paper investigates the wall-following task, which involves a robot maintaining a consistent distance from a wall while traversing a corridor. We introduce a theoretical framework to examine the stability of various control strategies for this task. Our analysis demonstrates that the closed-loop system for the proportional controller can exhibit unstable dynamics, and in specific scenarios, even an ideal controller may fail to stabilize the system. Furthermore, we show that the dynamic feedback law proposed by Sibley and Nelson (2001) is not unique; we derive a general form for dynamic feedback controllers and establish the stability conditions for their closed-loop behavior. Additionally, we identify a fundamental limit on the parameters of this general controller that ensures stability. These findings are validated through simulations and experimental data collected from the mobile platform developed by our team. The results indicate that the robot's behavior can display limit cycles and unstable dynamics, confirming the theoretical predictions. Ultimately, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the wall-following problem, offering valuable insights for the design of navigation controllers. The source code for our simulations is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/wall_following.

We demonstrate that the conductivity of extended dislocations is significantly higher than that of the superconducting bulk, a finding that aligns with recent experimental data. Furthermore, we show that the doping level and temperature critically determine the transition from bulk to dislocation-dominated conductivity. Finally, our analysis reveals that the power dependence of the microwave conductivity serves as a valuable tool for distinguishing between these two contributions. These insights are essential for accurately interpreting the microwave properties of high-$T_c$ superconductors. Additionally, our findings suggest that the anomalous microwave conductivity observed in various high-$T_c$ superconductors can be attributed to the presence of extended defects. This conclusion is supported by a comparison of the microwave conductivity of disordered YBCO with the specific density of extended defects identified in that material. The analysis also sheds light on the origin of the power dependence of microwave conductivity in high-$T_c$ superconductors. Specifically, the $E^2$ dependence is linked to the nonlinearity of the microwave response, whereas the $E^4$ dependence arises from the nonlinear transport of quasiparticles. These findings are consistent with the kinetic energy-driven superconductor model. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the high-field microwave cavity magnet (HFCM) technique. In this context, we observe that the microwave response of extended dislocations is largely independent of the microwave frequency, a characteristic that could be exploited to separate dislocation and bulk contributions. Consequently, the properties of these defects must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental data. Furthermore, our results suggest that the kinetic energy-driven superconductor model is a viable framework for describing the microwave response of high-$T_c$ superconductors. This is evidenced by the fact that the microwave response of disordered YBCO can be accurately described using the model. Finally, we note that the kinetic energy-driven superconductor model offers a unified explanation for the microwave response of high-$T_c$ superconductors, thereby eliminating the need for the controversial gapless superconductivity model. This paper introduces GrowSpace, a synthetic environment designed for growing spatial reasoning, a novel benchmark that mirrors real-world spatial challenges. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to apply 3D physics simulations as a basis for spatial reasoning tasks. GrowSpace leverages the versatility of the Unity game engine to create a rich, interactive 3D world where objects interact with one another. We have developed two spatial reasoning tasks within this space: Object Localization and Object Occlusion. To facilitate object tracking, we employed a state-of-the-art object detection model, YOLOv3. Our evaluation of GrowSpace involved training various deep learning models, including CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers, to solve these reasoning tasks. We found that GrowSpace effectively assesses both object localization and occlusion handling, with our best-performing Transformer model achieving 80% accuracy on Object Localization and 70% on Object Occlusion. Furthermore, we anticipate that this benchmark will inspire future research into solving complex, multi-step reasoning problems. We propose a novel application of the curvaton mechanism, termed the "running curvaton," which utilizes the scale dependence of the inflaton's potential to generate a dip in the primordial power spectrum. This approach offers a fresh perspective on explaining the origin of dark matter overdensities and the associated baryon overdensities observed in the distribution of matter within galaxy clusters. We demonstrate that the running curvaton mechanism can successfully account for the dark matter overdensity in the core of the Milky Way, designated as the Dark Matter Fossil (DMF). Furthermore, we show that the model can simultaneously explain the dark matter core of the Milky Way and the dark matter distribution in the Coma cluster. Our findings indicate that the comoving wavenumber of the dip in the primordial power spectrum must lie in the range $10^{-3} \lesssim k_{\rm dip} \lesssim 10^{-2} \, {\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ to reproduce the DMF, and $10^{-2} \lesssim k_{\rm dip} \lesssim 10^{-1} \, {\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ for the Coma cluster. Additionally, we establish that the curvaton field must constitute the majority of dark matter in the early universe, with its contribution exceeding $0.99$ in both scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be constrained using Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) observations. Our results suggest that the curvaton field must contribute less than $0.05$ to the total energy density during the epoch of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. These findings are consistent with the requirements of the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Consequently, we conclude that the running curvaton model provides a viable explanation for the dark matter distribution in both the Milky Way and the Coma cluster. This study represents the first attempt to explain the dark matter distribution in both the Milky Way and the Coma cluster simultaneously. Our findings indicate that the running curvaton model is a promising framework for understanding the distribution of dark matter in galaxy clusters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can be constrained using Big Bang Nucleosynthesis observations. Our results suggest that the curvaton field must contribute less than $0.05$ to the total energy density during the epoch of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. These findings are consistent with the requirements of the standard $\Lambda$CDM model.

This paper introduces a robust, data-driven approach to selecting robust estimators for generalized linear models, with a specific focus on logistic regression. Our primary objective is to identify an estimator that avoids interaction terms, rendering the resulting model more interpretable. We achieve this by minimizing a penalty term that quantifies the complexity of the design matrix derived from the covariate transformation. This optimization framework is applicable to any penalized logistic regression method. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposal through a simulation study and two real-world data applications. The first dataset concerns a 2012 study by the U.S. Department of Education on the factors influencing high school dropout rates. The second application involves a 2017 study by the U.S. Department of Education examining factors affecting the likelihood of high school students receiving a C or D grade. In both cases, we selected the Lasso and the Group Lasso to derive a robust estimator that excludes interaction terms. Our findings indicate that this framework successfully eliminates interactions while maintaining the key variables identified by standard Lasso and Group Lasso methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework offers a pathway for constructing confidence intervals for groups of variables, a capability currently lacking in logistic regression. We illustrate this advantage by applying the framework to a third dataset, which examines factors affecting the probability of a student receiving an A or a B. This application enables us to determine that the most significant factors are those related to the student's race and their parents' education levels. Finally, we extend the framework to the Case Correlation Score (CCS) estimator, a method developed by the authors for logistic regression that is robust against both outliers in responses and leverage points in covariates. We show that the framework performs effectively with the CCS estimator. The code required to replicate all applications is available at: https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/avoiding-interaction. Keywords: Generalized linear models; Group Lasso; Leverage; Interpretability; Logistic regression; Robustness. MSC 2010: 62J05; 62F35.

This work introduces a method for detecting mechanically generated headlines by analyzing the full context of their surrounding articles. We present a new dataset comprising news articles and their corresponding headlines, including both machine-created and human-created examples. A key insight is that the internal structure of mechanical headlines offers a more robust signal for identification than the headline-article pair itself. Leveraging this finding, we developed a transformer-based classifier that surpasses all current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we examine the model's behavior to understand its predictive capabilities. Finally, we outline avenues for future research, including the application of large language models to fact-checking and the identification of machine-generated content. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/robertkuczmierz/headline-classification.

We present a theoretical investigation into the ground state of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on the square lattice, considering both polycrystalline and amorphous configurations. By employing variational Monte Carlo simulations on clusters ranging from 16 to 100 sites, we identify the polycrystalline ground state as a valence-bond solid featuring strong quantum fluctuations that prevent the establishment of long-range magnetic order. Furthermore, we examine a configuration with random bond strengths, or "amorphous" geometry, and demonstrate that the Hall density, defined as the difference between antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic coupling contributions ($\rho_H = n_y - n_x$), exhibits a peak at the paramagnetic ground state. This finding is corroborated by amorphous systems containing up to 500 sites. We argue that this peak serves as a signature of a spin-liquid state, specifically the chiral spin liquid phase, which is recognized as a distinct quantum spin-liquid variant in the $S=1/2$ $J_1-J_2$ model. Consequently, we propose that the amorphous ground state of this model may offer a viable route to realizing a chiral spin liquid. Finally, we discuss the potential of this approach for experimental settings, such as spin ice materials, where geometric disorder is naturally present. Our results suggest that the polycrystalline ground state in these materials will also correspond to a chiral spin-liquid phase. This conclusion is supported by recent muon spin relaxation experiments conducted on the polycrystalline spin-ice material Dy$_2$Ti$_2$O$_7$, which revealed a paramagnetic phase with a non-zero Hall density. We contend that this phase is best described as a chiral spin-liquid phase. Our study thus establishes a framework for exploring quantum spin liquids in polycrystalline systems, a previously unexplored avenue. We anticipate that this work will stimulate both theoretical and experimental research into the possibility of chiral spin-liquid phases in polycrystalline systems. This paper introduces a new calibration algorithm designed to handle the substantial data volumes generated by modern radio interferometers. The proposed method achieves $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ scaling with respect to the number of antennas, provided the array is arranged on a regular grid. By utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), the algorithm efficiently processes visibilities and associated weights, thereby enabling the rapid calculation of correlation matrices and their inverses. This approach is applicable to a wide range of array geometries, including the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). The method is demonstrated through simulations of visibilities from a mock image of the Sun. Additionally, the study implements an iterative self-calibration procedure to refine the correlation matrix inverse and apply it to the visibilities. The resulting calibrated visibilities are inverse Fourier transformed to produce an image of the Sun, which is then compared against an FFT-generated reference image of the same region. Social media has become a primary channel for organizations to engage with customers, making it a vital component of modern digital marketing strategies. However, the rapid evolution of social platforms demands that businesses constantly generate fresh, engaging, and relevant content. This study examines the barriers and enablers that influence content creation across various social media channels. By analyzing social media attainability (SMA)—a metric that assesses the feasibility of creating content on a specific platform—we provide insights into the necessary content strategies for digital marketers. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and opportunities associated with developing these strategies. The findings are derived from a survey of 1,000 digital marketers, with the resulting data processed using the fuzzy Delphi method. This approach ensures that our conclusions are robust and reliable. Additionally, the research incorporates insights from digital marketing experts, including those from the International Association of Digital Marketing (IADM). The study's outcomes are expected to assist digital marketers in formulating effective content strategies and enable researchers to better understand the complexities of social media attainability. The paper concludes by outlining several directions for future research.

This paper clarifies the definition of the tensor product for hypergraphs and demonstrates that this product can result in multiple connected components. We explicitly calculate the tensor product of two specific hypergraph types and provide an explicit formula for their eigenvalues. Furthermore, we establish that for any hypergraph $H$, there exists a corresponding hypergraph $G_H$ such that the tensor product $H \times G_H$ possesses only one connected component. Finally, we explicitly construct $G_H$ for all $H$ where $H \times K_2$ yields a single connected component. Additionally, we calculate the tensor product of linear $2$-graphs and prove that their spectrum consists of a union of arithmetic progressions. This finding confirms a conjecture proposed by Bhowmik, Ghosh, and Mukherjee in their 2021 paper, "Tensor product of hypergraphs and its spectrum," published in *Linear Multilinear Algebra*, 79(10), pages 2703–2716. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is currently evaluating a medium-class space telescope, designated as the Indian Near-Infrared Space Telescope (INISAT), for its next space-based observatory. This paper outlines the scientific rationale and design parameters for INISAT, which are derived from the requirements of the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST). INISAT is envisioned as a near-infrared space telescope with a 1.2-meter primary mirror and a top wavelength of 2.4 micrometers. It will be equipped with two instruments: a multi-object spectrograph covering 0.8–2.4 μm and a wide-field imager spanning 0.8–1.6 μm. The spectrograph will support both low- and high-resolution modes, offering a low resolution of 1000 and a high resolution of 10,000. The imager will feature a 1.2-degree field of view and a pixel scale of 0.2 arcseconds per pixel. This study details the scientific case, instrument specifications, and a preliminary cost estimate for INISAT. The total estimated cost is approximately 1000 crores, with a projected launch date of 2028. This study investigates the use of natural cubic splines for modeling time in clinical trials aimed at assessing the efficacy of Alzheimer's treatments. We demonstrate that this approach offers a straightforward yet effective framework for characterizing time-dependent outcomes, enabling the simultaneous analysis of both the time-to-event and time-averaged effects of interventions. Furthermore, we establish that natural cubic splines yield optimal performance in this context and provide guidance on selecting the appropriate number of knots. The proposed methodology is validated through an analysis of data from a randomized trial evaluating the impact of donepezil on Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, simulations were performed to assess the method's performance regarding type I error rates and power. These findings are anticipated to be valuable for the design and analysis of Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. The proposed global optimization problem is resolved using a new algorithm that combines a novel local minimization method with a global optimization strategy. Our findings demonstrate that this method successfully identifies the primary transition routes for a broad class of systems, including those with multiple coexisting dominant transition routes and those influenced by both multiplicative and additive noise. Furthermore, we show that the primary action functional derived from the dominant action functional can be utilized to calculate the true system's stationary distribution. This enables the identification of dominant transition routes for a wide range of systems, such as those exhibiting metastability or multiple stable states. The method's efficacy is validated through its application to various systems, encompassing both finite- and infinite-dimensional cases. Notably, in the finite-dimensional context, we demonstrate that the method can identify dominant transition routes even when the system's dynamics are governed by non-Lipschitzian vector fields. Additionally, we extend the method to infinite-dimensional systems, including those defined by partial differential equations. Cross-domain Text-to-SQL serves as a critical bridge between natural language and database queries, enabling users to query databases using English. While recent advancements have leveraged pre-trained language models to enhance performance, the field still faces persistent challenges regarding data heterogeneity and sparsity. This paper introduces an auxiliary task-based approach that integrates auxiliary information into the end-to-end training of language models. By employing a two-stage training process, we first pre-train a BERT model on a specific corpus and then fine-tune it using auxiliary tasks. To improve the generalization capability of the text-to-SQL model, we utilize this pre-trained BERT as a feature extractor, feeding its output into the text-to-SQL architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches on both English and Chinese text-to-SQL datasets. This paper introduces a new Information-Focused Risk-aware Model Predictive Control (IFFMPC) framework designed for safe navigation in multi-robot systems operating within uncertain environments. The core concept involves utilizing a probabilistic risk-aware cost function that prioritizes the exploration of specific environmental uncertainties to enhance risk assessment accuracy during future missions. To achieve this, the framework employs a two-stage optimization process: the initial stage generates a nominal trajectory to maximize information gain, while the subsequent stage solves a Risk-aware MPC problem using that nominal path. This approach enables robots to actively reduce uncertainty regarding collision risks with obstacles. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed IFFMPC method successfully improves risk estimation, thereby facilitating safer navigation. Furthermore, the study confirms that the method achieves significant computational efficiency, allowing for real-time implementation. Finally, the IFFMPC's effectiveness is validated through simulations of multi-robot systems executing various mission profiles. These simulations reveal that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both computational efficiency and overall safety. Additionally, the results indicate that the multi-robot systems achieve a substantial reduction in path uncertainty, resulting in improved risk estimations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar123456789/Information-Focused-MPC. Keywords: Risk-aware Navigation, Multi-Robot Systems, Model Predictive Control, Information Gain.

We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a compact dwarf galaxy situated approximately 780 kiloparsecs from the Milky Way. This object was identified through a search for Andromeda satellites conducted with the VLT Survey Telescope. We present the results of a spectroscopic analysis of its brightest stars, which indicates a metallicity of roughly $-1.5$ dex and a radial velocity of $v_{\rm rad} = 370 \pm 10$ km/s. The And XXV system is located at a distance of $d = 2.4 \pm 0.1$ kpc from the Andromeda galaxy. We estimate its physical dimensions to be $L \approx 100$ pc and a stellar mass of $M_{\star} \approx 10^{4} M_{\odot}$. Based on these parameters, we classify And XXV as a compact dwarf galaxy. Furthermore, we estimate its age to be $\tau \approx 10^{9}$ years and derive a dark matter density of $\rho_{\rm DM} \approx 10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ pc$^{-3}$ within its core. This density is significantly lower than that of other known dwarf galaxies. We conclude that And XXV is likely a satellite of the Andromeda galaxy. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this discovery for the hierarchical model of galaxy formation. The identification of And XXV as a satellite of Andromeda supports the hypothesis that the Andromeda galaxy formed through the accretion of smaller galaxies. The existence of compact dwarfs like And XXV also suggests that the dark matter halo of the Andromeda galaxy may be more diffuse than previously thought. Finally, we propose that the presence of such compact dwarfs in the Andromeda halo could be used to constrain the mass of the Andromeda's dark matter halo. The low central dark matter density of And XXV may indicate that the Andromeda halo is more extended than earlier models predicted. This finding could be significant for the ongoing debate regarding the nature of the Milky Way's and Andromeda's dark matter halos. Non-orthogonal grant-free massive connectivity (GC) offers a promising solution for supporting a vast number of devices with sporadic transmission needs in future wireless networks. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm designed to generate a set of non-orthogonal sequences with a Hamming distance (HD) of $N/2$, where $N$ represents the sequence length. The initial stage employs a genetic approach to identify a local optimum with a high HD, which is subsequently refined in the second stage to maximize HD while minimizing the cross-correlation coefficient (CCC). The proposed method is validated through simulations, demonstrating that the generated sequences achieve an HD of $N/2$ and outperform existing methods in terms of CCC and error rate performance. Furthermore, these sequences exhibit superior CCC and HD characteristics compared to those derived from linear feedback shift registers. Additionally, the computational complexity of the two-stage genetic approach is significantly lower than that of other design methods. The effectiveness of the method is confirmed by its ability to reduce the block error rate (BLER) under specific channel conditions. Finally, the approach proves particularly advantageous in distinguishing small numbers of users (e.g., $U \leq 10$) transmitting with low sparsity (e.g., $K \leq 3$) over a range of signal-to-noise ratios (e.g., $-5$ to $10$ dB). The design parameters are $N=16$, $U=10$, and $K=3$. Keywords: Non-orthogonal grant-free massive connectivity, genetic algorithm, Hamming distance, cross-correlation coefficient.

This study examines various approximations for modeling humid air, focusing on equations of state and formulations for internal energy, enthalpy, and the specific heats ($c_p$, $c_v$). The analysis employs the thermodynamic coherence framework, which demands that these thermodynamic properties adhere to the fundamental thermodynamic relation. We demonstrate that ensuring thermodynamic coherence is more complex than merely satisfying the equations of state. Furthermore, we outline the specific conditions under which these approximations remain coherent and provide explicit thermodynamic potentials for each model. Finally, we investigate the possibility of constructing a thermodynamically coherent model using a polynomial in temperature and inverse volume for the equation of state. The resulting expressions for thermodynamic potentials are noted to be highly complex, and we show that such a model cannot be extended to include humidity. Additionally, we establish that the ratio of specific heats, $\gamma = c_p / c_v$, is not constant in this model; instead, it depends on temperature and density, a behavior that aligns with experimental data. We conclude by discussing the potential of this model for numerical simulations. We establish a novel characterization of the outer function and introduce a new criterion for segment convexity within the characteristic map of a matroid. The study also examines supermodular outer functions and their connection to the convexity of the base polyhedron. Additionally, we present a matroid-based generalization of the outer derivative and explore its relationship with rank functions on higher-dimensional lattices. Finally, we provide a matroid-based characterization of segment convexity for the base polyhedron of an integral polymatroid. As a consequence, we offer a novel proof of a theorem by Galbiati and Giorgetti. This paper introduces a new method for monitoring dialogue state using a speech-to-text (ASR) uncertainty model that tracks the probability of an utterance belonging to a specific label. We employ Word Confusion Networks (WCN) to represent ASR uncertainty and a new approach for aggregating this uncertainty into a sentence-level label score. Experiments conducted on the Microsoft Lady Gaga dataset demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses the baseline sentence-level confidence score by 11.5% in AUC. Furthermore, we show that the model can be fine-tuned to adapt to variations in ASR performance across different domains and languages. Finally, we illustrate how the model can be utilized to enhance dialogue system responses. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/DSM.

We introduce an efficient algorithm for computing the cohomology of sheaves on projective curves, leveraging the fact that on such curves, every coherent sheaf decomposes into a direct sum of stable sheaves. This approach is particularly well-suited for implementing in computer algebra systems, with a version already available in Macaulay2. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive survey of the algorithms for operations on sheaves on projective curves that are currently implemented in various computer algebra systems. The paper includes several examples and a Python library written for Sage. The Python code was developed using Macaulay2's extensive library of sheaf operations. We conclude by discussing potential extensions of these methods to higher dimensions. This study examines the minimum intrication required within a universal framework for the controlled entry of quantum states into a target subspace. We demonstrate that, unlike the minimal entry framework, a recently proposed generalization does not allow for the unconditionally unitary entry of an arbitrary quantum state, as this process would generally increase the state's intrication. Furthermore, we establish that utilizing intricated ancillary states can enable the unconditional unitary entry of any quantum state, and we determine the specific requirements regarding both the target subspace and the intrication of these ancillary states. These findings are applicable to any entry framework, including recent proposals for the universal absorption and cloning of quantum states. Additionally, we explore how these results can inform the design of new frameworks for quantum state absorption and cloning. Finally, we highlight the relevance of our research to the broader context of quantum state manipulation. Throughout this work, we restrict our analysis to pure states, as the extension of these results to mixed states remains an open question. We believe that the concepts and methodologies developed here will be valuable for advancing our understanding of quantum state manipulation. Our findings are supported by supplementary material and can be replicated through code available at https://github.com/eduardo-gonzalez-gonzalez/intricacy-of-universal-entry-frameworks. Furthermore, we have created an interactive application, accessible at https://eduardo-gonzalez-gonzalez.github.io/intricacy-of-universal-entry-frameworks/, which allows users to explore our results and visualize the intrication of quantum states. This application was built using Qiskit and the Qiskit Visualization Toolkit. We acknowledge that the interactive nature of this application may impose limitations on the complexity of the quantum states that can be analyzed. We hope this tool will inspire further research into the manipulation of quantum states. The authors thank their respective funding agencies for their support. We introduce a general framework for directly evaluating entanglement within systems of independent optical qubits. This method relies on a novel class of entanglement witnesses that are optimal across the full range of two-qubit optical systems. We demonstrate that these witnesses are indeed optimal for all such optical qubit configurations. Furthermore, we illustrate their application in experiments involving the generation and analysis of entangled photons. Our results are applicable to photon polarization and spatial mode degrees of freedom, as well as combined photon polarization-particle identity modes. Additionally, we show that these witnesses can detect entanglement in a generated state with a signal-to-noise ratio that is significantly lower than the threshold required by any other known method. This represents a substantial advancement in the direct detection of entangled optical qubit systems. Our proposed witnesses are valid for any physical implementation based on qubit optical systems. Finally, we provide a Python-based open-source tool to facilitate the practical application of these witnesses. This tool enables users to design their own optimal witnesses, analyze experimental data, and determine the necessary conditions for optimal measurement. This study provides the initial characterization of a novel electrostatic mode, identified as the "palm tree ELM mode" due to its visual resemblance to JET camera footage during island-dominated, pre-ELM phases. The paper outlines the conditions under which this mode emerges and details its fundamental properties, including frequency, amplitude, and spatial structure. Furthermore, it examines the relationship between the palm tree mode and the neoclassical tearing mode (NTM), supported by JET experimental data and gyrokinetic simulations. Finally, the work proposes a theoretical framework to explain the palm tree mode's origin and nature. This study represents the first comprehensive analysis of the palm tree mode, offering a robust basis for future investigations into its formation and the development of control strategies. Such advancements are essential for mitigating the detrimental impacts of these modes on tokamak performance. Additionally, the insights gained regarding the palm tree mode are expected to enhance our broader understanding of NTM behavior in JET and other tokamaks. Continual learning seeks to master a sequence of tasks over time while retaining the ability to handle previous ones. Recently, pretraining models on extensive datasets has become a standard approach for continual learning scenarios. However, this strategy often fails when the subsequent tasks are not representative of the general distribution, as the strong representation capabilities of pretrained models can lead to catastrophic interference. To address this, we introduce a straightforward baseline that leverages the flexibility of pretrained models to mitigate interference. Our method employs a dynamic regularization technique to continuously adjust the model's parameters, ensuring that knowledge from earlier tasks is not overwritten. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach not only surpasses the performance of many methods relying on pretrained models but also outperforms state-of-the-art techniques that do not utilize pretrained initialization. Furthermore, our method exhibits robustness against tasks with limited data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenChenchen/DRCL. This study examines how heterogeneity in neuronal degree distributions influences the synchronization of type-I neurons within random networks. We analyze two distribution types: a power-law form, $P(k) \propto k^{-\gamma}$, and an exponential form, $P(k) \propto e^{-\lambda k}$. Our findings indicate that both distribution types yield qualitatively similar outcomes, with network size and the specific parameters of each distribution playing crucial roles. Furthermore, we observe that networks featuring a heterogeneous degree distribution exhibit distinct synchronization patterns compared to those with a homogeneous distribution. Specifically, networks of any size containing a few highly connected hub nodes display qualitatively different phase diagrams. These hubs can either facilitate or hinder synchronization, contingent upon the network size and the specific nature of the heterogeneity. Additionally, we note that the critical exponent governing the order parameter near the synchronization transition is independent of the degree distribution. Finally, we discuss how these results extend to other neuronal models, including type-II neurons and networks with arbitrary topologies. Automated Program Repair (APR) has garnered significant research interest, yet existing methods often fail to address complex bugs. To address this, we introduce a novel technique called Antagonistic Patch Creation (APC), which generates antagonistic programs to expand the search space for bug fixes. These antagonistic programs are derived from original programs by integrating antagonistic change (AC) candidates. An AC candidate is a proposed modification that eliminates a specific bug in one program while inadvertently triggering a new bug in an antagonistic program. We evaluated our method using the most recent APR tool, Magenta, and the most comprehensive dataset, the main suite. The results demonstrate that APC substantially enhances Magenta's bug-fixing capabilities, achieving a 100% success rate on the main suite with a five-times improvement in bug-fix recall. Furthermore, we conducted a case study on the Defects4J dataset to illustrate the mechanism of AC candidates. Finally, we release the APC method as a standalone tool to facilitate future research. Our source code and test data are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/APC. Our findings indicate that APC is a versatile approach with the potential to significantly boost the efficacy of various APR techniques. Source code: https://github.com/ChenYi2000/APC. This study investigates the capability region of generalized interference-finite secret cooperation (GIFC). In this framework, the receiver's interference-finite channel is enhanced by the transmission of data from a helper, where the helper's data is modeled as a random variable possessing a spectrum defined by its entropy, mutual information, and cross-terms. The helper's transmission is constrained by a power limit, while the receiver's transmission is limited by a Decoding Error Probability (DEP) requirement. We demonstrate that the capability region of GIFC is the intersection of two mutual information regions, each defined by a linear program. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal GIFC receiver is a Maximum Likelihood (ML) receiver, and we propose a linear programming method to determine the probability distributions of the receiver's data. Additionally, we prove that the optimal GIFC receiver's data distribution exhibits a Markov property, allowing the search for the receiver's data distribution to be reduced to a linear program. Finally, we show that the GIFC capability region encompasses the capability region of a related scheme known as generalized interference channel secret cooperation (GISC). In GISC, the data transmitted by both the helper and the receiver is modeled as random variables with defined spectra, and the receiver's data is further constrained by an average power limit. The ability to characterize the GIFC capability region enables the analysis of various extensions, such as scenarios where the helper's data is constrained by an average power limit or an average energy limit. This paper presents a preliminary version of the GIFC capability region; a more comprehensive treatment will be published in a forthcoming book. We present a new technique for analyzing the collision dynamics of relativistic nuclei, designed to investigate the collision structure and the equation of state (EOS). This method relies on the three-dimensional flow variable, which is derived from the directed and outward flow components. The variable's 3-dimensional nature stems from its dependence on the longitudinal coordinate and the transverse momentum vector. By utilizing the directed flow component, the 3-dimensional flow variable offers a more comprehensive description of the complete flow field compared to the transverse flow component alone. Furthermore, the initial slope of the 3-dimensional flow variable versus the longitudinal coordinate provides a direct measurement of the 3-dimensional flow field, enabling the determination of the EOS. We have conducted 3-dimensional flow analyses of Au+Au collisions at various energies using the Isospin and Molecular Dynamics (IMDY) model. Our results indicate that the initial slope of the 3-dimensional flow variable is sensitive to the EOS; specifically, the collision dynamics are governed by the symmetry pressure at low energies and by the slope parameter $L_0$ of the EOS at high energies. Additionally, we have compared 3-dimensional flow variables with other previously used variables to assess their relative advantages. Our findings demonstrate that the 3-dimensional flow variable is a novel and promising instrument for examining collision dynamics and the EOS. This method is applicable to both heavy-ion collisions and other high-energy physics processes. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenJing1988/3dflow. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread illness and death, prompting a surge in research into diagnostic methods. While deep learning has proven effective for identifying the virus from chest X-rays, it often struggles with class imbalance and data leakage. This study introduces a novel framework that addresses these challenges while ensuring patient privacy. First, we employ a two-stage data augmentation strategy to mitigate class imbalance. Second, we utilize adversarial training to prevent data leakage. Third, we integrate the concept of differential privacy to safeguard individual data during training. Our model was evaluated on the public VQA dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing models. Furthermore, our method maintains differential privacy, a guarantee that prior approaches lacked. These findings suggest that our framework holds significant promise for future large-scale, privacy-sensitive diagnostic applications. This study investigates a wireless transmission system where a receiver collaborates with multiple cooperative nodes (CNs) to jointly infer the transmitted signal using a graph neural network (GNN). The joint GNN inference involves two phases: first, a message exchange phase where the receiver and CNs share a finite number of iterations of preliminary estimates; second, a processing phase where the receiver and CNs exchange a single message to compute final estimates. We formulate the problem of optimizing the network topology, the number of exchange iterations, and the GNN parameters to minimize the average mean square error (MSE) of these final estimates. We demonstrate that the optimal solution comprises a GNN with a one-hop network topology and a sufficient number of iterations to achieve a target MSE threshold. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity GNN design and an efficient algorithm for solving the topology optimization problem. Numerical results indicate that the proposed topology optimization achieves a significant performance gain over random topologies, while the proposed GNN design performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we observe that the proposed GNN is robust against channel estimation errors. Finally, we show that the proposed GNN outperforms existing literature-based GNNs in terms of performance. This is because the proposed GNN is specifically tailored to the inference problem, whereas other GNNs are designed for different applications. We also note that the GNN proposed in this work is applicable to other communication problems, such as joint detection and channel estimation. Homicide rates in Brazil have historically been high, with recent data indicating a surge in the early 2000s followed by a decline. This study analyzes the spatial distribution of homicides across the Brazilian province of Goiás between 2002 and 2014. The analysis reveals that the province contains two distinct homicide clusters: one in the north, characterized by high rates and a stable spatial pattern over time, and another in the south, marked by low rates that expanded geographically during the latter half of the study period. Furthermore, homicide rates in Goiás are significantly influenced by the province's socio-economic conditions, as well as the economic and social factors of neighboring provinces. These findings suggest that effective interventions to reduce homicide rates in Goiás must be tailored to the specific local context and address both economic and social determinants. The study concludes by outlining potential policy initiatives to mitigate the province's high homicide levels. Additionally, the research discusses the limitations of the analysis and proposes future directions for further investigation. The methodology employed is designed to be applicable to other regions facing similar challenges. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach to combat Brazil's persistent and severe homicide crisis. This paper introduces a new class of accelerated stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods that adapts to both issue and sound audio data. Specifically, when training deep learning models for speech enhancement, our approach leverages the statistical properties of the specific dataset to generate an adaptive step-size that is issue-specific. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this method achieves faster convergence on both issues, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, when compared to vanilla SGD, our proposed method yields superior performance in speech enhancement tasks. The Sun's core emits neutrinos and solar axions, both of which could be detected by the upcoming Gamma Ray Ballistic Imaging (BabyIAXO) experiment. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of axion fluxes from the solar core, evaluating the axion production rate and the instrument's sensitivity across the entire mass mixing parameter space. The research demonstrates that BabyIAXO can detect the Standard Solar Model (SSM) axillary neutrino flux with a 3.5 sigma significance over a 10-year exposure period. Furthermore, the analysis establishes a sensitivity of 0.15% for the SSM axion production rate, which corresponds to an effective axion-nucleon coupling constant of $g_{aN} = 1.5 \times 1^{-10} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$. This sensitivity is comparable to that of the current AMOS experiment. Additionally, the analysis is sensitive to axions produced via the magnetic catalysis mechanism, with a minimum mass of $m_a = 1.5 \times 10^{-10} \text{ eV}$. This surpasses the sensitivity of the proposed SHiP experiment, which has a similar mass range but a higher minimum mass threshold of $m_a = 1.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ eV}$. Finally, the analysis is also sensitive to the Sun's non-standard helium abundance, $Y_{sun}$, with a precision of 0.001, representing an improvement of one order of magnitude compared to the AMOS experiment. This enhanced sensitivity is attributed to the superior energy resolution of the Gamma Ray Ballistic Imaging technique. The results indicate that BabyIAXO will significantly advance our understanding of the Sun's core. This is the first study to explore the Sun's core using a Gamma Ray Ballistic Imaging instrument, and the analysis code is publicly available for future investigations. The findings are expected to be published in Physical Review D. This paper introduces a new class of self-exciting systems, extending beyond the well-known self-exciting point processes. While traditional models rely on the conditional intensity function, our proposed framework utilizes a novel concept called the \emph{potential function}. We demonstrate that the traditional self-exciting point process represents only a narrow subset of this broader category. Furthermore, we establish key properties of this new class, including \emph{quasi-monotonicity} and \emph{quasi-stability}, and provide a constructive method for generating them. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2 TSE) sequence designed for body imaging. The method employs a self-gating approach to retrospectively reconstruct free-breathing 4D T2 TSE datasets. To address flow artifacts in cardiac regions, a variable flip angle (VFA) scheme is applied, which lowers the effective flip angle in areas with free fluid flow. Furthermore, a respiratory motion correction technique is utilized to generate free-breathing 4D T2 TSE data into matched free-breathing 3D and end-expiration breath-hold 3D volumes. The study demonstrates that this free-breathing 4D T2 TSE approach yields high-quality results in both free-breathing 3D and matched breath-hold 3D modes. In the matched breath-hold 3D configuration, the VFA scheme successfully eliminates flow artifacts, while in the free-breathing 3D mode, self-gating combined with motion correction produces artifact-free images. Additionally, the 4D T2 TSE data reveals both respiratory and cardiac motion. This method offers a promising solution for free-breathing 4D body imaging, particularly in challenging areas like the heart where flow artifacts are typically problematic. The findings are illustrated using data from a healthy volunteer. Model compression is essential for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Data flow-preserving network structures, which maintain the original flow of information, have recently demonstrated superior performance compared to models that alter data flow. This paper presents a knowledge distillation approach designed to achieve data flow preservation during model compression. We introduce an intermediate layer distillation strategy that transfers knowledge from intermediate layers of the original model to the compressed model, thereby maintaining data flow throughout the network. Additionally, we propose a knowledge diversity distillation method to enhance the diversity of learned representations. Experimental results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques. Specifically, on CIFAR-10, our approach achieves 93.7% accuracy with a 30-layer ResNet (compared to 93.8% for the teacher), and 94.1% accuracy with a 18-layer ResNet (compared to 94.0% for the teacher). On CIFAR-100, the results are 84.7% accuracy with a 30-layer ResNet (versus 84.8% for the teacher) and 85.0% accuracy with a 18-layer ResNet (versus 84.9% for the teacher). Non-resident grazing, where livestock feed on vegetation without contributing to soil nutrient cycling, is a prevalent practice in arid and semi-arid regions. This study employs a dry-land plant model to investigate how such grazing influences plant dynamics. We developed a grazing model and analyzed its equilibrium points and stability. Our results indicate that both low and high grazing rates can destabilize the system, with the specific outcome depending on environmental conditions. Furthermore, we observed that non-resident grazing can trigger complex behaviors, including oscillations and chaos. These oscillations are characterized by both monotonic and non-monotonic approaches, demonstrating that grazing can either hasten or delay system stabilization based on parameter values. Additionally, grazing reduces the stability range of the non-resident plant, with this effect intensifying as the grazing rate increases. We also identified a critical threshold for the grazing rate beyond which the system becomes unstable, a point that shifts based on other parameter values. Finally, our analysis reveals that these dynamics can be either damped or undamped, with the nature of the damping determined by other parameter values. Overall, this research underscores the intricate impact of non-resident grazing on dry-land plant dynamics and emphasizes the necessity for careful management to mitigate adverse ecological effects. The study offers valuable insights for land managers and policymakers aiming to balance livestock grazing with vegetation conservation in dry-land ecosystems. Furthermore, the mathematical framework developed can serve as a foundation for future research into other ecological systems. The associated code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/Non-resident-grazing}. Over the past ten years, adaptive data structures have gained significant traction for their ability to deliver efficient online performance. This paper investigates the integration of adaptive structures with Sketches, a category of adaptive structures designed to address the streaming model. We introduce Adaptive CountSketch, which merges CountSketch with the "square root" technique. This method supports $n$-element updates in $O(\sqrt{n})$ time and $q$-element queries in $O(\sqrt{q})$ time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $O(\sqrt{n})$ time complexity of adaptive CountSketch is optimal. Additionally, we prove that for any linear Sketch, the $\sqrt{n}$ time bound of adaptive CountSketch is optimal, provided that the algorithm is permitted to perform $O(1/n)$ queries. Finally, we extend these findings to scenarios involving updates and queries on $n$ and $q$ elements, respectively, where each element appears $k$ and $l$ times. In this context, we establish that the time complexity is bounded by $O(\min\{k\cdot n, \sqrt{n}\} + \min\{l\cdot q, \sqrt{q}\})$, and we show that this bound is tight. Our proofs rely on a novel framework for analyzing adaptive data structures, which we believe will be applicable to other problems in this domain. Notably, this framework enables the reduction of any adaptive data structure problem to the Online Matrix Multiplication problem. Consequently, we derive a time complexity bound of $O(m^{2/3})$ for all operations in adaptive CountSketch, where $m$ represents the total number of updates and queries. This result is contingent upon the widely held conjecture that Online Matrix Multiplication can be performed in $O(m^{2/3})$ time. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of the Online Matrix Multiplication lower bound to adaptive data structures. Our work also yields a new lower bound for Online Matrix Multiplication, which is the first such bound to be tight for any non-trivial input distribution. We anticipate that these findings will be of interest to the Online Matrix Multiplication community. We have implemented adaptive CountSketch in C++ and made the code publicly available. This implementation is the first to achieve $O(\sqrt{n})$ time complexity for both updates and queries. We believe that the techniques employed in our construction will inspire further research into adaptive data structures. We hope that the community will continue to pursue this promising field

The code is optimized for both CPU and GPU architectures, featuring a straightforward implementation that delivers substantial performance gains. As a practical and efficient tool, ipie is well-suited for investigating new stochastic methods and applications. We investigate a dynamic, time-discrete market for a single good featuring one unit supply, a unit demand, and no initial endowments. The market comprises two agent types: "traders," who possess a specific trading strategy, and "brokers," whose income is derived from transactions facilitated by traders. Within this framework, brokers act as income maximizers, whereas traders aim to maximize their income relative to that of their broker partners. We analyze the dynamics of a "brokers' game" to determine an equilibrium where every broker is either maximally active or inactive, and no trader can increase their income by unilaterally deviating. Furthermore, we examine an iterative process where traders update their strategies to improve their income, demonstrating that this leads to convergence toward a brokers' game equilibrium. Finally, we present findings regarding the existence of such equilibria across various trader strategies. Additionally, we introduce a model where traders aim to maximize the income of the entire group rather than individual收益, deriving analogous results. Finally, we explore a scenario in which brokers also seek to maximize group income, proving that an iterative process can again yield a brokers' game equilibrium. This work extends our earlier research [10, 11, 12], which focused solely on the single-commodity case with a fixed number of brokers. We also address an open question from [11] concerning the existence of an equilibrium when the number of brokers varies. Our findings indicate that, in general, such an equilibrium does not exist; however, under specific assumptions, it does. In this study, brokers are modeled as minimizing cost functions, whereas [11] treated them as maximizing them. We also address the existence of equilibria in this cost-minimization scenario, a problem that was previously unresolved. Finally, we consider a variant where traders maximize group income, a topic that extends beyond the scope of [11]. In this context, brokers are also income maximizers, and we demonstrate that an equilibrium exists in this setting as well. Our results are supported by illustrative examples. The market dynamics described herein are applicable to various economic markets, including the foreign exchange market, where traders may be either active or inactive, and brokers may adjust their strategies to maximize their income. We report on the DUVET survey, a study of the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253, which utilizes a novel technique to map the three-dimensional structure of galactic outflows. By combining high-resolution observations of the ionized gas (via H$\alpha$) with high-sensitivity data of the molecular gas (via $^{12}$CO(3-2)), we identified a large-scale outflow originating from the central starburst region. This outflow extends approximately 1.5 kiloparsecs above the galactic plane and exhibits a collimated, jet-like morphology. Our analysis reveals that the outflow's spatial distribution aligns with the star formation rate surface density, indicating that star formation in NGC 253 is regulated by the outflow. Furthermore, the surface density of the H$\alpha$ emission within the outflow is comparable to that of the ionized gas in the galactic disk, suggesting that the outflow is not optically thin. We estimate the mass of the outflowing gas to be roughly $10^8$ solar masses, with a mass outflow rate of approximately $10^{-2}$ solar masses per year. The energy generation rate of the outflow is determined to be around $10^{42}$ erg/s, which is comparable to the star formation rate surface density in the galaxy's center. These findings suggest that galactic outflows driven by intense star formation are capable of suppressing further star formation in both the disk and the outflow itself. Consequently, NGC 253 serves as a critical case study for understanding how galactic outflows influence the star formation process. This study examines the impact of the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$) on triangular flow ($v_3$) within Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at a beam energy of 200 GeV. Utilizing the Multiphase Transport framework, we observe that a non-monotonic dependence of $v_3$ on $\eta/s$ exists for both central and peripheral collisions. Furthermore, we determine that the sensitivity of $v_3$ to $\eta/s$ is greater in peripheral collisions than in central ones for both systems. Additionally, our results indicate that $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions is more sensitive to variations in $\eta/s$ compared to Au+Au collisions. These findings suggest that measuring $v_3$ in small systems offers a more effective means of constraining the $\eta/s$ ratio of the QCD medium. Finally, we explore the potential for enhancing the precision of $\eta/s$ constraints through the use of higher-order flow harmonics. Our analysis reveals that $v_4$ in Cu+Cu collisions exhibits a more pronounced sensitivity to $\eta/s$ than $v_3$, whereas $v_5$ in Au+Au collisions shows greater sensitivity than $v_3$. These conclusions are supported by a detailed examination of the initial conditions and the evolution of the QCD medium. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of incorporating higher-order flow measurements to achieve a more precise determination of the $\eta/s$ ratio. The findings presented here are intended to guide future experimental efforts aimed at extracting the $\eta/s$ ratio in both large and small heavy-ion collision systems. The rise of autonomous driving has driven significant research into the intersection of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and Edge Intelligence (EI). IoV relies on vehicular networks to gather and share data, while EI leverages edge computing to process this information and enhance services. However, these two domains often lack a unified approach to safeguarding user privacy. This paper introduces a novel, integrated privacy protection framework designed to secure both data and model privacy within the EI context for IoV. The framework proposes a new mechanism that enables vehicles to jointly train an EI model while maintaining privacy through the combination of homomorphic encryption and differential privacy. Furthermore, vehicles can dynamically adjust privacy parameters to balance privacy levels with model accuracy. To validate the framework, we implemented a proof-of-concept using real-world traffic data from a specific city, demonstrating that the mechanism can accurately predict traffic congestion while effectively protecting user privacy. Experimental results indicate that the proposed mechanism outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both data privacy and model privacy. Additionally, we evaluated the framework's computational complexity and latency, confirming that it is feasible for deployment on resource-constrained edge nodes. Finally, we discuss the framework's potential for implementation in IoV platforms and its capacity to support advanced EI applications. The proposed solution is expected to facilitate the development of more intelligent and secure IoV systems. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the resulting system and explore its biological implications. Additionally, the stability analysis reveals that when all three Holling types induce the strong Allee effect on both species, the system's stability properties remain largely consistent. The paper introduces a novel homotopy method for solving linear programming problems, termed the "Aspect Pivot Simplex Technique" (APST). This approach constructs a continuous "homotopy path" that links a straightforward linear program to the target problem, enabling the solution of the latter by traversing the path. The study demonstrates that the APST path remains confined within a specific region, defined as a "hyper-pyramid," under a mild technical assumption. Furthermore, it proves that the corresponding solution path generated by the pivot-based apriori traversal algorithm is also bounded within this hyper-pyramid. These findings are supported by illustrative examples. Additionally, the authors conjecture that a specific pivot-based traversal of the path yields an optimal solution. The paper concludes by posing an open question regarding the existence of such a traversal that guarantees convergence to optimality. The primary contribution of this work is the demonstration that the APST offers a new method for solving linear programming problems with a provably bounded solution path. This result provides a fresh perspective on the P vs NP problem, as finding a point on this path constitutes a natural NP-hard problem. The authors anticipate that this finding will inspire further research into novel solution techniques for linear programming. This study investigates how off-shell effects and gluon splitting ($g\to t\bar{t}$) impact the extraction of the top quark pole mass from $t\bar{t}$+jet events. To address these influences, we employ a template fit method utilizing a likelihood function based on event shapes, specifically the invariant mass of the $t\bar{t}$+jet system. The analysis is conducted at both the hadron and leptonic decay levels, with detector effects incorporated through a data-to-simulation jet energy scale correction. The top quark mass is derived from a fit to the observed data, with the fit procedure also accounting for the $^{13}$B parton distribution function. Our findings indicate that off-shell and gluon splitting contributions are significant, particularly in the leptonic decay scenario. Furthermore, we observe that the extracted mass value varies depending on the included physics effects, a discrepancy that remains even after adjusting for the detector response. Finally, we compare these results with those from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The extracted top quark mass values range from $m_t = 172.2$ GeV to $m_t = 173.2$ GeV, showing good agreement with experimental measurements. However, the variation in the extracted mass due to varying physics inputs is substantial, reaching up to 1 GeV. This variation is more pronounced in the leptonic decay case, where it can reach 1.5 GeV. These findings underscore the critical need for precise modeling of off-shell and gluon splitting effects when extracting the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}$+jet data. Additionally, the large variation suggests that the current top quark mass extraction method is highly sensitive to the specific event selection criteria used. This sensitivity may stem from the fact that the fitted parameters are derived from a relatively small subset of the available data. To mitigate this, future analyses should aim to utilize a larger dataset and implement more robust selection criteria to ensure a more stable and accurate extraction of the top quark mass. Recent studies indicate that deep learning-based image generation models are increasingly vulnerable to automated exploitation by face manipulation attackers. This paper addresses the critical issue of the computational resources required by attackers to train deep neural networks for generating highly realistic face manipulations. To evaluate the computational efficiency of current deep learning generation models, we introduce a new benchmark dataset, FakeFace, comprising over 100,000 photorealistic face manipulations created using various deep learning generation models. We then assess the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning detectors on this dataset, analyzing how detector accuracy correlates with the computational cost of the generated images. Our findings reveal that vision transformers are the most computationally efficient models for creating deep learning-resistant face manipulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a lightweight convolutional neural network can match the detection accuracy of complex vision transformers while being up to 100 times more computationally efficient. Finally, we explore the potential of integrating a contrastive learning framework to further enhance the efficiency of deep learning detectors for face manipulation.
