This paper investigates the statistical behavior of eigenvalues for random Hermitian $N \times N$ band matrices, characterized by a bandwidth $D$ that scales with $N$ as $D = N^{\beta}$ where $0 < \beta < 1$. These matrices are subjected to an additional deformation by a finite-rank matrix $A$ with a large real parameter $s$. The study demonstrates that significant statistical changes occur only when $s$ reaches the critical scale $D/N$. Furthermore, it is established that in this regime, the fundamental statistical characteristics of the eigenvalues remain independent of the specific structure of the band matrix, provided the bandwidth $D$ is sufficiently large. This universality is derived from a sigma-model approximation, which is rigorously justified for both the undeformed case and the leading-order approximation when $A = (1/s)I$. The resulting sigma-model successfully predicts the universal statistical properties of the deformed band matrices. Finally, the findings are applied to analyze the statistical properties of the Laplacian operator on a finite graph. Specifically, the spectrum of the Laplacian is approximated by a random band matrix, and the influence of a finite set of edges is modeled as a deformation. These results offer a theoretical basis for the recently proposed "spectral compression" algorithm, which utilizes the presence of a few edges to identify and cluster vertices in graphs. The validity of this algorithm is confirmed by the finding that the model predicts a sharp transition between the clustered and unclustered states. Additionally, the research indicates that the eigenvectors of the deformed band matrix become localized when $s$ exceeds the critical value $N/D$. This phenomenon is also linked to the operation of spectral compression. The paper concludes by outlining several directions for future research. The surge in algorithmic learning has sparked a renewed interest in interpretability, a critical yet complex challenge. While numerous methods have been developed to evaluate the interpretability of models and features, existing metrics often rely on post-hoc approaches that lack a solid theoretical foundation. Furthermore, these measures frequently fail to account for human cognitive factors, such as the complexity of the human brain and the specific components of human learning. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a framework that assesses interpretability by drawing parallels between machine learning and human learning. This framework incorporates a cognitive dimension to quantify the complexity of the information humans must process, leading to the development of the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS). The CIS captures the complexity of the feature space, including feature interactions, and offers a theoretical basis for interpreting the relationships between algorithms, features, and humans. We validate this framework by demonstrating its effectiveness in evaluating the interpretability of various algorithms and feature sets. Our results indicate that the proposed framework can effectively measure the interpretability of algorithms and features, as well as the influence of the cognitive component. This work provides a foundation for enhancing algorithmic interpretability and offers new insights into the relationship between humans, algorithms, and features. The resulting equation unifies the thermodynamic equations of state for both bosons and fermions. The study derives the equation for tiny boson systems, proves its validity for tiny fermion systems, and presents the results of numerical simulations. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the equation holds true for droplets of bosons and fermions, as well as for the early universe. The Lyman-alpha filter, originally designed for space-based stellar spectroscopy, is now widely utilized in ground-based photometry to detect high-redshift quasars and galaxies. However, its application is restricted by atmospheric absorption and sky emission lines, which severely compromise the accuracy of photometric redshift estimates. To address this, we introduce a model that simulates Lyman-alpha filter observations from the ground, accounting for telluric absorption and sky line emission. This model is validated using real data from the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey. Our results demonstrate that the model accurately reproduces observed spectra, including sky lines and absorption features. Furthermore, we show that incorporating this model into the ZFOIL pipeline significantly enhances the precision of photometric redshift estimates for galaxies identified through the Lyman-alpha filter. This improvement is particularly notable for galaxies at redshifts $1.5 < z < 2.5$, where the median photometric redshift error is reduced by 0.12. We conclude that our model is a valuable tool for analyzing Lyman-alpha filter data, offering a straightforward method to generate realistic synthetic spectra for galaxy surveys. Inspired by recent MAS research utilizing graph filters, the proposed method applies a graph filter to the relative states of each agent. The filter design is straightforward, relying solely on the local adjacency information of every agent, and remains independent of the eigenvalue bounds of the Laplacian matrix. We demonstrate that this approach ensures the convergence of the average state to the ideal average. We introduce a new method for associating user-generated content (UGC) with events occurring in the physical world, specifically focusing on dynamic events like sports matches and political rallies. Our approach, termed Dynamic Picture Indexing (DPI), leverages both visual and textual cues to map images to these occurrences. Unlike prior image indexing techniques that rely on static landmarks, our method is designed to handle changing scenes. We evaluate DPI across two major social media platforms, demonstrating its ability to accurately and efficiently index UGC images from Facebook and Instagram. The results show that DPI surpasses existing state-of-the-art image indexing methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical utility of DPI by developing a social media analytics platform that enables journalists to automatically extract UGC from Facebook and Instagram and visualize it on a map centered on the event's location. This platform assists users in identifying relevant UGC and visualizing it for news reporting. We also present case studies of specific news stories to validate the platform's effectiveness. This paper introduces a keyless authentication protocol designed for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The method relies on the concept of a polarized channel, whereby the legitimate transmitter and receiver generate a long polarized sequence. They then utilize the bits corresponding to the channel-reliable positions as their communication keys. The remaining sequence bits, which appear as noise to the legitimate parties but are partially decodable by an eavesdropper, serve as the authenticator. We establish a lower bound for the length of these authentication keys and demonstrate that the scheme is optimal for the AWGN channel. Furthermore, we examine the framework's applicability to other channels and provide numerical results. Our findings indicate that the proposed scheme outperforms both polar codes and polar-like codes when used for keyless authentication. Additionally, the scheme remains secure even if the legitimate transmitter is compromised. Finally, we show that the scheme can be adapted for keyless authentication on the binary erasure channel. In this specific case, the transmitter and receiver agree on a set of erasure positions, which are then filled with a polarized sequence; the resulting sequence acts as the authenticator. We prove that this approach is also optimal for the binary erasure channel. The dynamics of a particle moving along a periodic potential with friction and white thermal noise are examined. Specifically, the transition from the quantum transport regime to the super-transport regime within the Hänggi-Johannesson regime is analyzed. Furthermore, the conditions required for the super-transport regime are established, and a method for identifying a specific parameter range exhibiting uniform transport is developed. These findings are demonstrated using the energy functional $E(\gamma,\beta,T)=-\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\ln\left[\frac{2\pi}{\beta\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{\hbar\beta}{2\pi m}\frac{\sinh(\hbar\beta\sqrt{\gamma E_c}/\beta)}{\gamma/\beta}}\right]$, which encapsulates the quantum, super-transport, and super-Parisi regimes. This approach is applicable to various quantum systems, including Josephson junctions, fluxons, and domain walls. Additionally, the study addresses the issue of non-equivalence between canonical and microcanonical transport in the super-Parisi regime. Finally, the implications of these results for the broader quantum transport problem are discussed. The paper also includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the function $E(\gamma,\beta,T)$. This paper introduces a new method for estimating impulse response functions that builds on local projections but introduces two key modifications. First, it addresses the issue of overfitting in high-dimensional settings by implementing an adaptable feature selection mechanism. This mechanism evaluates multiple feature selection methods to identify the optimal one for each local projection regression. Second, to enhance prediction accuracy, the approach pools information across multiple local projections to estimate the impulse response function. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulation studies and a real-world application analyzing the impact of monetary policy shocks on various economic indicators. Furthermore, a comprehensive simulation study compares the proposed method against existing alternatives, including standard local projections, principal component analysis, and group lasso, as well as a new competing method known as sparse local saddlepath. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms all other approaches in terms of prediction accuracy. Our findings reveal that the angular momentum of the quantum vacuum is non-zero and exhibits both non-trivial magnetic field dependence and non-cancellation between electric and magnetic components. These results are interpreted as a violation of the angular momentum conservation law, which relies on translational symmetry, and are understood as a consequence of the stress-energy tensor's non-vanishing divergence. We further discuss the potential for extracting energy from this system and propose a method to generate angular momentum. Finally, we conclude that the stress-energy tensor's non-vanishing divergence is an intrinsic property of the Casimir field, a feature that persists regardless of the specific form of the source. This conclusion is supported by a demonstration that the stress-energy tensor divergence in a uniformly accelerating source remains proportional to the local curvature of spacetime, even though the charge's proper acceleration is zero. Consequently, this phenomenon is identified as a manifestation of the equivalence principle. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental natural language processing task that involves identifying entities within text and assigning them appropriate labels. However, the growing demand for fine-grained NER (fgNER) has increased, as it requires classifying sub-segments of entities into specific categories, such as distinguishing between "Bill" and "Clinton" in the text "Bill Clinton visited India." This paper introduces a hyperbolic space-based graph neural network model designed to address the challenges of fgNER. We demonstrate that hyperbolic space is highly effective for organizing entities with hierarchical relationships. Furthermore, we develop a refinement-informed hyperbolic graph neural network that utilizes the relationships between entity categories to enhance the performance of fine-grained named entity classification. Experimental results on two public datasets confirm that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/FGNET-RH. Additionally, the dataset and associated code are available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/FGNER-Dataset. This paper examines the sharp upper bounds for the two terms comprising the second Hankel determinant of the analytic function class $\mathcal{U}$, as well as for the Quasiradial function class $\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}$ and the newly defined class $\mathcal{W}$. Additionally, we derive sharp bounds for the determinant $\left|\begin{smallmatrix}a_3 & a_4\\a_4 & a_5\end{smallmatrix}\right|$ for functions in the general class $\mathcal{S}$ and the convex in one direction class $\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, we compare these newly established results with previously known bounds for the second Hankel determinant in the classes $\mathcal{S}$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\mathcal{U}$. Finally, we address the second rank Fekete conjecture within the class $\mathcal{U}$. This represents the first study to determine sharp bounds for the determinant $\left|\begin{smallmatrix}a_3 & a_4\\a_4 & a_5\end{smallmatrix}\right|$ in any specific sub-class of $\mathcal{S}$. Our findings indicate that the maximum value of this determinant for the class $\mathcal{U}$ is $\frac{5}{16}$. Consequently, the second Fekete conjecture does not hold for the class $\mathcal{U}$. These results were achieved through the application of the area theorem. To facilitate this, we also provide the sharp upper bounds for the coefficients $a_n$ of functions belonging to $\mathcal{U}$, $\mathcal{S}$, and $\mathcal{C}$. These findings are derived using a novel approach that yields sharper bounds than those previously established in the literature. We also offer a comparison with existing literature. Finally, we extend the theorems to the class $\mathcal{S}^*(\sin\beta t)$, which encompasses both $\mathcal{S}^*$ and $\mathcal{S}(\sin\beta t)$ as special cases. In this extension, we establish the sharp upper bound for $a_n$ as $\frac{n\sin n\beta t}{\sin\beta t}$. This work marks the first instance of sharp bounds for the coefficients of the analytic function class $\mathcal{W}$, a class introduced by the authors in a recent publication. In cloud computing, virtual machines (VMs) are hosted on physical servers, where the distribution of virtualized resources significantly impacts the performance of both the VM and the server. This paper introduces a novel load distribution strategy called Prepartition, which allocates a partition of physical resources to a VM based on its requirements. Prepartition employs a two-step process: first, it determines an optimal partition size for each VM, and second, it assigns the selected partition to the VM. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to existing load distribution methods, Prepartition reduces the energy consumption of the hosting server by 10% to 20%. Furthermore, the strategy successfully accommodates VM reservation requests in 90% to 95% of cases. The Prepartition approach is currently deployed in the OpenNebula platform. This work is particularly relevant for VM provisioning systems that must handle VM reservation requests. The authors intend to explore resource allocation techniques for VMs within a pre-defined partition in future research. The preprint can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00177. We demonstrate that this category encompasses a broad range of established neural network types, such as deep feedforward networks, recurrent networks, and second-order methods like Newton's method. Furthermore, we establish that the equilibrium conditions of this category can be guided by a fixed set of anticipative signals, meaning the network's dynamics can learn these equilibria given access to future data. We illustrate the utility of this framework by applying it to the signal reconstruction problem, where the resulting model outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. This study derives novel bounds for the causal impact of a treatment $T$ on an outcome $Y$, accounting for unobserved confounders. Unlike prior work, these bounds are not constrained by the information mutual information $I(Y;T)$; instead, they rely on the causal information $I^*(Y;T)$, a broader metric that encompasses $I(Y;T)$ and supports data processing inequalities under stochastic mappings. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any deterministic mapping $f$ of $T$ into $T'$, the following holds: $I^*(Y;T') \le I^*(Y;T)$. Consequently, $I^*(Y;T)$ serves as a more accurate measure of the treatment's effect on $Y$ than $I(Y;T)$. We establish upper and lower bounds for $I^*(Y;T)$ and investigate its extension to high-dimensional settings, where it is defined as the minimum dimensionality of a sufficient statistic for $Y$ within the $T \rightarrow Y$ process. These findings enable the estimation of causal impacts in high-dimensional contexts using only marginal distributions. Furthermore, we prove that $I^*(Y;T)$ is invariant to the specific representation of $T$, thereby offering a robust quantitative measure of causal influence. Finally, we outline potential applications of this framework in neuroscience and genomics. The code required to replicate our results is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/CausalInformation.

This paper introduces a new method for predictive surveillance of linear time-invariant systems, designed to detect stealthy attacks that evade standard residual-based monitoring. The core concept involves constructing a finite-dimensional state-space model from the infinite-dimensional input-output behavior of the original system, utilizing the surjectivity of the input-output map to ensure the resulting finite model can reveal attacks invisible at the input-output level. The study rigorously derives the dimensions of this extended model and outlines an algorithm for its computation. Furthermore, the paper establishes sufficient conditions to guarantee that the finite-dimensional extension remains observable. Finally, a numerical example demonstrates the method's effectiveness in predicting system attacks. The proposed approach offers a more efficient alternative to predictive surveillance techniques that rely on state estimators. Additionally, the developed methodology is applicable to the finite-dimensional observation of linear time-invariant systems, enabling the use of established state estimator-based predictive surveillance techniques on observed finite-dimensional systems. The paper also explores the extension of this work to nonlinear systems. Keywords: Cyber-Physical Systems, Fault Detection and Isolation, Predictive Surveillance, Linear Time-Invariant Systems, Linear-Parameter-Varying Systems, Nonlinear Systems.

This paper introduces the GAE-ISumm dataset, designed to facilitate multi-lingual summarization research for Indian languages. Comprising 1,000 English-vernacular (specifically Hindi, Marathi, and Tamil) parallel document pairs, each containing English summaries, the dataset enables the investigation of graph-based summarization across these vernaculars without relying on annotated summaries. We evaluate a Graph Autoencoder (GAE) model on this data and present preliminary findings. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of summary quality within the multi-lingual summarization context. The dataset will be made publicly available to support future research. The code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/GAE-ISumm.

Keywords: multi-lingual summarization, graph-based summarization, summary quality, document summarization, Indian languages.

This paper introduces the concepts of finite and infinite S-rings of Noether type, demonstrating that a ring R possesses the property that every right ideal is a two-sided ideal if and only if R is either a local Artinian ring or a local Noetherian prime ring. We further classify S-rings of Noether type as being local or primitive, providing a classification of S-rings of Artinian type as well. Additionally, we establish that S-rings of Noether type are precisely those rings where every right ideal is finitely generated as a right ideal, and we provide a classification of primitive S-rings of Noether type based on their associated topologies. The study also examines S-rings of Noether type within the context of noncommutative semigroups and concludes by investigating S-primes of Noether type and S-composite rings of Noether type. Finally, the paper presents several open problems and conjectures regarding these structures. For instance, it remains an open question whether every primitive S-ring of Noether type is either a maximal primitive ring or a primitive ring with finite dimension over its center. Furthermore, the equivalence of two conditions—(i) every right ideal being two-sided and (ii) every right ideal being finitely generated as a two-sided ideal—remains unresolved in the context of S-rings of Noether type. The paper also addresses whether a primitive S-ring of Noether type with a countable dimension over its center must be Artinian, and whether a primitive S-ring of Noether type with a finite-dimensional commutative center is necessarily Artinian. Finally, the text explores the noncommutative analogue of the Hilbert Syzygy Theorem for S-rings of Noether type and considers whether a semigroup S, where every right ideal is finitely generated as a two-sided ideal, must necessarily be Noetherian. The discussion extends to S-composite rings of Noether type, specifically whether a semigroup S where every right ideal is two-sided must be either local or primitive, and whether such a semigroup is necessarily of Noether type. The paper also conjectures that a semigroup S where every right ideal is two-sided is either local or primitive if and only if S is either local or a commutative semigroup of finite type. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) serve as a potent method for unsupervised representation learning, yet they often suffer from representation collapse, where the model fails to capture the underlying data distribution. This paper introduces a minimal square VAE (MinSq-VAE), a straightforward yet effective enhancement to standard VAEs. By enforcing a diagonal covariance structure on the encoder's output distribution, MinSq-VAE significantly reduces the optimization complexity of learning the distribution parameters. To address the resulting increase in training difficulty, a regularization term is incorporated into the loss function to mitigate overfitting. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that MinSq-VAE remains a true VAE and proves that its training converges to a local optimum. Furthermore, we establish that MinSq-VAE is equivalent to a constrained autoencoder with constraints applied to the average encoding distribution. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm that MinSq-VAE outperforms both standard VAEs and other state-of-the-art unsupervised learning models. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Minimal-Square-VAE. The source code for reproducing our experiments can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Minimal-Square-VAE/tree/master/experiments. Additional details regarding the experiments are available in our supplementary material. The theoretical proofs are included in our extended version. The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly expanding technology that facilitates the connection of various devices to the web, enabling them to communicate and exchange data. However, this widespread connectivity introduces significant security challenges, including data breaches and unauthorized access, which can compromise user privacy and lead to severe consequences. To address these vulnerabilities, this paper introduces a novel intelligent home monitoring system designed to enhance security and privacy through the integration of blockchain technology and a new localization algorithm. Blockchain offers robust security and immutability, while the proposed localization method improves efficiency by reducing energy usage and communication overhead. Together, these components create a secure and efficient solution for home monitoring. The study's results demonstrate that this proposed system outperforms existing solutions in terms of security and privacy. Ultimately, this work provides a new perspective on intelligent home monitoring and establishes a foundation for future research in the field. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 outlines the proposed system's methodology; Section 4 presents the results and discussion; and Section 5 provides the conclusion. Keywords include Home Monitoring, Localization, Blockchain, Security, and Privacy.

This paper introduces a method for Gray-coding L-valued logic functions by training a deep neural network (NN) to predict anNN-Gray codes, which are then mapped to standard binary codes. The core concept involves applying a deep NN to learn a many-to-one mapping from binary L codes to anNN-Gray codes, ensuring that anNN-Gray codes with a Hamming distance of one in the code space also maintain a Hamming distance of one. This approach extends the traditional K-map method, which relies on human expertise. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed NN-driven technique yields significant improvements in both area and power consumption across various L-valued functions. Furthermore, the method is applicable to the automatic quantization of L-values derived from formal verification, enabling the efficient generation of test patterns for testing multiple signal lines simultaneously. The technique is highly efficient, requiring only a one-time training of the NN to generate the anNN-Gray codes. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed example of a 3-valued function to illustrate the proposed approach. The authors conclude that this technique is effective for minimizing the number of test patterns and enhancing the fault coverage of generated patterns. The technique is also highly scalable, capable of efficiently generating anNN-Gray codes for functions with a large number of L values. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the technique is robust, as the NN can be trained using different sets of minterms to produce the same anNN-Gray codes. The authors believe that this technique will be highly beneficial for the automatic quantization of L-values from formal verification and will enable the efficient generation of test patterns for multiple signal lines. The authors also note that the technique is versatile, as it can be used to generate anNN-Gray codes for both static and dynamic L-values. The technique is also highly flexible, allowing for the generation of anNN-Gray codes using different training parameters. This work examines several parameterized algorithms addressing the classical graph problem of determining if a directed graph $G$ admits an upward planar drawing. An upward planar drawing is a planar embedding of a directed acyclic graph where every edge points away from its source. We introduce a novel parameterization based on the number of edges violating upward planarity in a specific acyclic embedding, termed an "upward violation." Leveraging this metric, we develop a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm that decides upward planarity in $O(3^{\mu} \cdot n)$ time, where $\mu$ represents the count of upward violations and $n$ is the total edge count. Furthermore, we demonstrate that upward planarity is para-NP-complete when $\mu$ is defined as the number of edges violating upward planarity in an acyclic embedding, and it is W[1]-hard with respect to the number of source vertices. Finally, we establish that upward planarity is not even FPT when parameterized by the number of edges violating upward planarity in any drawing. These findings contrast with findings in general graph planarity, where parameters like the treewidth of the closure or the feedback vertex set size yield efficient algorithms. Additionally, we present an alternative parameter, $\mu'$, representing the number of downward violations in an acyclic embedding. We prove that upward planarity is para-NP-complete when parameterized by $\mu'$ and is para-NP-hard even when $\mu'$ is defined as the number of edges violating upward planarity in a drawing. This result stands in stark opposition to results for weakly directed planarity, where the problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable with respect to $\mu'$. Our findings indicate that identifying efficient parameterizations for upward planarity is significantly more challenging than for its undirected or weakly directed counterparts. Finally, we explore the upward $k$-outerplanarity problem and show that it is para-NP-complete when parameterized by $\mu$. However, we also provide an FPT algorithm for this problem using the treewidth of the graph as the parameter. The proposed algorithms are straightforward and rely on a straightforward extension of the classical $O(n)$ algorithm by Tamassia and Tamassia (1986). The paper concludes with a discussion on the relationship between upward violations and other graph parameters. This research investigates norms within transfer operator spaces associated with smooth semiflows. We demonstrate that, for sufficiently high Sobolev regularity spaces, the transfer operator norm decreases as regularity increases. This finding offers a partial resolution to a query posed by Baladi and Gentile. Furthermore, we apply this result to bound the Hölder continuous transfer operator norm of the Airy flow, thereby establishing the existence of nontrivial spectral gaps in certain Sobolev spaces. Additionally, we investigate whether the semigroup norm can be bounded by the norm of a specific linear combination of its generators, a property that holds true for the Airy flow. However, this property fails for the horizontal flow on the 2-torus, which precludes the existence of spectral gaps in any Sobolev space for this specific flow. Finally, we examine the validity of this norm diminution property for general semiflows, identifying a class of semiflows where the norm remains constant. We also present examples where the conclusion is false, including the time-one map of the time-independent flow $F(x) = x^2 - 2$. We contend that thermal photons and dileptons emitted during the viscous hadronic phase can precisely map the specific shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$) of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). This capability stems from the directional flow of thermal photons, observable through their anisotropy coefficients $v_n$ in non-central heavy-ion collisions. Our analysis demonstrates that these anisotropies are significantly amplified by viscous corrections linked to $\eta/s$ in both dilepton and photon spectra. Consequently, we propose that thermal photon (or dilepton) directional flow offers a unique method for measuring the QGP's $\eta/s$ ratio. This approach complements traditional methods that rely on comparing heavy-ion collision data with ideal hydrodynamic simulations. We illustrate this proposal by examining the $\vec{v}_2$ flow of thermal photons and dileptons emitted during the viscous hadronic stage, demonstrating its sensitivity to the QGP's $\eta/s$ using the PHENIX dataset from $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV Au+Au collisions at RHIC. Furthermore, we show that this viscosity sensitivity is accessible across a broad energy range, from 7.7 GeV to 5.02 TeV, covering both RHIC and LHC experiments. Our findings indicate that the $\vec{v}_2$ flow of thermal photons and dileptons can distinguish between the QGP's $\eta/s$ values predicted by various QCD equations of state. This insight is particularly valuable for future analyses of high-energy heavy-ion collisions, such as those conducted by the ALICE experiment at the LHC. We conclude that the directional flow of thermal photons and dileptons represents a novel and promising probe for QGP viscosity. Additionally, we outline the necessary experimental and theoretical efforts required to fully exploit this capability in future heavy-ion studies. Finally, we emphasize that this approach is applicable to all heavy-ion facilities worldwide, including RHIC, LHC, FAIR, NICA, and the proposed Energy Upgrade at the LHC (E@LHC). We anticipate that this research direction will yield significant insights into QCD matter under extreme conditions. Identifying effective interventions is a critical challenge across numerous scientific fields, including medicine, public health, and social sciences. Through extensive simulations and an analysis of a real-world large-scale experiment, we demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing FDR procedures in terms of FDR control and statistical power. A fundamental tenet of cosmology is the uniform expansion of the universe, which is quantified by the Hubble law. This study examines whether the expansion of the solar system adheres to a similar law, specifically investigating the relationship between the Sun's recession velocity and the orbital radii of the planets. By analyzing data from the NASA JPL Horizons on-demand system, the research calculates the rate of the Sun's retreat from each planet's current position. The findings reveal a strong correlation between these recession velocities and the orbital distances, indicating that the solar system is expanding at a rate approximately 10 orders of magnitude slower than the universe. These results are statistically significant and cannot be attributed to measurement errors or biases within the NASA ephemerides. The study further explores potential explanations for this phenomenon, including the influence of dark matter and dark energy. Additionally, the paper addresses the apparent contradiction between the solar system's expansion and the lack of observable effects on planetary orbits, suggesting that this paradox may be resolved by a probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics. Finally, the paper proposes that the expansion of the solar system could serve as a viable alternative to the recently proposed "Baade's paradox." Temporal action localization (TAL) is a crucial task for video analysis. While numerous supervised methods exist, they depend on labeled data, which is often scarce and expensive to obtain. To address this, we introduce SSCAP, an unsupervised framework designed for temporal action localization. SSCAP operates by learning a self-supervised representation of action semantics from the video content itself. Our approach consists of two primary components: (1) a self-supervised co-occurrence action modeling module that generates pseudo-labels for actions within video segments, and (2) a contrastive learning module that extracts features from these segments to facilitate action recognition. We evaluate SSCAP across various video datasets, including UCF101, HMDB51, UCFSports, Kinetics-400, and SSv2. Software testing education is a critical component of computer science curricula, yet it remains difficult to teach effectively. A primary obstacle is the absence of a clear, inquiry-driven framework that enables students to grasp the fundamental concepts of testing. This paper introduces and examines the Utility of Inquiry-Based Conceptual Responses (UB-TR) as a pedagogical tool for assessing student understanding of core software testing principles. The study compares UB-TR with the Traditional Detailed Evaluation Mechanism (TM), a conventional testing approach. Through an empirical investigation involving 120 undergraduate students, the research demonstrates that inquiry-based testing education utilizing the UB-TR method is more effective than traditional approaches based on TM. The findings indicate that UB-TR facilitates a deeper comprehension of essential software testing concepts and enhances students' ability to apply these concepts in practical scenarios. Additionally, the paper outlines the limitations of the study and proposes several directions for future research. This work is anticipated to assist educators in delivering effective software testing instruction. The authors have made the inquiry-based testing materials referenced in this study available online for educational use. Furthermore, the authors are currently developing an automated grading system for the UB-TR method to support software testing education. Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing label scarcity in image classification. However, most existing methods rely on access to both source and target training data during the adaptation phase, a constraint that often fails in real-world scenarios where target data is inaccessible. To overcome this, source-free domain adaptation has recently gained significant attention. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages semi-supervised learning to facilitate source-free domain adaptation. Specifically, we propose a method that utilizes a compact model, trained solely on source data, to guide a larger model during inference on the target domain. This framework enables the large model to achieve state-of-the-art performance on domain adaptation tasks without requiring any target training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art results across three standard benchmarks for image recognition. Additionally, we show that our approach can be seamlessly integrated with several existing source-free domain adaptation techniques. Finally, we evaluate the efficacy of our proposed framework in two practical scenarios: source-free domain adaptation and continual learning. Experimental results confirm that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in these applications. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2020/S2S4DFC}. This paper outlines the design and analysis of a gas-core reactor suitable for space propulsion in remote missions. The study examines the reactor's operating regime, the thermodynamic cycle of the proposed propulsion system, and the materials required for construction. Additionally, we provide an overview of the reactor's performance across various operational modes. The analysis demonstrates that such a reactor can deliver high specific impulse while offering adjustable thrust levels. Furthermore, the paper addresses the challenges associated with material selection and their potential solutions. Finally, the reactor's performance is illustrated using two specific case studies. Ultimately, the paper concludes that a remote gas-core reactor represents a viable option for deep space missions. These reactors would be deployed in orbit around a planet or moon, where they could be manufactured, tested, and maintained before being launched into deep space. This approach avoids the need to develop, test, or maintain the reactor within the deep space mission itself. The paper also discusses the challenges and opportunities involved in producing such a reactor in orbit. Finally, we suggest that these reactors could be manufactured in orbit using a combination of existing and emerging space manufacturing technologies. The paper also explores the benefits of utilizing space-based manufacturing facilities, such as the proposed Asteroid Redirector Rendezvous Vehicle (ARRV), to produce these reactors. Overall, the paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the remote gas-core reactor concept and its application to space propulsion. It also addresses several open issues and research gaps that need to be resolved to advance this concept. The paper concludes by suggesting potential areas for future research. Specifically, we recommend investigating the use of space-based manufacturing facilities to produce these reactors, as well as studying the operational and maintenance requirements of the reactors once they are in deep space. Additionally, we suggest researching the impact of the local radiation environment on the reactor's performance and the development of advanced materials and coatings to mitigate radiation damage. Finally, we recommend further research into the thermodynamic cycle and heat transfer characteristics of the propulsion system, as well as the effects of non-equilibrium chemistry on system performance. The paper also addresses the issue of fuel supply for the reactor and suggests exploring the use of fuel depots in orbit or on celestial bodies to ensure a continuous fuel supply for the reactor. Additionally, we recommend researching the effects of long-term operation on the reactor's performance and the development of advanced monitoring and diagnostic systems to detect and mitigate any performance degradation. Finally, we suggest further research into the effects of microgravity on the reactor's performance and the development of advanced numerical methods to simulate the reactor's behavior in microgravity.

Recent years have seen a surge in astroparticle experiments designed to detect rare events, driven by the field's critical role in addressing fundamental questions in cosmology and particle physics. These experiments rely on sophisticated sensor systems to identify target phenomena amidst background noise. This study introduces a domain-informed neural architecture that leverages the spatial arrangement of astroparticle experiment sensors to precisely localize interactions. We validate this model using a simulation of a cubic volume containing 1,000 scintillator spheres, where the spatial configuration of detected signals serves as input. The proposed architecture outperforms a standard Transformer model, achieving 99.9% accuracy in signal localization, compared to 98.3% for the Transformer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model's performance is robust across various experiments with different volumes and sensor densities. Our findings indicate that domain-informed neural architectures are essential for optimizing astroparticle experiment performance. Additionally, we show that these architectures can be enhanced through the integration of auxiliary models that incorporate domain-specific knowledge. This approach not only boosts performance but also facilitates the identification of anomalies, such as dark regions within the experiment volume. Finally, we highlight that domain-informed neural architectures can be adapted to other sensor-based experiments, including those in medical imaging. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/astroML/interaction-localization. Atmospheric observations of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets have become increasingly common, yet the interpretation of these data remains a significant challenge. This difficulty stems from the intricate chemistry and physics governing these environments, which necessitate complex numerical models to derive accurate atmospheric compositions. We introduce EXOPLINES, a comprehensive repository of molecular absorption cross-sections designed to accelerate the interpretation of future atmospheric studies. This database includes cross-sections for 18 key species: H2, H2O, CH4, CO, CO2, NH3, HCN, HNC, CS, TiO, VO, CrH, FeH, Cr2, NiH, NiH+, Cr2+, and TiO2. These values were computed using the Molecodes suite of programs, which employs the Born-Oppenheimer approximation and the Born-Huang perturbation method. The collection is accessible online at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~wright/exoplimes.html. We anticipate that EXOPLINES will serve as a valuable resource for researchers utilizing retrieval codes to analyze brown dwarf and exoplanet spectra. Furthermore, we outline the procedures for adding new species to the repository. Our goal is to facilitate the creation of extensive molecular absorption cross-section databases, thereby simplifying the modeling of brown dwarf and exoplanet atmospheres. We intend for EXOPLINES to be a freely available, freely accessible, and free-for-profit online resource. Contributions from the community are welcome, and we encourage interested individuals to contact the authors to join the effort. This work investigates the relationship between classical logic programming and answer list programming, introducing a language called classol that bridges classical logic and answer set programming. We demonstrate that classol can model the semantics of answer list programming, thereby facilitating the reasoning required for grounding in answer set programming. Additionally, we examine how classol can represent the stability semantics of answer set programming. Our primary contribution is a declarative framework that encapsulates the grounding and stability semantics, enabling the utilization of efficient classical SAT and model counting solvers. We illustrate this language with examples derived from answer set programming and provide an implementation. The proposed language serves as a foundation for developing efficient grounders and solvers for answer set programming. Furthermore, we have integrated this language into the open-source ASP solver ASPCore, which includes a grouder capable of handling answer set programs. We present experimental results comparing our grouder against state-of-the-art alternatives. These results indicate that, for the tested benchmarks, our grouder is competitive with leading solvers, particularly when answer set programs are formulated using the answer set programming with constraints (ASPcore2) format. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential future research directions.

This work establishes the initial phase of a comprehensive law governing universal quantum resource theories. We demonstrate that for any set of free transformations within such a theory, a monotone can be constructed to characterize every channel in the theory; this construction method includes free entropies and generalized resource relative entropities as specific instances. Furthermore, we prove that these entropies satisfy the chain rule, thereby enabling the formulation of an initial law for the generalized resource relative entropy. Additionally, we derive an integral representation of the free probability distribution and utilize it to demonstrate that free entropy remains invariant under free transformations. These findings are applicable to the study of coherence and entanglement. As a practical application, we introduce a novel measure of entanglement for bipartite states that surpasses existing bounds on resource relative entropy and provides tighter constraints on the distillation rate of Bell pairs. Finally, we illustrate how these methods can be utilized to derive new upper bounds on the distillation rate of entanglement. These results are also relevant to the analysis of other universal resource theories.

This study addresses inference challenges within non-stable, non-stationary multivariate time series, offering both theoretical and numerical insights. We introduce a non-stationary stochastic volatility model featuring power-law distributed innovations, analyzing its asymptotic behavior and developing estimation techniques. Our primary theoretical contribution establishes the asymptotic normality of the estimator under appropriate regularity conditions. Additionally, we propose a test for normality in the innovation distribution, demonstrating its consistency. Numerical experiments further illustrate the performance of our estimator and normality test. Finally, we apply these methods to a non-stationary, heavy-tailed time series derived from high-frequency financial data. The analysis reveals that the stochastic volatility component is non-ergodic, a finding that complicates the estimation of the power-law innovation distribution. However, we successfully estimate the heavy-tailedness parameter, which remains stable across various estimation windows. These findings underscore the necessity of heavy-tailed stochastic volatility models for non-stable time series and suggest that stochastic volatility can induce apparent heavy tails in financial time series. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/JuliaTimeSeries/NonStableHeavyTails. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor Jean Jacod. Efficient decoding of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes is a critical component for achieving reliable communication over noisy channels with linear-rate capacity-achieving codes. However, current LDPC code designs lack decoders that operate in linear time, $O(n)$, relative to the codeword length $n$. This study introduces a novel class of LDPC codes equipped with linear-time decoders. Specifically, we present a family of rate $R$ LDPC codes where decoding can be accomplished in $O(n)$ time using $O(n)$ space. These codes are constructed by concatenating a rate $1/2$ polar code with a rate $1/2$ LDPC code featuring rate $1-R$ and constant relative distance. The resulting linear-time LDPC codes exhibit a rate-distance product of $R\epsilon n$ and a relative distance $\epsilon > 0$. The proposed linear-time decoder utilizes a non-iterative algorithm that combines belief propagation with min-sum decoding. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these linear-time LDPC codes achieve an error probability of $e^{-\Omega(n^{\alpha})}$ for some $\alpha > 0$ when transmitted over the binary symmetric channel. Such error performance is characteristic of LDPC codes with rate $1-R$ and constant relative distance, which are decoded using the same non-iterative method. Our work extends the class of efficiently decodable LDPC codes, complementing recent advancements by other research groups. Our codes maintain the advantages of existing LDPC designs, including high rates, constant relative distances, and low decoding complexity. Additionally, we establish that these linear-time LDPC codes are quasi-cyclic, enabling the implementation of efficient parallel decoders. Quasi-cyclicity is a valuable trait for many applications, including physical layer network coding and quantum error correction. Notably, this class of LDPC codes can be directly adapted for use as check matrices in quantum LDPC codes. We demonstrate that these linear-time quantum LDPC codes possess a rate $R' = \Omega(1/\sqrt{n})$ and constant relative distance, achieving an error probability of $e^{-\Omega(n^{\alpha'})}$ for some $\alpha' > 0$ over the quantum depolarizing channel. Quantum LDPC codes with rate $1-R'$ and constant relative distance can also be decoded in linear time using our non-iterative approach. A distance $r$ dominating set of a graph $G$ is defined as a vertex set $D$ where every vertex in $G$ is within distance $r$ of at least one member of $D$. The distance $r$ domination number, denoted by $\gamma_r(G)$, represents the minimum cardinality of such a set. This paper investigates the size of distributed distance $r$ controlling sets, specifically those sets $C$ that can extend to a distance $r$ dominating set by adding vertices from $V(G)\setminus C$. We demonstrate that for graphs $G$ with girth $g$ and maximum degree $\Delta$, there exists a constant $c$ dependent on $r$, $g$, and $\Delta$ such that $\gamma_r(G)/|V(G)| \leq c$ holds whenever $|V(G)|$ is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we establish that for sparse graphs where $g$ and $\Delta$ are large, the ratio $|C|/\gamma_r(G)$ is bounded by a function of $r$, $g$, and $\Delta$ for any distributed distance $r$ controlling set $C$. These findings are achieved through a novel analysis of graph colorings. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to determine if a given set $S$ constitutes a distributed distance $r$ controlling set. Finally, we examine the scenario where $G$ is a random graph formed by selecting vertices from a graph with girth $g$ and maximum degree $\Delta$. In this context, we prove that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a constant $c$ depending on $r$, $g$, and $\Delta$ such that $\gamma_r(G)/|V(G)| \leq c + \epsilon$ with high probability, provided the vertex count is large enough. A mass-boundary correspondence is proposed for disordered higher-order topological (HOT) materials, extending the well-known bulk-boundary correspondence found in ordinary topological systems. This framework classifies the reduction of topological protection caused by mass terms into three categories: complete loss, partial loss, or preservation of topological protection. The study examines a generalized Su-Schrieffer-Anderson (SSA) model featuring corner states and an SSA-like hinge state model. Furthermore, the results are applied to the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) on a square lattice and a three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ HOTI. Finally, the mass-boundary correspondence is demonstrated in a three-dimensional mass-deformed Chern insulator exhibiting hinge states. These findings offer a novel perspective on the topological properties of higher-order topological systems and establish a foundation for investigating their physical characteristics. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to other emergent topological phenomena. Solar jets are believed to originate from magnetic reconnection occurring in the low corona, yet their precise formation mechanisms remain unclear. This study presents LOFAR observations of a piston-driven surge, offering new insights into the dynamics of such events. The surge's leading edge moves at approximately 100 km/s, while the following jet exhibits a much higher velocity of about 300 km/s. The jet's front displays a braided structure, and the surge's leading edge appears as a thin, bright arc. The spatial relationship between the surge and the jet suggests they are physically linked, with the jet likely accelerating the surge. Furthermore, the surge's leading edge seems to mark the boundary between the jet and the low corona. This interpretation is supported by the surge's size and the magnetic field strength derived from LOFAR data. The observed velocity of the surge's leading edge aligns with the Alfvén speed calculated using the derived magnetic field strength. These findings indicate that the surge is driven by a jet acting as a piston, pushing against the ambient magnetic field. This research demonstrates that LOFAR data can be utilized to investigate dynamics within the low corona. Additionally, the study confirms that piston-driven surges are a common phenomenon in the low corona. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be efficiently executed by quantum devices but difficult for classical machines. This study examines the entanglement within the final state of this protocol, specifically measuring it through negativity. Our findings indicate that while global entanglement grows with the number of photons, it saturates as the count of optical modes increases. Furthermore, we observe that the probability distributions of multi-mode negativity and three-mode negativity follow distinct patterns. These results offer new insights into the entanglement characteristics of bosonic systems. Finally, we propose an experimental approach to verify these findings using the quantum state tomography of photonic systems. This method involves reconstructing the complete state vector and calculating negativity across all possible multi-mode partitions. Although the computational cost of this analysis scales exponentially with the number of modes, it remains feasible for small-scale experiments. Consequently, our findings are particularly relevant to recent achievements in boson sampling involving up to 50 modes. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1992/BosonSampling_entanglement. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a computational framework for agents to acquire skills through interaction with their surroundings. Within the model-based RL category, agents utilize a belief state to represent their understanding of the environment and plan their future actions. Cognitive multi-level frameworks have been developed to analyze single- and multi-player games with incomplete information, typically involving one or two hierarchical layers. This study extends that methodology to multi-player games characterized by multiple layers of incomplete information. We introduce a sequence of Bayesian games to represent interactions among agents at various cognitive layers, where each agent engages in a specific action-based signaling game with adjacent layers. We examine the existence and characterization of Bayesian Nash equilibria within these Bayesian cognitive layers games. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these games can model scenarios where agents possess different information regarding other agents' types and cognitive levels. Finally, we establish a limit theorem that enables the derivation of a unique fixed point for a sequence of such games. This limiting game features only two layers: a bottom layer where agents know their types but remain unaware of others' levels, and a top layer where agents are aware of both their own and others' types and levels. We also provide an example illustrating how this framework can represent information diffusion within a social network. Additionally, we explore the application of these games to multi-level reasoning in multi-agent path finding. Our analysis of a two-level, two-agent path finding instance reveals that Bayesian cognitive layers games can capture situations where agents differ in their knowledge of each other's types and levels. We further show that the probability of type uncertainty vanishing in the limit results in a unique equilibrium for these Bayesian cognitive layers games. This unique equilibrium corresponds to a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in a top-level game where all agents know each other's types and levels, and this top-level game can be solved via a path finding algorithm. Consequently, this finding offers a novel method for determining a unique equilibrium in Bayesian cognitive layers games. Finally, we discuss how these findings can facilitate the design of mechanisms for multi-level reasoning in multi-agent path finding. Specifically, we demonstrate that a mechanism can be constructed to incentivize agents to truthfully report their types and levels, thereby inducing a unique equilibrium in the Bayesian cognitive layers game that projects to the unique equilibrium of the top-level game. We also extend the limit theorem to handle cases where type uncertainty does not vanish in the limit. We present the two collections within this class with the smallest and largest estimated values, designated as the minimum FPF collection (min-FPF) and the maximum FPF collection (max-FPF), respectively. The min-FPF collection applies a filtering technique to track the minimum value, whereas the max-FPF collection employs the same technique to monitor the maximum value. Both the FPF collection and its variants are founded on a new data structure called the \emph{gap tree}, which we demonstrate offers superior performance compared to the gap-free tree proposed by Datta et al.~\cite{Datta2019}. Furthermore, we extend min-FPF and max-FPF to support the estimation of the range, minimum, and maximum of a set of real numbers. We further generalize min-FPF to handle the estimation of the union of $k$ disjoint intervals on the real line and the maximum of $k$ disjoint intervals. Additionally, we adapt max-FPF to estimate the size of the intersection of $k$ disjoint intervals on the real line. Finally, we demonstrate that min-FPF can be extended to estimate the minimum of $k$ disjoint intervals. Experimental evaluations indicate that min-FPF and max-FPF are more efficient than their corresponding gap-free tree variants. Our results show that min-FPF outperforms min-FPF$^*$ by a factor of 1.5 to 2 in terms of space usage and by 1.2 to 2 in terms of query time. Mafia is a well-known social board game where players act as either "Citizens" or "Mafias" and attempt to identify one another. Finally, we compare these results with data from a small-scale experiment conducted among our colleagues. Additionally, we observe that the presence of a Sheriff significantly boosts Citizen victory rates, particularly in shorter games. The electronic behavior of multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) is governed by two primary mechanisms: direct electron transfer within the inner shell and phonon-mediated transfer from the inner to the outer shell. Furthermore, the resonant transmission of electrons from the inner MWCNT shell to the SWCNT is suppressed at temperatures above 100 K, whereas the transition from the outer shell to the SWCNT is enhanced. These results indicate that phonons play a critical role in enabling electron transfer from the inner to the outer shell of MWCNTs. This discovery holds significant implications for the design of carbon-based electronic devices, particularly in optimizing electron transport between adjacent carbon nanotubes. Additionally, it suggests a potential pathway for enhancing electron injection into the intertube space of MWCNTs. Finally, this research offers a novel approach for populating the electron system of MWCNTs, a factor essential for investigating their intrinsic electronic properties. This is achieved by utilizing the SWCNT as a shell-to-shell electron transfer channel, thereby facilitating the study of the intrinsic electronic properties of MWCNTs. This paper introduces a novel fuzzy k-means approach that incorporates variable feature weights. We recognize that in high-dimensional datasets, certain features often possess greater significance than others. To address this, we propose an entropy-driven method for calculating these weights. First, we compute the entropy value for each feature; subsequently, weights are assigned inversely proportional to these entropy values, ensuring that features with lower entropy (higher relevance) receive higher weights. The resulting model, termed Entropy-driven Variable Feature Weighted Fuzzy k-means (EVFKM), was validated across multiple real-world datasets. Our findings demonstrate that EVFKM consistently outperforms the standard fuzzy k-means algorithm in terms of clustering accuracy. Furthermore, we observe that EVFKM scales linearly with the number of features, confirming its suitability for clustering in high-dimensional spaces. Finally, we illustrate how EVFKM can be applied to identify patient subgroups based on clinical data. The source code for this method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/EVFKM.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which combine multiple expert networks with a gating network to assign weights, have long been a staple in probabilistic modeling. Despite their widespread use across various domains, current algorithms struggle with the "deadlock" problem, where the gating network becomes trapped in a local minimum. This issue stems from the non-convex nature of the loss landscape, which prevents standard gradient descent methods from effectively training the gating network. Consequently, the gating network often fails to activate the intended experts, leading to poor performance. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm that integrates a perturbation mechanism with a trust region strategy, enabling gradient descent to navigate out of local minima. We have rigorously proven that this approach avoids deadlock and successfully identifies a near-optimal point. Additionally, we propose a new algorithm that merges a gradient method with a non-convex optimization technique, demonstrating its ability to converge to a second-order stationary point. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our proposed algorithms outperform existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we have applied these methods to large-scale MoE models for classification and clustering tasks, achieving significant improvements in both training efficiency and model performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi2001/MoE. Finally, we have released a user-friendly Python package, PyMoE, which streamlines the implementation of MoE models and their training. This study investigates the disruption of global symmetries within quantum gravity frameworks, specifically focusing on the potential breaking of Peccei-Quinn symmetry and its influence on cosmic birefringence. We demonstrate that the absence of such symmetry disruption is a necessary condition for the viability of the axion model in explaining the recently observed global birefringence signal. Furthermore, we establish that this conclusion remains robust even when accounting for Planck-scale effects. We analyze these effects through two lenses: first, by evaluating the stability of the axion decay constant against quantum gravity effects, and second, by examining whether the global symmetry can be redefined via vector fields. Our analysis of decay constant stability indicates that the Planck-scale limit is not strictly required, as a sufficiently high Planck-scale value is adequate. Additionally, we find that the symmetry breaking scenario is not favored, as it necessitates fine-tuning of the model's parameters. Consequently, we conclude that quantum gravity effects do not significantly disrupt the Peccei-Quinn symmetry. Finally, we provide a discussion of the broader implications of these findings. A transferability guarantee ensures that a model trained on one dataset can be deployed on another. This paper challenges the conventional view that a classifier's agreement with human labels across two training datasets serves as such a guarantee. We argue that, absent further evidence, high agreement merely indicates that the model fits the training data well, rather than ensuring correct labeling of the second dataset. To support this, we introduce the "overfitting hypothesis," which posits that deep neural networks can achieve high agreement through overfitting. We demonstrate that an adversarial model can replicate this high agreement while systematically making errors on the second dataset. Furthermore, we show that the adversarial model's behavior mirrors that of a standard model trained with a strong L2 regularization term. Finally, we contend that existing literature on the significance of Two Agreement is flawed because it overlooks the possibility that Two Agreement is simply a manifestation of overfitting. We conclude by proposing four alternative hypotheses that could explain the observed relationship between deep model transferability and Two Agreement. These alternatives suggest that current research on the interpretability of deep learning models may be misleading the community. We hope these perspectives inspire new investigations into the true nature of overfitting in deep learning. The structural characteristics of real-world networks are intricate and often defy simple description. A prominent feature is a "small-world" architecture, characterized by high connectivity and the presence of tightly bonded clusters. This study investigates how such network topology influences the dissemination of information within complex networks. We demonstrate that modularity plays a critical role in regulating the velocity of information spread. Specifically, networks with low modularity facilitate the rapid diffusion of information, whereas highly modular networks significantly impede the diffusion process. Our findings are supported by both a theoretical model and numerical simulations. Furthermore, we show that the theoretical predictions align with numerical results across various real-world networks. These insights offer a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics governing information diffusion in networked systems. Additionally, our results suggest that the topology of real-world networks can be engineered to control the rate of information diffusion. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these findings in the context of epidemic modeling. This research was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period marked by the rapid global spread of the virus. Our results provide a new perspective on the mechanisms driving the rapid diffusion of infectious diseases. Moreover, our findings indicate that the speed of viral transmission can be controlled by modifying the network topology. This conclusion is supported by empirical evidence from the real world. For instance, the adoption of a lockdown policy in Italy led to a substantial decline in the speed of the virus's spread. This aligns with our findings, as lockdowns restrict human mobility and alter the network topology, thereby reducing its modularity. Our results also explain the observed variations in the speed of the pandemic across different regions. For example, the virus spread more rapidly in the densely populated northern regions of Italy compared to the sparsely populated south, a disparity attributed to differences in network modularity. Our findings have significant implications for controlling epidemics. By understanding the relationship between network topology and the speed of disease transmission, we can develop strategies to mitigate the impact of epidemics. For example, our results suggest that increasing the modularity of a network can be used to slow down the spread of a virus. This could be achieved by implementing targeted interventions, such as social distancing measures, which would reduce the connectivity of the network and increase its modularity. In conclusion, our findings provide a new perspective on the mechanisms driving the spread of infectious diseases and offer a potential pathway for controlling epidemics. By manipulating the network topology, we can influence the speed of viral transmission and mitigate the impact of the pandemic. This approach could prove instrumental in the ongoing fight against COVID

This paper introduces the concept of distinctiveness for Lagrangian submanifolds within Calabres-Finsler manifolds, demonstrating its quantitative nature. We establish that the distinctiveness of a Lagrangian $L$ can be expressed through Calabi's relative functional, mirroring the relationship between massiveness and Calabi's $F$-functional observed in Kähler manifolds. Furthermore, we prove that the distinctiveness of $L$ serves as a sufficient condition for the existence of special Lagrangian gradient flow lines originating from $L$. This finding extends the Thomas-Yau theorem, which previously held only for Lagrangian submanifolds in Calabi-Yau manifolds. Additionally, we show that the massiveness of calabi-Yau domains, as defined by Chen and Tian, is equivalent to the distinctiveness of their boundary Lagrangians. Finally, we provide a sufficient condition for the existence of holomorphic discs with Lagrangian boundaries based on the concepts of massiveness and distinctiveness. These findings offer a quantitative perspective on the Lagrangian massiveness proposed by Chen and Tian. The study begins with a review of Calabi's relative functional and its connection to massiveness, followed by an analysis of the relationship between massiveness and distinctiveness. The paper then proceeds to establish the main theorems. This paper introduces a precision analysis for the time-domain standard perturbation model (TSPM) applied to unamplified links. By deriving the probability of bit error ($P_b$) for the TSPM, we demonstrate that it aligns with the Gaussian model (GM) under low jitter conditions and converges to the Sarma bound (SB) in high bit-rate scenarios. Furthermore, we prove that the TSPM's $P_b$ is always superior to or equal to the SB, thereby establishing the Sarma bound as a conservative estimate for amplified backbones. Additionally, we propose a method to calculate the TSPM $P_b$ in the time domain, which avoids the need for extensive simulations. Finally, we present a procedure for generating realistic jittered pseudo-random binary sequences (PRBS) that accurately reflect the $P_b$ of the TSPM. These sequences can be used to simulate the eye diagram of an ideal receiver, thereby validating the precision of existing TSPM $P_b$ calculations. Numerical results confirm the accuracy of these proposed methods. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive precision analysis of the TSPM, offering a clear understanding of its limitations and enabling its effective application in practical systems. Recent theoretical work has suggested that moderate interactions can trigger reentrant incompressible quantum Hall phases at low filling factors, such as the reentrant 5/2 state. This study investigates the stability of such a phase using variational Monte Carlo simulations. Our results indicate that an incompressible reentrant 5/2 phase does not form; instead, the ground state evolves continuously from the reentrant to the unique 5/2 phase as interaction strength increases. This contrasts with theoretical predictions, which anticipated a first-order transition between these phases. Furthermore, we observe that the 5/2 phase becomes thermodynamically unstable relative to the reentrant 7/2 phase at moderate interaction strengths. These findings align with earlier theoretical predictions regarding the reentrant 7/2 phase. Additionally, we demonstrate that the reentrant 3/2 phase is thermodynamically unstable compared to the 5/2 phase across all interaction strengths. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the reentrant 5/2 phase within the context of the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface. The recent discovery of gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers has sparked significant interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) as a potential dark matter candidate. This motivation has driven numerous studies aiming to establish cosmological constraints on the mass function of these PBHs. However, many of these works rely on the Thakurta metric to describe cosmological black hole dynamics, which is now recognized as flawed. In this paper, we demonstrate that the core issue lies in the metric's incorrect treatment of the cosmological horizon, leading to the erroneous conclusion that the accretion rate of gas by merging black holes is independent of the Hubble parameter. Consequently, the LIGO-Virgo constraints on PBHs derived from this method are invalid. We provide the correct derivation of the accretion rate and re-evaluate the cosmological constraints on the PBH mass function, finding no significant differences compared to the results obtained using the flawed approach. This indicates that the fundamental conclusions regarding the PBH mass function remain consistent. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the current LIGO-Virgo constraints on PBHs are not compromised by the misuse of the Thakurta metric. Furthermore, we have made our updated code publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. Our conclusions are expected to apply to all studies utilizing the Thakurta metric to derive cosmological constraints on the PBH mass function. This study investigates how planet formation via pebble accumulation is influenced by dust density fluctuations. We developed a one-dimensional model that integrates the evolution of dust density with the growth of a protoplanet. Our results indicate that clumps with higher-than-average dust density significantly accelerate planetary growth. Specifically, if the dust-to-gas mass ratio is 0.01, a planet can form within 10 million years in a region where the dust density exceeds the average by a factor of 100. Furthermore, the planet's final mass is directly proportional to these local dust density enhancements. This mechanism offers a potential solution to the long-standing puzzle of how planets with masses exceeding 100 Earth masses can form within the short lifespans of protoplanetary disks. Additionally, we demonstrate that planets created through this process retain a substantial amount of pebbles, suggesting that such a density-amplification mechanism is essential for pebble-nucleated planet formation. Consequently, this model may help explain the existence of super-Earths and the volatile content observed in some exoplanets. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for this dust density-amplification mechanism to operate. We conclude that the process is likely active in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, where dust density is enhanced by the pressure bump generated by a planet gap. This implies that the dust density amplification mechanism and pebble-nucleated planet formation are likely linked. Future research should focus on the physical processes driving dust density amplification and on planet formation models that incorporate dust density evolution. Such efforts are crucial for understanding the initial mass and composition of planets. Furthermore, we must explore the relationship between pebble-nucleated planet formation and the current exoplanet population. By examining the density fluctuations of dust and gas in protoplanetary disks, we can better understand the formation of exoplanets. Ultimately, this research will contribute to unraveling the mystery of planet formation. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the pebble-nucleated planet formation model; Section 3 introduces our proposed dust density-amplification mechanism; Section 4 presents the model results; and Section 5 summarizes our findings. Additionally, Section 6 discusses the implications of this dust density-amplification mechanism for pebble-nucleated planet formation. Overparameterized models are common in machine learning, where the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. This paper examines the learning of concept classes from samples under the constraint that learners must be efficiently computable. We demonstrate that when computational limits are imposed, error can be learned efficiently with a sample size that is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors, yet remains superlinear. This finding contrasts with the standard realizable setting, where sample complexity is linear, and the computationally unconstrained PAC setting, which allows for sublinear sample complexity. Consequently, our findings indicate that the interplay between overparameterization and efficient computation can result in learning problems that are strictly harder than those arising from overparameterization alone. Finally, we prove that the hardness of learning concept classes under computational constraints is equivalent to the existence of one-way functions. This equivalence extends to scenarios involving overparameterized learners, provided they are computable within a slightly broader class of functions. To our knowledge, this represents the first time the hardness of overparameterized learning has been characterized in terms of cryptographic assumptions. Our results further imply that overparameterization can render learning problems intractable for any learner, even one possessing unlimited computational power. Additionally, we explore the relationship between our findings and the hardness of learning overparameterized neural networks, suggesting that resolving open questions in this area could yield insights into the hardness of overparameterized learning in general. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for understanding the hardness of overparameterized learning in overparameterized models. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where the hardness of overparameterized learning is established in an overparameterized model. We conclude by outlining several open problems in this domain.
