This paper investigates Bohr topology features of infinite abelian groups, specifically examining the minimality of their Bohr compactification and the existence of infinite Bohr-definable subgroups within them and their compactifications. The primary focus lies on infinite (necessarily discrete) Bohr-topologized groups that are countable sums of finite groups, with an emphasis on the Boolean groups $V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Z}_2$. The study primarily addresses the second scenario. The findings reveal that the Boolean group $V$ possesses a rich structure of infinite Bohr-definable subgroups, yet its Bohr compactification $K$ lacks a minimal structure. This conclusion is derived from an analysis of Boolean-valued models $M_K$ associated with $K$. Furthermore, this result extends to broader classes of groups, including those formed by direct sums of finite cyclic groups and finite simple groups. The proofs rely on a novel method for identifying infinite Bohr-definable subgroups, which is the outcome of an intricate interplay between model theory and topological dynamics. This methodology is also applicable to other significant questions in these fields. The paper concludes with several remarks and a list of related problems. Alzheimer's disease (AD) represents a progressive neurodegenerative condition characterized by the gradual deterioration of cognitive functions, including memory, language, and reasoning. While the disease progresses through distinct stages—ranging from mild impairment to severe dementia—the specific transition from a mild cognitively impaired (MCI) state to full Alzheimer's remains poorly understood. This study investigates the feasibility of predicting this progression using MCI patient data obtained via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We introduce a novel deep learning architecture called Deep InfoMax, which integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a variational autoencoder (VAE) to extract robust features from 3D brain MRI scans. These features are subsequently utilized to forecast AD progression. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an accuracy of 70.5%, outperforming other methods. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's performance, highlighting its potential for early detection and prediction of Alzheimer's progression. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Deep-InfoMax. This research was conducted as part of the Kaggle 3D Medical Prognosis competition, available at https://www.kaggle.com/c/3d-medical-prognosis. The competition organizers provided MRI scans of MCI patients, and our objective was to predict AD progression using the Deep InfoMax model. This work serves as a proof of concept for the competition, and we hope it proves beneficial to the community. Future endeavors will focus on refining the model to achieve even higher accuracy. This paper introduces a new model for interpreting language semantics that leverages word embeddings and an interaction-driven recurrent neural network. We contend that the semantic relationships between words are inherently dynamic and interactive, evolving as they engage with one another within a sentence. To capture this phenomenon, we propose a novel feature extraction method that models word interactions through a dynamic feature matrix. This matrix is generated by integrating the initial interaction state of the recurrent network with the embeddings of interacting words, where the initial state is determined by a word's identity and its interactions with other words. Experimental results demonstrate that our interaction-driven approach outperforms existing methods in extracting semantic features, achieving state-of-the-art performance in sentence classification and semantic similarity tasks. The interplay between spin-orbit interaction (SOI) and electron-electron interactions is a fundamental aspect of correlated electron systems. This study investigates how interactions influence SOI within a correlated metal by examining the SrIrO$_3$ perovskite oxide. We introduce a new class of three-dimensional asymptotically flat spacetimes that exhibit metastability. These spacetimes feature a disconnected domain consisting of two asymptotic regions linked by a smooth, finite, and minimal bridge. At the extreme limit, this structure degenerates into two separate asymptotic regions connected by a maximal minimal surface. We term this limiting configuration the "confocal conformal shadow," which serves as the conformal compactification of the static Schwarzschild solution, connecting both asymptotic regions at infinity. We demonstrate that our spacetimes possess a continuous symmetry group that includes an isometry subgroup, and we outline the methodology for generating them. Furthermore, we establish that these spacetimes are asymptotically safe, with their shadows remaining smooth and minimal everywhere. Finally, we examine the behavior of test particles within these geometries. Specifically, we show that while null geodesics can transition between the two asymptotic regions, timelike geodesics are confined to a single connected component. Deep learning has achieved remarkable success across numerous artificial intelligence applications, including medical image analysis. However, the widespread adoption of deep learning tools in clinical settings is hindered by their limited generalization capabilities when faced with distribution shifts, such as variations in patient demographics or imaging equipment. Consequently, there is a critical need for robust artificial intelligence tools capable of handling these distributional changes. This study introduces a robust testing framework that integrates distribution-free prediction intervals with conformal forecasting to evaluate the performance of artificial intelligence tools under distribution shift. We validate this framework using three deep learning models applied to medical image analysis tasks involving distribution shift. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively assesses the performance of artificial intelligence tools under distributional shifts, offering a more comprehensive evaluation than traditional point-based metrics. Furthermore, this approach holds significant potential for enhancing the robustness of artificial intelligence tools in medical settings by facilitating the development of reliable prediction intervals. We introduce a straightforward and efficient technique to enhance the sampling of molecular conformations, specifically for DNA, by applying a small constant force to the base pairs. This approach, termed Stiff Base Biasing (SBB), utilizes a spring with a high force constant to exert this force. Our findings indicate that SBB generates an effective free energy landscape that is significantly smoother than the original, thereby facilitating the exploration of broader conformational spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the SBB methodology is straightforward to implement within standard molecular dynamics software. We successfully applied SBB to sample conformations of both B-DNA and Z-DNA. In the B-DNA case, the technique revealed a landscape featuring a single minimum alongside a series of metastable states. For Z-DNA, SBB facilitated the transition from a high free energy barrier region to a lower one, allowing for the characterization of metastable states and the identification of the free energy landscape. Additionally, we show that SBB can be integrated into free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations to improve the sampling of DNA conformations. These results confirm that SBB is a versatile and effective method for molecular dynamics simulations. The accompanying Python code is accessible at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1234/SBB. This study evaluates the ANS entropy compression algorithm's performance on various datasets. We assess its effectiveness across six categories of entropy-coded compressed files generated using different compression methods, ranging from simple run-length encoding to sophisticated context models. Our results indicate that ANS achieves compression ratios comparable to those of entropy coding techniques. Additionally, ANS offers the benefits of rapid compression and decompression speeds, along with high algorithmic simplicity. Given these advantages, ANS is well-suited for applications requiring tight integration of compression with other functionalities, such as data encryption. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexeykuznetsov/ans-c.

The dielectric response of cementitious materials is influenced by the electric properties of their constituent phases, including the aggregate, cement paste, and the interfacial boundary between them. This study employs a multi-phase dielectric model to examine how the dielectric constants of the aggregate, cement paste, and pore fluid influence the material's overall dielectric constant. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of interfacial polarization within cementitious composites. Our findings indicate that the dielectric constant of the pore fluid exerts a more significant influence on interfacial polarization than that of the cement paste. Additionally, the dielectric constant of the pore fluid has a greater effect on the dielectric constant of cementitious materials when using a low-dielectric constant aggregate compared to one with a high dielectric constant. These results offer valuable insights into the dielectric behavior of cementitious materials, which can be utilized to develop non-destructive testing methods for assessing their condition. These techniques may facilitate the detection of microcracks, moisture content, and residual strength in structures such as concrete, bridges, and dams. Ultimately, this research aids in developing non-destructive testing protocols for evaluating the integrity of cementitious materials. Additionally, the methodologies employed can be applied to analyze the dielectric characteristics of other composite materials. The findings presented in this study are supported by experimental data. This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the properties of heavy-heavy hadronic clusters, specifically $QQ$ and $Qq$, where $Q$ denotes a heavy quark and $q$ a light quark. The study employs the $1/N_c$ expansion, with $N_c$ representing the number of colors, alongside the $1/m_Q$ expansion, where $m_Q$ is the mass of the heavy quark. Utilizing the heavy quark effective theory (HQET), we analyze the masses of these clusters to explore their potential applications. Furthermore, we examine the binding energies of heavy hadronic clusters within the framework of the potential non-relativistic QCD (pNRQCD). Our findings indicate that the masses of $QQ$ and $Qq$ clusters are nearly independent of $N_c$, a result that contrasts with the well-established $N_c$ dependence observed in heavy quarkonium. Additionally, we investigate the binding energy dependence on $N_c$ and demonstrate that it increases as $N_c$ grows. These conclusions are supported by numerical calculations. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the existence of such heavy-heavy hadronic clusters. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable cosmological probe, allowing researchers to study the distribution of dark matter halos and the thermal state of the intergalactic medium (IGM) through the three-dimensional clustering of absorption systems. This study demonstrates that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest can be modeled as a collection of discrete absorption systems, where the mean density of these systems is directly proportional to the Lyman-$\alpha$ density contrast. Consequently, the three-dimensional correlation function of the absorbers is derived from the mean Lyman-$\alpha$ density contrast, which is subsequently converted into a comoving correlation function. By applying a spherical top-hat smoothing kernel to the Lyman-$\alpha$ density contrast, we calculate the mean number density of dark matter halos with a virial temperature of $T_{\rm vir}=10^4$ K. This halo number density is then used to derive the halo mass function. Furthermore, we examine the temperature of the IGM at redshift $z=2.5$ by analyzing the thermal state of halos with $T_{\rm vir}=10^4$ K. Our findings indicate that the thermal energy of these halos is primarily determined by the IGM temperature, with a contribution of approximately 90% at $z=2.5$. Finally, we compare our results with previous studies and discuss the implications of these findings. Ultimately, the three-dimensional clustering of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest offers a robust cosmological test for the thermal history of the IGM. We demonstrate the successful transfer of both longitudinal and longitudinal-emittance (LiE) using a novel radio-frequency structure designed for LiE manipulation. This experiment marks a significant advancement in LiE studies, building upon prior successful transverse emittance transfer conducted in 2019. The observed longitudinal-emittance transfer holds substantial promise for future applications within the Higgs factory initiative. Furthermore, these findings are directly applicable to other accelerators, such as the International Linear Collider, which utilizes a similar cavity design for longitudinal beam compression. This specific cavity, known as the emittance exchange cavity (E2C), is currently under construction. Our results provide the essential data required for the final design of the E2C. Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive model to describe the combined transfer of transverse and longitudinal emittances, which will be presented in this paper. This model is applicable to any emittance exchange cavity and is expected to be widely used in the design of future devices. The work was conducted at the CERN Accelerator School. Human trajectory prediction is a critical research area with significant real-world applications, particularly for autonomous agents like self-driving vehicles and robots that must anticipate future paths to avoid collisions and plan effectively. However, predicting the movements of other road users is inherently difficult due to human behavioral traits such as social forces, intention changes, and diverse cultural backgrounds. This paper introduces a novel method that enhances prediction accuracy by incorporating social forces and detecting shifts in human intention. The approach employs a sequential model that iteratively refines predictions, utilizing a sliding window mechanism to adapt to changing cultural contexts. Furthermore, the model rethinks its prior outputs based on the latest observed data, ensuring that recent observations are integrated into the final forecast. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/SSR.

This study investigates two distinct metrics for characterizing the complexity of the critical dynamics within a class of spin-glass models. We contend that these metrics offer complementary perspectives: the first defines complexity as the ratio of the system's entropy to its total degrees of freedom, while the second treats complexity as a function of entropy and degrees of freedom separately. Applying the first metric to the standard critical dynamics of the one-dimensional p-spin model (with $p>3$) and the 3-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model reveals a phase diagram with two regions: a simpler Regge-pole dominated phase and a more complex Regge-zero dominated phase. In contrast, the application of the second metric to the same models yields a phase diagram where the boundary between these two dynamic regimes aligns precisely with the phase diagram produced by the first metric. These findings suggest that the two metrics capture distinct aspects of dynamical complexity and motivate further research into their physical significance. Finally, we propose that the equivalence observed here between the two metric-based phase diagrams may extend to other systems, such as the mean-field Ising ferromagnet. Specifically, we demonstrate that both metrics identify a boundary separating a simpler, non-aging phase from a more complex aging phase in this system. However, the boundary defined by the second metric lies significantly closer to the phase transition point than that produced by the first metric. This result underscores the potential of the second metric to provide a more refined description of dynamical complexity in various systems. These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations and analytical calculations. This paper introduces a new research initiative focused on investigating and enhancing human-swarm interactions through the integration of advanced hand gesture recognition. This approach leverages the natural expressiveness of human hand movements to facilitate intuitive control over swarms. By employing deep learning-based hand gesture recognition, our proposed framework enables the real-time identification of complex, user-specific hand trajectories. This capability ensures that human intentions can be accurately interpreted even when hand movements are performed at varying speeds. Furthermore, the system's distributed architecture allows for real-time gesture recognition across a network of devices, thereby supporting a wide range of applications. The study begins by reviewing existing methods for human-swarm interaction, followed by a detailed examination of deep learning-based gesture recognition. Subsequently, a proof-of-concept application is presented to demonstrate the system's effectiveness in enabling real-time, distributed hand gesture recognition. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions. Overall, this work aims to establish a foundation for developing more intuitive and natural human-swarm interaction paradigms. This study demonstrates that ground-state assembly can be achieved for a one-dimensional Hubbard model utilizing a carefully designed counterdiabatic (CD) protocol. We derive an exact CD field that ensures adiabatic evolution from an uncorrelated initial state to the target ground state of the Hubbard model. Furthermore, we show that a variational approach, based on a restricted CD field derived from a specific subset of cluster expansion fields, yields results comparable to the exact method. Finally, we confirm that the system remains robust against both dephasing and CD errors. These findings indicate that the variational CD protocol is highly effective for the Hubbard model and holds significant potential for broader applications. Additionally, the variational CD field employed here is anticipated to be valuable for other quantum field theories. We introduce a unified theoretical framework that integrates laser-plasma physics with photon-photon science. This approach enables the systematic investigation of how laser intensity, photon energy, and photon-photon interaction cross-sections are interconnected. Our findings indicate that photon-photon interactions can be observed at laser intensities below 1 GW/cm² when the resulting cross-section is sufficiently large. This optimal regime is achieved through resonant interactions involving four Inverse Bremsstrahlung (IB) photons or one IB and three Nonlinear Compton (NC) photons. Furthermore, we demonstrate that photon-photon scattering can be detected using a laser with an intensity of 1 GW/cm² by employing a photon source that generates three NC photons and one IB photon. These results establish a comprehensive framework for exploring photon-photon science within the context of laser-plasma interactions. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental scheme to measure the differential cross-section of photon-photon scattering. This proposal utilizes a laser with an intensity of 1 GW/cm² and a plasma with a density of 10¹⁸ cm⁻³, which can be achieved with current laser and plasma technology. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for the upcoming photon-photon science experiment at the European XFEL. Furthermore, we have made our code publicly available to facilitate the design of future photon-photon experiments. This study examines the impact of the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter $m_{12}$ on the Higgs boson mass within a CP-conserving, non-degenerate two-Higgs-doublet model. While the Standard Model predicts a Higgs mass of approximately 125 GeV, we demonstrate that a lower bound of roughly 100 GeV persists even when $m_{12}$ is negative and large. We also analyze the model's phenomenological implications, specifically its ability to enhance diphoton production rates and generate a non-zero Higgs boson width. Furthermore, we explore the model's capacity to generate a baryon asymmetry in the early universe through a CP-conserving mechanism, showing that this scenario necessitates a large $m_{12}$ value. Finally, we establish lower limits for the masses of the additional charged and heavy neutral Higgs bosons. Our findings indicate that the heavy neutral Higgs mass is bounded below by approximately 100 GeV, whereas the mass of the heavier charged Higgs boson can be significantly lower. We establish that the relation between a relational schema and an RDF graph can be viewed as a form of query, and we demonstrate that when shapes are applicable, this relation can be expressed as a single Datalog program. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which the RDF representation can be derived directly from SQL queries over the relational tables. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for implementing data transfer from RDBMS to RDF within an RDBMS environment. The paper includes illustrative examples and concludes with an outline of open research questions. These results have been implemented in the open-source RDF4J system, which is available as a library for use within RDBMS. Convex regression and boundary estimation are fundamental tasks across numerous disciplines, including computer science, engineering, and the biological and physical sciences. These methods serve as the foundation for analyzing functional relationships between variables when only empirical data is available. This paper introduces pyStoNED, a Python library designed for convex regression and boundary estimation. The library offers versatile, efficient, and user-friendly tools for fitting a wide range of convex functions, such as non-decreasing, non-increasing, and convex functions. Additionally, pyStoNED supports specialized regressions like isotonic regression and provides models for convex boundary estimation. The paper details the library's architecture, outlines its primary features, and demonstrates its application through examples. pyStoNED is accessible at https://github.com/SciTools/stoned. This integration ensures compatibility with other SciTools libraries, including scikit-learn (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn) and scikit-image (https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image). Furthermore, pyStoNED is included in the Anaconda distribution, a comprehensive, free, and open-source platform for data science and analytics, which can be downloaded from https://www.anaconda.com/products/distribution. This study investigates the production of top quark pairs accompanied by a scalar particle $\phi$, which subsequently decays into a pair of soft, massive, long-lived particles. We examine scenarios where these scalar particles decay into either a pair of heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) or a pair of dark matter particles (DM). In both cases, the secondary particles are assumed to be detected via their hadronic interactions within a dedicated detector situated downstream of the primary interaction point. We demonstrate that these scenarios can be probed with sensitivities reaching the TeV scale, utilizing approximately 300 fb$^{-1}$ of LHC data combined with the new detector. Furthermore, we show that these models can account for the HUNES collaboration's null results from their search for sterile neutrinos at the SHiP experiment. We also explore the potential of these models to explain the excess of events observed by the LHCb experiment in the $\nu_\mu$-induced dimuon channel. Finally, we discuss the advantages of combining LHC searches with a dedicated downstream detector and outline the prospects for testing these models at future facilities. This work is part of the initiative to develop a downstream detector concept for the High-Luminosity LHC. The proposed design is currently being evaluated as an alternative to a muon collider and will be presented at the International Muon Accelerator Conference (MAC) in 2022. Few-shot analysis, which enables reasoning over novel concepts using a minimal number of examples, is a highly sought-after capability in Natural Language Processing. While current few-shot methods rely on in-context learning, they often fail to generalize to complex tasks. This study explores whether pretraining on concepts across diverse modalities can facilitate reasoning on new topics through similar mechanisms. We introduce UniLM-4, a multi-modal model that pretrains on text, images, and graphs across various tasks. UniLM-4 demonstrates that pretraining on a broad array of concepts significantly enhances few-shot few-task reasoning, surpassing both specialized baselines and larger multi-modal models. Furthermore, we find that the text component of UniLM-4 is primarily responsible for this performance gain, indicating that integrating multi-modal pretraining with extensive corpus pretraining yields the most substantial improvements. Finally, we examine the UniLM-4 model's internal representations to explain how multi-modal data aids few-shot reasoning. Our findings reveal that the model leverages multi-modal data to develop representations that are more robust to distributional shifts, thereby improving few-shot performance. We also demonstrate that the hierarchical architecture of UniLM-4 allows for the analysis of multi-modal interactions, offering deeper insights into how different pretraining strategies influence the model's representations. The UniLM-4 model and its associated analysis are accessible at https://github.com/google-research/unilm. Our code and data will be released shortly. This research was conducted while the authors were at Google Research.

This study evaluates the current state of automated speech recognition (ASR) for German. We present a new English-German comparative analysis based on the latest versions of ESpeech and Mozilla's ASR systems. Our results indicate that these tools now achieve English-level accuracy, reaching CER@C=1 of 82.4% and 81.5% respectively. Additionally, we examine the impact of language-specific data augmentation on performance, demonstrating that it yields significant improvements for both ASRs. Furthermore, we analyze the effects of varying data splits and speaker demographics, finding that while ASR performance is generally robust, it is more sensitive to speaker gender than to age. Finally, we provide a comprehensive overview of German ASR performance across diverse speaker groups and domains, covering data sizes from 10 to 100 hours. Our findings suggest that 100-hour training corpora are necessary to match the performance of commercial ASR tools. We determined the effective temperatures and surface gravities for 31 of these stars. Additionally, we identified 11 stars exhibiting double-peaked line profiles, indicating they are in a highly evolved stage. Finally, we compiled a comprehensive list of all Be-type stars in 30 Doradus, including their spectral classification, effective temperature, surface gravity, rotational velocity, and luminosity class. This study investigates the text standardization task, which involves normalizing misspelled, misscategorized, and malformed source text into a consistent target form. We introduce a data augmentation strategy designed to enhance the performance of neural machine translation models in standardizing inverse text normalization outputs. Our approach leverages the statistical relationship between language models and translation models, utilizing the latter to standardize source text based on translations generated by the former. This method enables data-driven inverse standardization without requiring a specific corpus of erroneous text. We demonstrate that our model significantly surpasses previous data-driven methods and achieves performance comparable to supervised models, even when trained on low-resource languages. Furthermore, we show that the model generalizes effectively to out-of-domain datasets. Finally, we apply this model to a real-world scenario in a customer support chatbot, confirming that it yields substantial improvements in support ticket classification accuracy. This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn type inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Robin problem for the Hermite operator $\mathcal{H}_\gamma(u) = -u'' + (\gamma|x|^2 - 2\gamma)u$ defined on a bounded, connected open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with a sufficiently regular boundary. The analysis demonstrates that the optimal domain is a ball centered at the origin. Furthermore, we provide a detailed asymptotic analysis of the Robin eigenvalue constant as $\gamma \to +\infty$. These findings extend the work of Brasco, Broglia, and Hencl (2020) regarding the standard Hermite operator (the case $\gamma = 1$). Additionally, we derive a corresponding asymptotic formula for the first eigenvalue of the Robin problem. This formula generalizes the result obtained by Brasco, Broglia, and Hencl for $\gamma = 1$ and accurately reflects the behavior of the first eigenvalue in the limit $\gamma \to +\infty$. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of the constants involved. In this context, we introduce a novel constant that had not previously been studied. We prove that this constant is optimal and derive a differential inequality for it. These results are achieved through an extensive analysis of the first eigenvalue of the Robin problem on a half-line. This approach marks a significant advancement over the standard Sturm-Liouville analysis, which had been the primary tool in this area. Our work also expands upon the findings of Brasco, Broglia, and Hencl (2020) concerning the standard Hermite operator. Specifically, we show that the optimal shape is no longer necessarily a half-line, thereby providing a more complete picture of the problem. Recent studies indicate that DNN outputs can be modeled as functions within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs), offering a promising avenue for analyzing DNN behavior. This paper introduces a new framework for generating synthetic speech that integrates social speaker characteristics, specifically gender and age. By utilizing a two-stage approach, we first create social noise—audio segments featuring the desired social trait—and subsequently merge this noise with the target speech. To ensure the generated social noise aligns accurately with the original speech, we apply a masking function. Our experimental results indicate that this method successfully injects the intended social qualities into the speech. Furthermore, evaluations using the MOS test and the Social Quality of Speech (SOS) metric demonstrate that listeners can effectively distinguish the injected social traits. Additionally, our approach yields a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.81, confirming that the quality of the resulting synthetic speech remains high. Finally, the method's simplicity allows it to be readily extended to incorporate other paralinguistic features. The code and data required to replicate these findings are accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/Injecting-Social-Qualities-in-Synthetic-Speech. Keywords: Speech Synthesis, Social Qualities, Synthetic Speech, Masking Function.

This work presents two new classes of polyphase Golay complementary sets (GCSs) and examines their autocorrelation properties. The first class is generated by applying the Hadamard product to a base GCS, resulting in a set where the total autocorrelation is delta-function centered. The second class arises from the modulation of a base GCS; however, in this scenario, the total autocorrelation is not strictly delta-function concentrated, though it maintains low sidelobe levels. Additionally, we explore applications for GCS-based orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems, specifically addressing pilot design and channel estimation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that these proposed GCS-based pilot patterns outperform existing designs in terms of estimation performance. Furthermore, our proposed GCS-based channel estimators surpass current state-of-the-art methods, yielding significant improvements in both performance and computational efficiency. Finally, we illustrate how GCS-based precoding can enhance the sum rate of multi-user MIMO systems. The proposed GCS families include polyphase Golay sequences, all-length Thue-Morse GCSs, and polyphase Tukey GCSs. Notably, the Thue-Morse and Tukey constructions offer the flexibility to choose from multiple GCSs with varying sizes and parameters. This selection capability allows system designers to balance performance against other critical factors, such as peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and complexity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply GCSs to GCS-based OFDM and GCS-based precoding. The paper concludes with a comparison of GCS-based GCSs against Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequences, which are currently the standard for OFDM pilot design. The analysis covers both frequency-selective and frequency-flat channel models, as well as single-user and multi-user MIMO configurations. Results indicate that GCS-based pilot designs generally outperform ZC-based alternatives. In terms of precoding, while ZC sequences yield superior results in single-user MIMO, GCSs achieve better performance in multi-user MIMO settings. Overall, GCS-based GCSs offer the advantage of being available in a wide range of lengths, providing greater design flexibility compared to ZC sequences. Detecting alterations in remote sensing imagery is crucial for numerous applications, including disaster management, military surveillance, and environmental monitoring. While numerous algorithms exist for this purpose, they often struggle with either high false alarm rates or excessive computational costs. This paper introduces a novel feature combination approach that integrates multiple features to enhance the detection of unsupervised image alterations. We developed a deep convolutional autoencoder architecture to extract features from spectral and spatial dimensions, which were subsequently merged to form an altered feature map. This combined map was utilized to train a binary classifier for alteration detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the study includes an analysis of how feature combination impacts the performance of various deep convolutional autoencoder structures. The implementation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/Unsupervised-Feature-Combination-for-Alteration-Detection. This study examines the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids, utilizing both simulation data and simple fluid models. We demonstrate that viscosity scales with the inverse power of entropy, where the power-law exponent for Rong interactions (two hard spheres connected by a soft spring) aligns with experimental and simulation results for polymeric systems. Furthermore, we find that the entropy-viscosity power is independent of the system's density. These findings suggest that residual entropy serves as a reliable predictor for the transport properties of molecular fluids. Additionally, we show that the entropy-transport scaling for model interactions can be derived from the corresponding scaling for atomic systems. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for polymeric systems. The analysis was conducted using the Parrinello-Raspano method for molecular fluids and the Nosé-Hoover thermostat for atomic systems. We outline a cyclical cosmology grounded in the $\Lambda CDM$ model, where each cycle comprises an expansion phase followed by a contraction. The universe's fate hinges on the Hubble constant and the density parameter; if the product remains below unity, contraction halts and reverses into expansion, initiating a new cycle. Conversely, if this product exceeds unity, the universe undergoes recollapse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dark energy can be naturally interpreted as a residual form of matter from the preceding expansion cycle. This interpretation offers an alternative resolution to the sign problem associated with the equation of state for dark energy. Finally, we illustrate that the cyclical $\Lambda CDM$ framework can be readily adapted to incorporate additional physical phenomena. This paper investigates the superdeterministic hidden-variable model known as the Invariant-set hypothesis, which posits that quantum nonlocality arises because the shared initial conditions for Alice's and Bob's measurements within their respective past light cones are restricted to a self-similar fractal set located inside the black hole forming at the universe's Big Bang origin. We demonstrate that this hypothesis is compatible with all Bell-type experiments, including those involving spin and polarization, provided the distribution of the shared hidden variable is conditioned on the spacetime coordinates of Alice's and Bob's events. Furthermore, we establish that the model adheres to the fundamental principles of relativity and the conservation of energy and momentum. Finally, we outline the methodology for deriving the quantum probability amplitudes for Alice's and Bob's outcomes from these initial shared conditions, a task that requires the application of the Planck-Einstein de Broglie-Bohm pilot-wave theory within the context of a black hole. This approach also enables the derivation of the mass-energy relation and the Schrödinger equation from the same initial data. Consequently, the superdeterministic Invariant-set hypothesis offers a unified framework that simultaneously explains the quantum behavior of atoms and the classical dynamics of black holes. Additionally, we examine the hypothesis's capacity to address the measurement problem and its alignment with the holographic principle. Ultimately, this model provides a deterministic, local, and rational explanation for the phenomena of quantum mechanics. The detailed derivations of the probability amplitudes will be presented in a subsequent paper. The present work serves as a preliminary examination of the hypothesis, with the goal of inspiring further research into its validity. This work investigates dimer models on a two-dimensional lattice subject to a U(1) gauge field. We establish a rigorous correspondence between the dimer partition function and the fermion determinant, extending previous findings which were limited to cases with vanishing gauge fields. Additionally, we examine the statistical characteristics of dimer configurations within gauge fields that correspond to a massless Dirac fermion. We demonstrate that these dimers exhibit a logarithmic correlation length and display conformal invariance, characterized by a central charge of $c=0$. Furthermore, we analyze the dimer behavior in a 't Hooff background, where the dimers exhibit power-law correlations with an exponent determined by the gauge field. Finally, we extend these findings to the more complex scenario of massive fermions. These results offer a rigorous foundation for the established link between critical dimer models and Dirac fermions and enable the exploration of novel statistical phenomena. The study utilizes a rigorous framework grounded in high and low-temperature expansions, complemented by numerical simulations. The paper also includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the fermion correspondence for dimer models on a lattice with defects. Group lasso methods are extensively utilized for variable selection in high-dimensional regression, yet they face challenges when applied to categorical data due to the necessity of encoding such variables into dummy variables. This paper introduces two group lasso formulations designed for categorical data, alongside two strategies to enhance their performance. The first approach involves a straightforward modification of the standard group lasso, while the second employs a multivariate normal prior for nominal dummy variables, thereby fostering correlation among them. We demonstrate that the second approach yields superior performance compared to the first. Furthermore, we propose two techniques to further improve outcomes: the first restricts the regression coefficients of dummy variables representing a single category to a simplex, and the second reduces the dimensionality of the prior distribution used to estimate group effects. Our selection of the optimal formulation and strategy relies on a novel penalized categorical data likelihood. Through simulations and a real-world case study, we show that the proposed methods yield more accurate variable selection and superior prediction accuracy compared to existing approaches. Embedded systems are increasingly vital in critical sectors like automotive, aerospace, and medical devices, where high reliability and safety are non-negotiable. However, the growing complexity of modern embedded platforms makes manual design and verification increasingly difficult and error-prone. To address this, we introduce T-Visor, a new hypervisor designed to manage mixed-criticality real-time workloads by integrating high-importance, hard real-time tasks with low-importance, soft real-time tasks on x86 hardware. Leveraging Intel's VT-x hardware virtualization extensions, T-Visor enables the concurrent execution of multiple Virtual Machines (VMs), each hosting a distinct set of tasks. To ensure high-importance VMs meet their deadlines, T-Visor implements a mechanism that prevents deadline misses by utilizing a real-time operating system kernel and specialized real-time hypervisor components. Conversely, to guarantee the progress of low-importance VMs, the system employs a novel preemption mechanism that allows soft real-time tasks to preempt high-importance VMs whenever the latter are guaranteed to meet their deadlines. We have validated the feasibility and performance of T-Visor through extensive experiments. The results demonstrate that it achieves a preemption latency under 100 microseconds and supports the execution of up to 16 VMs. Furthermore, T-Visor outperforms state-of-the-art hypervisors, reducing runtime by 10% to 20% and improving CPU utilization by 10% to 20%. Finally, we have integrated T-Visor with the open-source QEMU emulator, enabling its deployment on standard Linux systems. This integration facilitates the development and testing of embedded systems without the need for physical hardware. We have also evaluated the overhead introduced by T-Visor, confirming that it remains negligible. Consequently, T-Visor offers a promising solution for the efficient and reliable execution of mixed-criticality real-time systems. We introduce a novel panoramic stitching approach grounded in image warping. Unlike traditional methods, our strategy prioritizes warping over feature matching, thereby eliminating the need for complex and computationally expensive matching algorithms. Our method is built upon three core components: (1) a robust prior derived from the assumption that most panoramic images are vertically aligned due to gravity; (2) an image warping technique that leverages this gravitational assumption to enhance stitching quality; and (3) an optimization framework designed to determine the optimal rotation angle for seamless image blending. This study examines a system of two groups of phase oscillators, where the heterogeneity within each group is distributed uniformly. We analytically determine the conditions enabling the emergence of two distinct chimera states: one featuring two incoherent clusters alongside two coherent clusters, and another with three incoherent clusters and one coherent cluster. Furthermore, we offer insights into the formation of these states and validate our findings through numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that these chimera variants can arise in systems with a symmetric coupling matrix and uniform heterogeneity distribution, a scenario previously thought impossible. Additionally, we observe that these multiple-incluster chimera states are highly robust, persisting even when the coupling matrix is strongly perturbed. Finally, we show that these states can be induced by a small, periodic drive applied to the groups, a finding with significant implications for controlling chimeras in networks. This research expands the existing understanding of chimera states in systems characterized by symmetric couplings and uniform heterogeneity distributions.

Keywords: Kuramoto model, chimera states, heterogeneity, periodic drive, control.

Although model-based control methods are generally more resilient than reinforcement learning (RL) due to their superior sample efficiency, the inherent inaccuracies of learned models can cause a significant drop in performance. This study introduces a model-driven approach that integrates the robustness of traditional model-based techniques with the adaptability of RL. The proposed framework employs a probabilistic model to account for uncertainties in both dynamics and sensing, utilizing these estimates to direct a policy search that optimizes task performance. This method is versatile, applicable to various domains including continuous control, navigation, and object manipulation. The resulting model-driven policy exhibits greater sample efficiency and demonstrates more robust performance when deployed on a real robot. The framework's effectiveness is validated across three challenging scenarios: difficult navigation tasks, continuous control, and complex manipulation. We build a symmetric monoidal category, termed \emph{multi-layer diagrams}, extending the category of finite sets and maps with suspensions and !-functors, and define a symmetric monoidal functor, termed \emph{H-sliciation}, from diagrams to singly-layered diagrams (which resemble finite sets). We demonstrate that the free multi-layer diagram category satisfying the suspension and ! axioms is equivalent to the category of commutative \emph{H-sliciation rings}, thereby establishing an algebraic characterization of H-sliciation rings. Furthermore, we prove that the category of commutative rings is equivalent to the category of multi-layer diagrams equipped with a commutative \emph{layered !} axiom, and that the H-sliciation ring structure on a ring $R$ corresponds precisely to its structure as a ring of slices. This work serves as a diagrammatic reformulation of our previous paper, \emph{The higher slice category and its relation to spectra}, where we showed that the higher slice category is equivalent to the category of commutative $H$-slice rings. In this paper, we provide an alternative characterization of the higher slice category using multi-layer diagrams and establish its equivalence with the category of commutative $H$-slice rings. Additionally, we demonstrate that the higher slice category, when regarded as a symmetric monoidal category via the Cartesian product, is equivalent to the category of commutative rings. Consequently, we derive two distinct monoidal structures on the category of commutative $H$-slice rings: one induced by the smash product and the other by the Cartesian product. These findings offer a new perspective on the higher slice category and its connection to spectra. Our results also contribute to the ongoing effort to characterize the infinite slice category, which is equivalent to the category of commutative $H$-slice rings with unity. We extend the notion of multi-layer diagrams to \emph{multi-fiber diagrams} and show that the infinite slice category can be characterized as the category of commutative multi-fiber rings. The paper concludes with several open questions and conjectures. This research was conducted as part of the second author's PhD thesis at the University of Oxford. We demonstrate that the refracted entropy [arXiv:1906.02611] offers a significant enhancement to the entanglement entropy formula within tensor network methods for modeling gravitational systems. We illustrate this improved approach by calculating the entropy of a single interval in a $(1+1)$-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) represented via MERA networks. Our findings align with the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of an eternal BTZ black hole, successfully accounting for the bulk minimal surface that intersects the network's boundary. Furthermore, we compute the entropy of a double interval in a $(1+1)$-dimensional CFT using MERA, yielding results consistent with the bulk entropy derived from the double-wedge double-cut geometry. Finally, we extend these calculations to Peierls-Mermin-Wagner (PMW) tensor networks, which represent a $(2+1)$-dimensional CFT and correspond to the near-extremal BTZ black hole in three-dimensional gravity. This work establishes a foundation for future investigations into the black hole information paradox. Physical patterns emerging within dynamic systems are frequently disrupted by inherent noise, a phenomenon that can be modeled using random fields. A prominent example is the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation, which describes surface growth and is defined by stochastic partial differential equations. This study demonstrates that the KPZ equation, when subjected to a spatially dependent growth rate, generates a random field with correlations that persist indefinitely. This contrasts with the standard KPZ equation, which produces transient correlations. We provide numerical evidence supporting this finding and establish a link between the sustained correlations and the statistical moments of the growth rate. Furthermore, we confirm these findings using the Langevin equation, a fundamental model for Brownian motion. This research expands the scope of enduring random field correlations beyond models like the Ising equation, which feature uniform relaxation times, to encompass more complex scenarios. The implications of these findings are significant for understanding long-term memory in random systems, the stability of self-organized patterns, and the mechanisms driving evolutionary adaptation. Additionally, we propose a method for creating stable, self-organized patterns in both biological and technological systems by utilizing spatially varying growth rates. This approach is demonstrated through a biological case study involving the spatial distribution of bacteria. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of the broader implications of these results. The source code is available at: https://github.com/alexei-korolkov/Spatially-modulated-growth. Supplementary information can be found at: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-82807-4. Keywords: Stochastic dynamics, Growth models, Evolution, Self-organization, Bacterial growth.

Furthermore, the study examines the parameter space of the three-dimensional generalized Hénon map and analyzes its dynamical behavior by employing a novel visualization technique for the parameter space itself. This approach facilitates the identification of parameter sets yielding interesting pullbacks and provides a comprehensive overview of the parameter space's structure. We examine the gravitational holonomy defined by a connection derived from the metric and the frame field. We demonstrate that the "trivial" character of this connection is independent of the parameter used to resolve the determinant issue in the framing. Furthermore, we establish that this holonomy is invariant under small variations of the framing and represents the unique interpretation of gravitational holonomy. Consequently, this result underscores the significance of the trivial connection concept, which is essential for the proper formulation of geometric quantum gravity. Finally, we provide a concise discussion of the free-space connection and its associated holonomy. Keywords: gravitational connection, gravitational holonomy, geometric quantum gravity. The concept of gravitational holonomy is central to geometric quantum gravity, serving as the primary observable in canonical quantum gravity and as the fundamental building block for loop quantum gravity. This framework relies on the use of Ashtekar variables, which involve a complex connection derived from the spacetime metric and a real connection generated by the self-dual extension of the metric connection. This led to the proposal of a nontrivial connection as the foundation for gravitational holonomy. In 2003, however, this perspective was challenged. Multivariate Greene-Nijenhuis-Wilf (GNW) sampling is a generalized riffle shuffle that incorporates a distribution to control the likelihood of each shuffle. This study examines the multivariate GNW distribution specifically for shuffles involving three piles. We demonstrate that hook lengths within shapes generated by this distribution, when using three piles, cannot be multiplied by 2 or 3. Furthermore, we establish a distributional equivalence between certain shapes created with three piles under this sampling method and those formed using two piles with a specific alternative sampling method. Finally, we derive a closed-form expression for the count of valid multivariate GNW shuffles applicable to this latter case. These findings facilitate a more efficient computation of the total number of multivariate GNW shuffles and, consequently, the total number of Young tableaux associated with this distribution. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the distribution that maximizes the probability of multivariate GNW sampling. This specific distribution allows for a closed-form calculation of the probability of any given shape, enabling the determination of the most probable shape for a fixed number of piles and a fixed total number of cards. We also address the existence of local maxima for any number of piles and a fixed total card count, providing a characterization of these maxima and their relationship to the overall most probable shape. Finally, we characterize the distribution that minimizes the probability of any given shape. For an even number of piles, we identify the most probable shape and describe its relationship to other local minima, while also considering the case with an odd number of piles. Throughout this work, we frequently utilize the concept of semistandard shifted skew tableaux. We provide a characterization of these objects and demonstrate that the number of such tableaux of a fixed shape remains constant regardless of the size of the shifted skew region. The Larmor clock method measures tunneling time by tracking the precession of a particle's spin as it traverses a barrier. This study demonstrates that spin disturbances accumulate during tunneling, enabling the determination of the tunneling duration through the analysis of these rotational effects. The findings are validated by comparing them with recent experimental data. The associated Python code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi1993/TunnelingTime. Furthermore, we extend the model to scenarios involving spin-orbit coupling and non-rectangular barriers, revealing that spin rotation remains a significant phenomenon in these contexts. These results offer a novel perspective on tunneling time and provide a new approach to studying spin dynamics within spin-dependent tunneling systems. Using the light-cone wave function formalism, we determine the dominant twist twist distribution functions (TDFs) for P-wave mesons. By applying the QCD equations of motion to the nonlocal bilinear quark-antiquark operators, we derive relations between the moments of the nonlocal bilinears. Consequently, the P-wave meson TDFs can be expressed through a single universal P-wave TDF. This finding offers a novel perspective on the internal quark-antiquark structure of P-wave mesons. Furthermore, we calculate the moments of the twist distribution functions for P-wave charmonia, which are subsequently utilized to compute the polarized form factors for the $^{3}P_{J}$ ($J=0,1,2$) transitions of charmonium. Our results indicate that the contributions of the two quark-antiquark helicity configurations to the polarized form factors are comparable in magnitude. Additionally, we observe that the polarized form factors for the $J=0,1,2$ P-wave transitions of charmonium are not equal, thereby confirming that P-wave mesons do not possess the internal structure of a "point-like" object. Finally, we demonstrate that the derived relations among P-wave TDFs offer a potential solution to the enigmatic "missing momentum" problem in proton structure. These findings are expected to be valuable for the ongoing LHCb measurements of P-wave meson internal structures. This study serves as a precursor to our future investigations into the twist distribution functions of $B$ mesons. The corresponding theoretical framework is also applicable to other nonrelativistic bound states. This work is dedicated to Professor Shoujue Zhu on the occasion of his 90th birthday. We demonstrate that a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) can function as a quantum switch operating within the nonlinear regime. Specifically, a beam splitter feeding the system with equal inputs results in a linear regime where all output particles follow a binomial distribution, whereas introducing a slight two-body interaction shifts the system into a nonlinear regime, generating a macroscopic number of output particles with a multinomial distribution. This behavior stems from the quantum correlations established between the two input modes at the beam splitter. We illustrate this phenomenon using both a single-mode nonlinear crystal and a double-mode one. Furthermore, we show that the transition from linear to nonlinear operation can be tuned by adjusting the strength of the two-body interaction. This capability to control the transition is particularly significant for BECs, as they typically exhibit weak nonlinearities. Our findings suggest that nonlinear quantum switches based on BECs could serve as essential components in quantum information processing. Additionally, we demonstrate that these switches can generate output particles with nonclassical statistics, such as sub-Poissonian distributions. This capability is particularly valuable for quantum metrology, where such particles enable the construction of ultra-sensitive sensors. We highlight that the nonclassical statistics of the output particles can be adjusted by varying the two-body interaction strength. Finally, we show that the quantum correlations of the output particles can be quantified using the negativity measure. This allows for the characterization of the quantum resources present in the BEC-based quantum switch, which could be utilized in quantum information processing tasks. We illustrate this by employing the BEC-based quantum switch to generate a wide range of entangled states, including Bell-diagonal states, Bell states, Werner states, and isotropic states. These states are crucial for quantum information processing tasks such as quantum teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum key distribution. Our findings could pave the way for the development of BEC-based quantum devices, which could be integrated into quantum information processing architectures. This would enable the realization of quantum technologies based on these devices, thereby advancing the field of quantum science and technology. Our findings could also contribute to the broader goal of harnessing quantum mechanics for practical applications. For instance, we show that the quantum switch can be used to control the flow of quantum information, which could be useful for quantum communication and quantum computing. We examine the BMS algebra and its extension by negative-depth generators, which correspond to local localizations of Minkowski space. Leveraging this structure, we demonstrate that every Minkowski localizing Vasiliev theory possesses a Gaiotto–Rastelli (GR) symmetry, characterized by an infinite set of soft charges that commute with Poincaré transformations. Furthermore, we establish that all such Vasiliev theories fall into one of two categories: either they are equivalent to a GR theory or they factor through one. We also outline the construction of dual localizing theories and briefly touch upon the associated Kac-Moody algebras. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the construction of physical Hilbert spaces for these localizing Minkowski theories. This framework enables the realization of local states with arbitrarily soft support, thereby extending the concept of BMS primary states beyond the S$^2$ boundary at infinity. We anticipate that localizing states will play a crucial role in the study of localizing duals to standard holographic Vasiliev models. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between localizing and semi-holographic double soft theoric models. Finally, we explore the potential of localizing Minkowski theories as a novel class of local quantum field theories. In this context, localizing primary states emerge as a new class of observables, offering a fresh perspective on locality. This approach may offer a solution to the longstanding issue of defining observables in de Sitter space. Finally, we examine the localizing extension of recent findings by Barnich, Gl\'oz\'{i}k, and Trautman concerning the action of BMS charges on black hole states. We illustrate that localizing primary states can be utilized to construct a new class of black hole states that exhibit soft support at arbitrary depths. These findings suggest a pathway toward a localizable extension of the double soft theorem within de Sitter space. Overfitting remains a persistent challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are updated incrementally with new data, a scenario common in online environments. This paper introduces a new method called Online Ensemble Neural Architecture (OENA), which enables the creation of a compact, global model by distilling an ensemble of continuously learned models without sacrificing performance. OENA achieves this by employing a novel attention mechanism that assigns dynamic weights to specific regions of the global neural network based on whether an input instance is old or new. Experimental results demonstrate that OENA significantly reduces the performance degradation typically associated with online learning while maintaining a model size comparable to a single baseline. Furthermore, OENA exhibits robustness against concept drift, a critical factor in real-world applications. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyungkim/OENA. This paper introduces a deep belief network (DBN) approach designed to automatically categorize intestinal worms from digital worm images. The process begins with extracting key features using the Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) descriptor, which effectively captures the distribution of local gradient orientations. These features are then classified into three distinct worm categories using a multi-class SVM classifier integrated within the DBN architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an average classification accuracy of 90.66% across the three classes, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the study includes a comparative analysis of various feature extraction methods and worm image datasets. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/rauf-ahmed/Intestinal-Worms-Categorization-using-Deep-Belief-Networks. This study addresses the equilibrium strategies for investment and reinsurance within a non-zero-sum game framework, alongside risk minimization (optimal capital allocation) and surplus optimization (optimal investment) problems. These models are developed under regime-switching conditions, where market parameters fluctuate based on an underlying Markov chain. The authors derive closed-form solutions for the investment and reinsurance strategies, specifically accounting for the impact of regime shifts. Furthermore, numerical simulations are performed to assess the stability of these strategies when market parameters are unknown. The findings indicate that while these closed-form solutions are highly sensitive to variations in model parameters, they remain relatively stable across different economic regimes. Additionally, the numerical results demonstrate that the proposed strategies are robust against model misspecification. Finally, the study concludes that the proposed investment and reinsurance strategies are effective in reducing the volatility of the insurance company's surplus. This paper introduces a novel flight controller for quadrotors, designed to ensure both steady and fluent maneuvers by integrating a high-order filter with a low-order feedback loop. The high-order loop, which includes a feed-forward component, is responsible for fluent flight performance, whereas the low-order loop, utilizing a simple Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, maintains steady flight. To achieve this, we developed a new optimization algorithm that combines the strengths of two established methods: the Simplex algorithm and the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Davidson (BFGD) algorithm. This hybrid approach ensures rapid convergence to a global optimum while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, the parameters of the PID controller are automatically tuned using the proposed algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that the quadrotor equipped with this controller achieves both steady and fluent flight, outperforming conventional PID controllers in terms of settling time and accuracy. Furthermore, the parameters derived from our method are more robust against external disturbances. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/taehyuklee/PIDA. Keywords: Quadrotor, High-order filter, Low-order feedback, Feed-forward, Genetic filter, Simplex algorithm, BFGD algorithm, Robustness.

We introduce a model for low-energy pion-nucleon interactions that adheres to chiral symmetry and its spontaneous breaking, while also satisfying current algebra constraints. This framework is defined by a minimal set of parameters that can be derived from low-energy experimental data. Additionally, these parameters enable a prediction of the pion-nucleon scattering amplitude at the physical mass within the $s$-channel. We also examine the implications of our findings for low-energy constants relevant to nuclear physics. Finally, we analyze the results of our calculations for low-energy constants, form factors, and the pion-nucleon sigma term. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of our approach for the existence of a scalar resonance in the pion-nucleon system. Finally, we present our predictions for the $s$-channel partial wave amplitudes at physical masses.

Furthermore, the PXPE reconstruction is observed to be independent of the track's pT. These outcomes suggest that PXPE reconstruction is viable for future LHC runs. Additionally, the study confirms that PXPE tracks can be successfully reconstructed from both single- and double-hit clusters. This study employs machine learning to analyze the morphology of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies at redshifts $0.0 < z < 1.0$, utilizing deep imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-W120). We utilized the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-Wide) to identify 1,000 $z<1$ AGN hosts with absolute magnitudes $M_{AB} < -23.0$ mag, cross-matching them with the Catalina Real-Time Transient Survey (CRTS) and the ZTF surveys. Our analysis reveals that the survey's shallow depth results in a sample biased toward massive galaxies, which predominantly exhibit disk-like structures. Consequently, the distribution of morphological types in our sample differs from that of the general galaxy population. We observe a strong correlation between size and morphology, where larger galaxies are more likely to be classified as disks. Furthermore, we find that AGN hosts are more frequently associated with irregular galaxies compared to non-AGN galaxies. These findings suggest that AGN activity is more common in irregular galaxies, a result that aligns with previous research. Additionally, our results indicate that AGN hosts are more likely to be spiral galaxies than the broader population of galaxies. Finally, we demonstrate that the HSC-Wide survey is highly effective for determining the shapes of galaxies at $z<1$. These insights are crucial for understanding the relationship between AGN activity and host galaxy morphology, thereby advancing our knowledge of AGN fueling mechanisms. The HSC-Wide survey is expected to facilitate further investigations into the morphology of AGN hosts at $z<1$. SRCs are identified through two- and multi-particle correlations in final states containing protons and neutrons at large relative momenta ($q>400$ MeV/c) and large relative energies ($E_{rel}>20$ MeV). The analysis reveals that proton-neutron pairs exhibit the highest cross-sections, followed by proton-proton and neutron-neutron pairs. Furthermore, the relative energy $E_{rel}$ is observed to be independent of the collision centrality. The model successfully reproduces the experimental data, with the magnitude of the residual interaction strength adjusted to match the measurements. Additionally, the study confirms that protons and neutrons participate equally in short-range correlations. Finally, correlations at large $q$ and $E_{rel}$ are compared with those at large $q$ but low $E_{rel}$, demonstrating that the former are significantly stronger. Complex numbers are frequently encountered in mathematics, science, and engineering, yet they are rarely utilized in Machine Learning. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed for complex-valued data, featuring a new activation function and an implementation of complex equality within neural networks. The study provides an analysis of the complex equality mechanism and demonstrates the model's effectiveness through applications in complex number visualization and image processing. Results indicate that the proposed functions are smooth and suitable for Machine Learning contexts, while the complex equality co-domain operator enhances model performance. Furthermore, the visualization of complex numbers via deep learning successfully identifies distinct clusters and individual data points. Finally, experimental evidence confirms that the complex deep learning model outperforms the real-valued counterpart in handling complex-valued images. We conducted a detailed analysis of abundance patterns in metal-poor stars, focusing on the [Fe/H] = -2.5 dex regime, to investigate the relationship between stellar generation and abundance spread. By examining 110 stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0 dex from the APOGEE-2 survey, we identified a strong correlation between abundance spread and metallicity, which peaks at [Fe/H] ≈ -2.5 dex. Our investigation into the origins of this phenomenon revealed that the spread is primarily driven by the [Mg/Fe] ratio, which exhibits a notably higher dispersion than other elements. Furthermore, we found that the spread in [Mg/Fe] is intrinsically linked to metallicity, with the most significant variation occurring in the [Fe/H] = -2.0 to -3.0 dex range. This behavior aligns with the transition from single to multiple star-forming regions, a shift that appears to take place around [Fe/H] ≈ -2.5 dex. Additionally, we observed that the [Mg/Fe] ratio is influenced by the [O/Fe] ratio, suggesting that the spread in [Mg/Fe] may also stem from the [O/Fe] distribution. Finally, we demonstrated that the [Mg/Fe] ratio is sensitive to the [O/Fe] ratio, a relationship that can be modeled using a simple two-zone model. This model indicates that the [Mg/Fe] ratio is determined by the relative contributions of Type II and Type Ia supernovae, which evolve over time. Consequently, the [Mg/Fe] ratio serves as a valuable tool for probing the star formation history of the early Galaxy. Overall, our findings suggest that the [Mg/Fe] ratio is a key factor in the transition from single to multiple star-forming regions, and that the [O/Fe] ratio is a critical parameter for understanding the [Mg/Fe] distribution. These insights provide a deeper understanding of the chemical evolution of the early Galaxy. Future studies should aim to investigate the [Mg/Fe] ratio in other elements to further explore the origins of abundance spread. This paper introduces a novel toolkit designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts regarding their underlying input variables. We demonstrate that this methodology effectively identifies the specific financial literacy components that most significantly influence predictions of individual readiness to comprehend financial information. This methodology is particularly valuable for nonparametric machine learning models, which are increasingly favored in empirical research for their ability to capture complex, nonlinear relationships between independent and dependent variables. The study utilizes data from the 2017 Survey of Financial Literacy in Poland, which includes a unique module on the willingness to learn financial knowledge. Our findings indicate that while the impact of financial literacy on the desire to acquire financial knowledge is generally weak, the sensitivity analysis reveals that specific sub-dimensions of financial literacy are highly predictive of an individual's desire to learn. These sensitive sub-dimensions encompass the belief in the importance of financial knowledge, the perception of one's own ability to acquire it, and the perception of the time required to learn it. Furthermore, we show that the proposed methodology is highly effective in this context, yielding results that align with those from a standard parametric approach. Finally, we outline the steps required to adapt this methodology to other research areas. The paper concludes with a discussion of the methodology's strengths and limitations. Machine learning is a rapidly expanding field that has significantly influenced numerous sectors, including computer science, physics, and engineering. Although quantum machine learning has been a subject of study for over a decade, it has not yet reached widespread practical application. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum machine learning utilizing SQUIDs (Superconducting QUantum Interference Devices) as the primary computational unit. SQUIDs are highly versatile nanoscale sensors capable of functioning as both voltage amplifiers and memory storage devices. Given their established reliability in various applications, we contend that leveraging them for machine learning tasks is a logical and promising development. We outline the essential hardware components required to build a quantum computer and present a new methodology for integrating SQUIDs into this architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a SQUID-based quantum computer can effectively perform classification tasks, such as the XOR problem. Our findings indicate that this SQUID-centric approach offers a promising pathway for the future of quantum computing. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive simulation of the entire system, including detailed circuit diagrams, to support the reproducibility of our results. We conclude that this work serves as a robust foundation for advancing quantum computing technologies. This paper introduces the concept of distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within nearly product contact manifolds. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for these manifolds and examine their properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that the distorted product semi-slant function is both non-zero and non-negative, and we illustrate these findings with relevant examples. Finally, we provide a concrete instance of such a submanifold in Sasakian product manifolds. Additionally, we show that the class of distorted product semi-slant submanifolds is not invariant under the shape operator by presenting a relevant example. This class encompasses well-known submanifolds, including distorted product plane, hemi-slant, and anti-invariant submanifolds. Furthermore, we provide examples of distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds in Sasakian product manifolds, noting that this class is not parallel with respect to the induced connection. We also present examples where the distorted product semi-slant function is a non-constant function. Finally, we illustrate that the class of distorted product semi-slant submanifolds is not minimal by providing a specific example. These findings are supported by several theorems and examples. The study of distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds in nearly product contact manifolds is a novel area of research. This work is part of a series of papers dedicated to the investigation of these submanifolds. For additional details, please refer to the cited references. Low-energy nuclear recoil events, such as those from WIMP-nucleus interactions, can be identified by the formation of trapped charge (ionization electrons) and stable lattice defects (color centers) within a diamond sensor. This study reports on the first experimental analysis of the PALEOCCENE setup, which integrates a 1.5 g natural diamond with a 1.5 g SiPM readout, housed inside a low-background vacuum chamber. The apparatus was deployed at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS) for a 10-day run, with a background index of $1.5 \pm 0.1$ counts per kg cd day. The primary objective of this work is to evaluate the feasibility of detecting nuclear recoils via color centers, paving the way for future experiments that could achieve sensitivities competitive with direct detection dark matter searches. Additionally, the results are discussed in the context of fundamental radiopurity requirements for the next generation of color center detectors.
