Research into the dynamics of colloidal particles has revealed that many systems are driven by non-equilibrium forces, including those of entropic and nonequilibrium activity in origin. This study examines the motion of dynamic colloidal particles subjected to gradients of such activity. We demonstrate that particles exposed to nonequilibrium activity gradients exhibit asymmetric diffusion, whereas those in entropic force gradients display asymmetric mobility. These findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental data. Furthermore, we show that the nonequilibrium activity strength can be quantified through the asymmetry of particle diffusion. These results offer a deeper understanding of the dynamics of asymmetric colloidal particles within non-equilibrium environments and establish a method for characterizing non-equilibrium activity in such settings. Additionally, our findings are applicable to a wide range of biological systems. Specifically, we apply our results to the diffusion of proteins in living cells, revealing that the cytoplasmic environment generates an activity gradient. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these findings for the directed transport of particles in active matter. This paper introduces a geometric approach to the problem of identifying and clustering the sources of epidemics within networked populations. The proposed algorithm relies on the observation that, under specific assumptions, a community of infected nodes originating from a single outbreak can be defined as the intersection of two geometrically constructed sets. The study presents a theoretical analysis of this method, demonstrating its relationship to the stochastic outbreak model and the community structure of the underlying network. Furthermore, the method is illustrated using both synthetic and real-world networks. The results indicate that the approach performs exceptionally well on sparse networks and remains effective across a broad range of epidemics on other network types. Additionally, the method proves to be computationally efficient, capable of clustering outbreaks in large networks with millions of nodes within seconds. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future extensions. Keywords: outbreaks, networks, epidemics, outbreaks, outbreaks. This study presents a straightforward method for avoiding spurious X-shaped artifacts centered on point sources when creating maximum likelihood (ML) maps from CMB data. These features, which resemble the source but are significantly larger, have previously been suppressed using pixel-based deconvolution. We demonstrate that the root cause of the X-shapes is the point source's location on the map grid. By shifting the map grid so the source does not align with a pixel center, we eliminate the issue without needing to deconvolve the point sources. This approach is particularly beneficial for constructing ML maps, as deconvolution can introduce artifacts that complicate subsequent analysis. We illustrate this technique using the Planck 2015 High Frequency Separation (HFI) data to generate ML maps. Furthermore, we show that this grid-shifting strategy is applicable to any CMB dataset. Finally, we confirm that the resulting maps produce likelihoods comparable to those obtained with pixel-based deconvolution. The code used to generate these maps is publicly accessible.

This study investigates how to train language-guided, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning agents to execute complex tasks using natural language. We introduce a new training framework that employs a latent variable model to represent both the referent of an ambiguous sentence and the specific point in time to which a goal instruction applies. This model is integrated into the reward function, allowing the agent to learn a distribution over potential interpretations of those instructions. Our approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin on a difficult, multi-step task from a recent benchmark. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method facilitates more sample-efficient learning and produces agents whose policies are more robust to variations in instruction wording. Finally, we analyze how the agent's policy distribution evolves during training and how this evolution influences the policy's sensitivity to linguistic ambiguities. The code and data required to replicate our experiments are accessible at https://github.com/mburda/ambiguity. These resources also support a recent paper by our team, which builds upon the same codebase. That paper explores how self-play can enhance the performance of reinforcement learning agents in a multi-agent setting. Our findings indicate that self-play enables agents to learn more sample-efficiently and yields policies that are more robust to ambiguities in communication. The results from both papers are available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00058 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00059, respectively. We believe that the code, data, and insights from these two studies will be valuable to the broader community. We hope this work inspires others to investigate how RL agents can acquire a shared language for coordinating joint actions and how their sensitivity to ambiguity in interpreting others' intentions can be reduced. Additionally, we aim to inspire research into how self-play can improve the performance of RL agents in multi-agent environments. Our work is part of a broader research program focused on learning to communicate and coordinate in RL agents. We introduce a shadow procedure tomography method designed to characterize quantum channels. Our approach relies on preparing a comprehensive collection of diverse input states, executing the quantum channel on each state, and subsequently analyzing the resulting outputs. We demonstrate that this method is both optimal and universally applicable to any quantum channel. Additionally, we illustrate its utility by presenting efficient strategies for the full tomography of specific channels, such as the depolarizing and dephasing channels. Our findings indicate that the number of measurements required to estimate the parameters of these channels scales logarithmically with the dimension of the Hilbert space. Furthermore, we extend this methodology to the comprehensive description of quantum supermaps. To achieve this, we employ higher-order channels, which function as supermaps acting upon quantum channels. We prove that the measurement count needed to estimate the parameters of these higher-order channels also grows logarithmically with their dimension. Finally, we examine the application of our method to certain noisy channels that exhibit non-Markovian dynamics. In these scenarios, we successfully reconstruct the complete dynamics of the noisy channel. Our results suggest that the number of measurements needed to estimate the parameters of these dynamics remains logarithmic with respect to the Hilbert space dimension. Consequently, this approach offers a pathway to fully characterize quantum systems exhibiting non-Markovian behavior. Our study thus paves the way for future research into efficient methods for shadow tomography of quantum systems. This finding underscores the method's potential to enable the efficient description of numerous other quantum resources. This paper introduces and examines keen inequalities related to the Cheeger constant of planar convex bodies. We demonstrate that the unit disk maximizes the Cheeger constant among all convex bodies with a fixed area, a result that follows from the isoperimetric inequality. Furthermore, the disk minimizes this constant when the perimeter is held constant, and the disk's Cheeger constant is strictly positive. These findings constitute a two-dimensional analogue of the Minkowski inequality for isoperimetric profiles. Additionally, we present and prove a corresponding inequality for higher dimensions, which also addresses the Minkowski inequality regarding isoperimetric profiles in that context. The proof relies on the Brunn-Minkowski inequality and the fact that the isoperimetric profile of n-dimensional Euclidean space is known. Finally, we establish that the n-dimensional ball is the maximizer of the Cheeger constant among all convex bodies with a given volume, and we provide an explicit formula for this constant for the n-dimensional ball. The proof utilizes the Alexandrov-Fenchel inequality, which is itself a consequence of the Minkowski inequality. This work extends the authors' previous study published in \emph{J. Geom. This study investigates the renormalization group behavior of a Coulomb-interacting two-dimensional graphene system, specifically focusing on bilayer graphene where low-energy excitations are described by quadratic dispersion relations. The analysis reveals that the Coulomb interaction remains marginally irrelevant in this context, a finding that contrasts with the marginal relevance of the interaction in single-layer graphene, which is characterized by linear dispersion. Furthermore, the renormalization group analysis demonstrates that the interlayer hopping parameter is an irrelevant parameter within the system. Consequently, the fixed point governing the system is identical to that of single-layer graphene, where the interlayer hopping is also irrelevant. This result implies that the universal properties of quantum Hall effect in graphene are independent of whether the system consists of a single layer or multiple layers. Finally, the study examines the instability of this fixed point in the presence of multiple-body interactions, such as three-body interactions, and analyzes the impact of such interactions on the density of states at the Fermi level. The findings indicate that three-body interactions are irrelevant in the quadratic dispersion model, whereas they exhibit relevance in the linear dispersion model. Additionally, the analysis explores the instability of the fixed point when a two-body interaction is present. The relevance of the interaction is also influenced by the presence of a dielectric medium, which can alter the renormalization group flow of the interaction. Overall, the findings suggest that the quantum Hall effect in graphene is a robust phenomenon that is insensitive to the specific form of the Coulomb interaction. The structural and electronic characteristics of endohedral fullerenes are significantly influenced by the nature of their internal atoms. This study employed scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to examine the properties of Sc2TbN@C80. Our STM findings reveal that the average height of Sc2TbN@C80 molecules varies with temperature, suggesting a conformational change. Furthermore, the STM data indicate that the molecules are oriented with the C2 axis perpendicular to the C80 cage surface. DFT calculations demonstrate that the C2-M (M = Sc, Y, La, Dy, Ho, Er, Tb) @C80 molecules adopt two distinct conformations: C2-M@C80-I and C2-M@C80-II. The C2-Sc@C80-I structure aligns with our STM observations, whereas the C2-Sc@C80-II configuration corresponds to the high-temperature state. Additionally, the C2-Sc@C80-II structure is more stable than the C2-Sc@C80-I structure by 0.10 eV. These results suggest that the molecules observed at room temperature adopt the C2-Sc@C80-I conformation, while they transition to the C2-Sc@C80-II conformation at elevated temperatures. The electronic properties of C2-Sc@C80-I and C2-Sc@C80-II were also investigated. Finally, STM measurements of the density of states (DOS) at the Fermi level (EF) indicate that the C2-Sc@C80-I structure is more favorable than the C2-Sc@C80-II structure. This work provides valuable insights into the structural and electronic properties of C2-M @C80 molecules. The findings are anticipated to contribute to the development of new materials with promising applications in nanotechnology. The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast network of devices capable of communicating with one another, facilitating data exchange and enabling users to manage their devices remotely. However, the IoT ecosystem is expanding rapidly, with billions of devices expected to be online within the next few years. This surge in connectivity creates significant security and privacy challenges, as these devices often suffer from limited computational power, small memory capacity, and low energy efficiency. Consequently, there is a critical need for lightweight cryptographic algorithms tailored for IoT security. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art lightweight cryptosystems, offering a comprehensive analysis of their security and performance characteristics. Furthermore, it examines the security threats facing IoT devices and proposes strategies for securing them using lightweight cryptography. Finally, the paper outlines the authors' future research directions in this field. Given the current lack of a complete survey on the subject, this work aims to provide valuable insights and guidance for future research. The paper is structured into seven sections, beginning with an introduction, followed by a review of the state-of-the-art, and concluding with the authors' proposed future research avenues. Section 3 provides an overview of the Internet of Things. Section 4 details the state-of-the-art lightweight cryptosystems, while Section 5 explores security threats and solutions within the context of IoT security. The paper concludes in Section 6 with the authors' proposed future research directions. The primary contribution of this work is a thorough survey of lightweight cryptosystems, offering detailed security and performance analyses, alongside a survey of security threats and potential solutions for IoT environments. Sequential decision-making is a prevalent challenge across numerous fields, where Bayesian methods offer a robust framework for integrating prior knowledge with new data. This study focuses on adaptive Ramsey measurements, which determine magnetic field amplitudes by sequentially adjusting the $\pi/2$ pulse duration. We introduce a Bayesian decision theory to guide the adaptive process, aiming to minimize the posterior variance of the magnetic field. Our results demonstrate that this sequential approach achieves a comparable final measurement precision to an optimal Ramsey scan with only a 10% reduction in efficiency. Furthermore, we show that this method surpasses the efficiency of the adaptive Ramsey technique previously reported by Li et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 112, 110501 (2014)]. Finally, we generalize this sequential decision-making model to other adaptive experiments, such as quantum feedback control. This work provides a practical method for optimizing adaptive decision processes and establishes a foundation for future research in sequential decision-making. We introduce a novel centrality metric grounded in the comparison of actual distances between nodes with the minimum possible distance allowed by the triangle inequality. This approach, which we term Gromov centrality, leverages the concept of triangle inequality surplus (TIS) to highlight network regions where the triangle inequality holds as an equality. Gromov centrality enables the identification of key nodes within the network's backbone, which is defined as the minimal subgraph necessary to maintain all pairwise distances. Furthermore, this method offers a multi-scale analysis of centrality, as the backbone can be determined at any resolution by adjusting a threshold for acceptable TIS. The effectiveness of Gromov centrality in revealing backbone nodes is demonstrated across various network types, including random graphs, scale-free networks, small-world networks, and real-world social networks. Additionally, we show that Gromov centrality is particularly effective at detecting nodes that bridge distinct network communities. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of Gromov centrality and utilize it to analyze the complex contagion dynamics of the 2002 Florida power grid failure. In this context, the nodes identified as most central correspond precisely to the critical components of the power grid that, when removed, triggered the cascading failures. These findings suggest that Gromov centrality serves as a valuable tool for vulnerability analysis in infrastructure networks. The Gromov centrality code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robertkelly/GromovCentrality. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant no. 1803920. This paper introduces a novel gravitational theory, designated as AZS (for Azimuthally Symmetrical), which relies on a tensor metric and a diagonal connection. The connection components are derived from the metric through a specific formula that ensures general covariance. The field equations, which are second-order differential equations, are derived from a Lagrangian that depends on the metric, the connection, and their first derivatives. The Lagrangian is constructed to be linear in the derivatives of the metric and quadratic in the derivatives of the connection. When the connection is expressed via the Christoffel symbols, the Lagrangian simplifies to the Hilbert Lagrangian, thereby recovering General Relativity. The theory's validity is confirmed by its ability to reproduce General Relativity's results in weak gravitational fields and by its satisfaction of the equivalence principle. Furthermore, the theory remains applicable to strong gravitational fields, including those involving black holes. In such scenarios, the theory yields novel results, such as a new form of gravitational waves and a distinct expression for the Schwarzschild metric. Additionally, the field equations impose no restrictions on the connection, allowing for a broader class of solutions compared to General Relativity. This broader solution space enables the derivation of a new set of conservation laws, including a conservation law applicable to all diagonal connections. These findings are detailed in this article and its companion, AZS-2, which together establish the foundation for this new gravitational framework. This work also serves as the foundation for our upcoming book, *A New Theory of Gravity*, which will provide a comprehensive exposition of the theory. Keywords: General Relativity, Black Holes, Gravitational Waves, Diagonal Connections, Conservation Laws. (Abridged)

This paper examines sets of matrix pencils that are closed under rigorous equivalence. We demonstrate the structure of such sets by distinguishing between those containing at least one symmetric pencil and those with no symmetric members. Furthermore, we identify all collections consisting entirely of non-singular pencils. Our primary instrument in these developments is a newly introduced canonical representation for symmetric pencils under rigorous equivalence. Additionally, we provide a complete classification of these canonical forms within the context of rigorous equivalence. The study also explores the relationship between symmetric pencils and those possessing definite Hamiltonian matrices. Finally, we present a classification of sets of strictly regular pencils based on their closedness under rigorous equivalence. Notably, within the strictly regular domain, there exist sets that are closed under rigorous equivalence but contain no symmetric pencils. We characterize these exceptional sets and offer a classification of their elements via an appropriate canonical form. The theoretical framework is substantiated with illustrative examples. The paper concludes with an outline of several promising avenues for future research. This work extends the findings of [10] and [11] to the context of rigorous equivalence. The term "rigorous equivalence" was proposed by [12] to describe a specific equivalence relation between matrix pencils, defined by a pair of transformations: one acting on the pencil and another on its associated Hamiltonian matrix. This concept is particularly significant for control-theoretic applications, as it ensures that key properties of the Hamiltonian matrix remain invariant. Specifically, the rank of the nullspace corresponding to the eigenvalue zero—which determines the number of Jordan blocks associated with this eigenvalue—is preserved under rigorous equivalence. Given that matrix pencils play a crucial role in control theory, particularly in analyzing Hamiltonian matrices, the focus on rigorously equivalent sets is well-motivated. Rigorous equivalence is a natural extension of strict equivalence, which itself extends projective equivalence. While projectively equivalent matrices share the same projective eigenvalues, rigorous equivalent pencils maintain the same eigenvalues. Consequently, matrix pencils under rigorous equivalence possess a distinct structure compared to matrices under projective equivalence. The study of these pencils is essential for applications in control theory, where matrix pencils are frequently employed. For instance, eigenvalues derived from matrix pencils are vital for analyzing Hamiltonian matrices, which are central to control theory. Furthermore, matrix pencils offer a more natural framework for projective equivalence than matrices do for projective equivalence. We develop a generalized T-duality framework for Lie group manifolds with constant curvature by employing a non-abelian Lie algebra. This approach maintains the constancy of the Riemann curvature tensor, ensuring that dual metrics remain Einstein. We present explicit examples of this generalized T-duality, including the well-established Abelian T-duality on sphere backgrounds, dualizing $SU(2) \times \mathbb{R}$, and the recently discovered non-Abelian T-duality on the $\text{AdS}_3$ background. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dual metrics are connected through a specific type of conformal transformation. Finally, we examine the dual of a specific example from reference [1] using our framework and compare the resulting dual metric with the one obtained in that same reference. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for the holographic principle. This paper serves as a foundational step toward investigating T-duality on twisted tori. We demonstrate that every metric space with treewidth $t$ admits a small treewidth embedding into $\ell_1$-spaces, specifically bounded by $O(t^2 \log^2 t)$. This space can be represented as the $1$-type space of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where every node and edge carries a weight of $1$. Leveraging this representation, we establish that any planar graph subject to a lower bound on face sizes can be embedded into a graph with treewidth $O(\sqrt{t \log t})$. Furthermore, we show that minor-free graphs, even when non-planar, possess a small set of separators under a similar face size constraint, enabling their embedding into graphs with treewidth $O(\sqrt{t \log t})$. Finally, we prove that metrics with bounded treewidth can be approximated by graphs with comparable treewidth, thereby extending prior findings by Demaine et al. and Dvo\v{r}\'{a}k et al. to the metric setting. All logarithmic factors are suppressed. Additionally, we present a metric space with treewidth $t$ that cannot be embedded into $\ell_1$ with a treewidth smaller than $\Omega(t^2 / \log t)$. This construction is derived from a straightforward treewidth $t$ graph that fails to embed into $\ell_1$ with a treewidth below $\Omega(t^2 / \log t)$. We also examine the case where face sizes are permitted to be small. In this scenario, we illustrate that minor-free graphs may require a treewidth blowup of $2^{\Omega(t)}$ for small treewidth embeddings, and we conjecture that this exponential lower bound is tight. Our findings are supported by an extended abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07000. The paper includes an appendix by Piotr M\'{e}sz\'{a}ros, who proves that planar graphs with $t$ as the maximum face size can be embedded into a graph with treewidth $O(t^{2.5})$. We conjecture that the optimal treewidth for such embeddings is $O(t \log t)$. We demonstrate that a broad category of smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time dynamical systems exhibits chaotic behavior, including periodic orbits across all periods, the creation and annihilation of fixed points, and the emergence of periodic and chaotic attractors from invariant sets of infinite period. This category encompasses the time-reversal of any smooth strongly monotonic map, such as the Lorenz system, the Ricker model, and the discrete Mackey-Glass system. Our findings are based on the observation that the global behavior of such systems is largely determined by the local Jacobian structure, which features an invariant cone field and a cone contraction property. We establish that these geometric characteristics are closely linked to the global dynamics of arbitrary smooth strongly monotonic systems, with the cone contraction property playing a pivotal role. Furthermore, we prove that the cone contraction property holds for all strongly monotonic systems where the product of singular values of the Jacobian along a specific direction remains sufficiently small. This result extends the theory of cone contraction and its associated dynamics, as developed by Mallet-Paret and Sussmann, to a wider range of strongly monotonic systems. We illustrate the application of this theory to various strongly monotonic systems, including the Ricker model, the discrete Mackey-Glass model, and the Lorenz system. Additionally, we show that the cone contraction property is satisfied by the time-reversal of the Mackey-Glass system, thereby enabling the analysis of its global dynamics. Finally, we outline the methodology for constructing periodic orbits and chaotic attractors within this class of strongly monotonic systems. These results are derived from the theory of cone contraction and cone nonexpansion, which we have expanded to cover a more general class of strongly monotonic systems. Our work also provides a new proof of the existence of cone contraction in strongly monotonic systems, utilizing the theory of nonstandard analysis. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the theory of nonstandard analysis; Section 3 presents the theory of cone contraction and cone nonexpansion; Section 4 reviews the dynamics of strongly monotonic systems; Section 5 introduces the concept of a strongly monotonic system with a cone structure; Section 6 defines the class of strongly monotonic systems under study; Section 7 outlines the global behavior of this class; and Section 8 provides a proof of the cone contraction property for the class. Variational quantum eigensolvers (VQE) are designed to determine the ground state energies of quantum systems. However, in many scenarios, the standard initial guess for the VQE parameters fails to converge to the true ground state. This study investigates the potential of an adaptive VQE (AVQE) approach that incorporates qubit excitations. We demonstrate that initializing the AVQE with qubit excitations derived from a prior excited state yields superior results compared to starting from the ground state. This strategy is particularly advantageous for systems where excited states lie significantly lower in energy relative to the ground state. Furthermore, we examine the impact of these qubit excitations on both the convergence rate and the number of required circuit measurements. Our findings indicate that this method is especially effective for molecular systems featuring degenerate ground states. Additionally, we outline a potential extension of this approach to other quantum systems. Finally, we present results for the hydrogen molecule ($H_2$) and the pyrazine molecule ($C_2H_4N_2$) to illustrate the efficacy of qubit excitations in driving VQE convergence. These examples were simulated using both the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA) and the unitary coupled cluster ansatz (UCC). The proposed method is anticipated to be highly beneficial for future VQE implementations on near-term quantum hardware. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/Quantum-Computing-Research-Lab/QCRL-AVQE. Although generative models are theoretically capable of serving as decoders, current practice typically employs discriminative architectures for this role. This paper investigates the potential of employing a generative decoder. We demonstrate that this approach can be highly effective, particularly when integrated with a potent decoders-to-encoders distillation strategy. Our evaluations on image classification benchmarks reveal that our generative decoder surpasses the state-of-the-art. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's versatility by adapting it to various other tasks, including image generation, denoising, and segmentation. Notably, our segmentation model achieves performance comparable to top-tier convolutional networks while utilizing significantly fewer parameters. We also examine the application of this technique to natural language processing, where it yields promising results. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the training dynamics to deepen the understanding of this powerful decoder. This study examines the accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation within the $\Lambda$CDM framework, incorporating a stochastic gravitational-wave background (GWB) with a power-law frequency dependence of $\Omega_{\rm GW} \propto f^{\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ is a free parameter. This approach models the long-wavelength limit of inflationary gravitational waves, where the spectrum is dominated by super-horizon modes that remain nearly constant over time. We demonstrate that this "rigid-amplified" GWB can be effectively approximated by a white noise component, $\Omega_{\rm GW} \propto f^0$, when analyzed using current and near-future cosmological datasets. Consequently, we apply this simplified model to recent observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), and Advanced LIGO-Virgo (ALV) data. Our findings indicate that the white noise approximation yields a GWB amplitude of $\Omega_{\rm GW,0,1} = 1.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^{-9}$ and a Hubble constant of $H_0 = 69.1 \pm 1.1$ km/s/Mpc, resolving the Hubble tension. Furthermore, we show that a narrow range of the power-law index, $-0.2 \lesssim \alpha \lesssim 0.2$, is permitted by the data, a range that encompasses predictions from both single-field and multi-field inflationary models. This suggests that a primordial origin for the GWB is consistent with current observations. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for future experiments, including the Pulsar Timing Array NANOGrav, the space-based LISA, and next-generation cosmological surveys such as DESI and HST. Our analysis indicates that NANOGrav will constrain the index to $-1.0 \lesssim \alpha \lesssim 1.0$, while LISA will achieve a precision of $\Delta \alpha \sim 0.01$. These findings support the hypothesis that the recently detected NANOGrav signal originates from a primordial source. The ALMA Atacama Compact Array (ACA) was employed to investigate the neutral gas composition of Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a heliocentric distance of 3.0 AU. Observations conducted on 2018 June 10 revealed a CO emission structure measuring 1000 x 1000 AU², with a nucleus radius of 0.5 km derived from the outgassing rate. The observed CS-to-CO abundance ratio of 0.0016 aligns with values reported for other comets, suggesting that the ACA's sensitivity is sufficient to detect CS in cometary atmospheres. Furthermore, the study proposes that the observed CS abundance may be influenced by a background emission component originating from the interstellar medium. This finding supports the hypothesis that a portion of the molecular cloud's carbon reservoir is replenished by cometary material. The research concludes by outlining future observational strategies for the ACA to enhance the detection of CS in cometary environments. Additionally, the paper presents a novel method for determining the production rate of CS, which is applicable to other molecules. This approach involves subtracting background emission from the total observed signal to isolate the cometary contribution. The study also explores the potential for using this background subtraction technique to identify CS emission from other sources, such as the solar wind. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for the carbon cycle within the solar system. The data utilized in this study can be accessed via the ALMA Science Archive. This study introduces an unsupervised, end-to-end approach to generating speech without relying on annotated transcriptions. Our method employs a novel technique to create synthetic speech by sampling from an implicit distribution, utilizing a new conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that integrates a transformer-based autoregressive decoder. We demonstrate that our CVAE can learn to synthesize speech from text input and decode audio into corresponding text. Furthermore, experiments indicate that the proposed CVAE outperforms a TTS system trained on a limited dataset regarding both average and minimum generation quality. This study examines Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) as a dark energy candidate within a Quintessence framework, utilizing a complex parameter $\alpha+i\beta$ to model the equation of state. The analysis focuses on a cosmological model where the THDE field interacts with the matter sector, employing a matter-dominated universe for the infrared cutoff. The resulting model is evaluated against Type Ia supernovae (SN1a) data alongside baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) and Hubble parameter ($H(z)$) measurements. The study further investigates the model's stability and thermodynamic properties. The primary objective is to determine the values of parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that best fit the observational data. The findings indicate that the model is viable for the parameter range $-0.15 \leq \alpha+i\beta \leq 0.15$. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the THDE model can account for the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. This work extends our previous research, which relied solely on SN1a data. The inclusion of baryon acoustic oscillation and Hubble parameter data strengthens the model's validity and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the universe's evolution. This study represents a significant advancement in our understanding of the dark energy sector and its role in cosmic evolution. The methodology employed can be applied to other cosmological models to investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for future research in cosmology. The authors hope this work will inspire further investigation into the nature of dark energy and dark matter. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in real-world applications, yet they are notoriously difficult to solve, often requiring the use of approximations. This paper introduces a hybrid approach combining Multi-Criteria Genetic Algorithms with Branch and Bound (MCGBB) techniques. The method begins with a Multi-Criteria Genetic Algorithm (MCGA) that utilizes a Niching technique to identify a diverse set of non-dominated solutions. Subsequently, these solutions serve as starting points for the Branch and Bound (BB) algorithm, which refines them into true non-dominated solutions. The process is iterative, continuing until the Niching algorithm converges. The primary contributions of this study are: (i) the introduction of the MCGA-BB method as a novel hybrid strategy, (ii) the development of a new Branch and Bound variant grounded in local optimization, and (iii) the provision of a comprehensive numerical analysis supported by 1000 runs across various test cases. The results demonstrate that this method effectively generates high-quality solutions for MO-MINLP challenges. Furthermore, the paper addresses a specific challenge in multi-criteria optimization: the lack of a reliable method to verify the completeness of the obtained solution set. To tackle this, we propose a new metric called the "Non-Dominated Coverage Ratio" (NDCR), which quantifies the percentage of a reference set covered by the generated solutions. The study concludes that the proposed MCGA-BB method is capable of identifying the entire Pareto front. The study's website is available at: http://www.scielo.org.ar/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1667-82682019000100009. Linked Lie groups, which form monads over the point in any topos possessing a natural numbers object, serve as the generalization of group objects within the category of spaces. By extending the definition of Lie groups to this broader context, we demonstrate that every linked Lie groupoid is connected and simple, and linked Lie monads are group objects that are integral complete. These findings are derived through a differential calculus constructed from the internal logic of any locally locally cartesian closed topos with a natural numbers object. Furthermore, we establish that the monad of directed linked Lie groupoids over the point is self-adjoint within this topos. These results are specifically validated in the well-established model of synthetic differential geometry. The proof strategy relies on the fundamental theorem of Lie theory, which connects the internal logic of the topos with the theory of Lie theory. This theorem asserts that the point is a universal object for linked Lie groupoids, enabling the derivation of the aforementioned results from the corresponding properties of the point. Additionally, we provide a novel proof of the classical completeness theorem for Lie groups using the framework of synthetic differential geometry. Finally, we extend these findings to the more general setting of linked monads. This work contributes to the emerging field of categorical Lie theory, which aims to generalize the classical theory of Lie groups by utilizing category theory to elucidate their fundamental properties. The paper is structured into three sections: the first presents the general theory of linked monads, the second details the theory of Lie theory for linked monads within an arbitrary topos featuring a natural numbers object, and the third applies these concepts specifically to the synthetic differential geometry model. The accessibility of high-performance computing and data resources has become a cornerstone for scientific progress. However, sharing data from trusted Cyberinfrastructures (CI) with external CI partners or individual researchers presents significant security challenges. To address this, we introduce a novel security model designed to enable safe and efficient data exchange between CIs and between CIs and trusted researchers. This model relies on a gateway that acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to interact with CI resources as if they were internal members, while the gateway itself manages all external communications. We have developed a proof-of-concept implementation of this gateway and successfully tested it within the European Bioinformatics Centre (EBI) CI. Our results demonstrate that this approach effectively facilitates data exchange between the EBI CI and the Grid5000 CI, as well as between the EBI CI and individual researchers from Grid5000. Furthermore, we show that the gateway can be remotely administered by EBI staff without compromising security, thereby enabling the management of numerous external users and significantly enhancing scalability. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this gateway to support data exchange between EBI and other trusted CI partners. This paper was originally presented at the 11th European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys 2016). The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/ebicloud/gateway. Aspect-Sentiment Pair Classification (AS-PC) involves predicting the sentiment of an aspect within a given sentence. While prior research has focused heavily on extracting aspect terms, aspect phrases, or aspects from knowledge bases, aspect-based sentence representations remain underexplored. This study introduces a pre-training model that utilizes supervised contrastive learning to generate aspect-specific sentence representations. By training a classifier on these pre-trained representations, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on the SemEval AS-PC task. Furthermore, we integrate the model into the SemEval aspect extraction pipeline, yielding state-of-the-art performance in aspect phrase extraction. Additionally, the model demonstrates the ability to identify implicit aspect sentiments, a capability that reveals its robustness and generalizability. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/SC-PRE-TRAIN.

This study investigates the mediation analysis of a binary outcome influenced by both an exposure and a binary mediator within a case-control study framework. We demonstrate that, under a linear structural equation model, the standard regression coefficients for this design can be interpreted as causal parameters provided that: 1) the exposure and mediator are conditionally independent in the absence of the exposure, and 2) the joint distribution of the exposure, mediator, and outcome adheres to a specific factorization pattern. Furthermore, we establish that these two assumptions can be evaluated directly in a case-control setting. Finally, we propose a computationally efficient method for estimating the causal parameters and their standard errors, which involves fitting a series of logistic regression models. This approach remains valid even when the joint distribution of the exposure, mediator, and outcome deviates from the assumed factorization pattern. We illustrate the application of this method using data from a case-control study involving lung cancer patients. Additionally, we have made our R code available to facilitate replication. Our findings indicate that, among current and former smokers, a one-standard-deviation increase in pack-years of smoking leads to a 10% rise in the probability of a positive sputum cytology result, with a 30% indirect effect mediated through chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This result is consistent with a previous analysis of the same data under a logistic structural equation model. However, applying a logistic structural equation model to this design yields a different estimate for the indirect effect, suggesting that the linearity assumption is more appropriate for this context. We also observe that the indirect effect is more pronounced in former smokers compared to current smokers. These results highlight the critical role of the structural equation model's functional form in mediation analysis. Our proposed approach offers a practical solution for addressing this issue. Finally, we discuss the extension of this work to other sampling designs and models. (This work was supported by NIH grant R01ES021201). This study examines a multiuser secure communication system supported by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS). The RIS comprises N reflecting elements, each modeled with hardware imperfections, and the system employs multiple transmit antennas alongside a passive jamming antenna to enhance security. The jammer is positioned to maximize the secrecy rate by directing signals toward the worst-case user. To address the resulting non-convex optimization challenge, the authors propose a low-complexity secure transmission design utilizing a semidefinite relaxation (SDR) method. This approach involves optimizing a rank-one matrix that represents the combined power allocation for both the main transmitter and the passive jammer, alongside the optimal RIS configuration. The proposed Riemannian manifold optimization technique ensures the resulting reflector power remains non-negative. Furthermore, the study analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the optimal objective value and the corresponding RIS configuration as the number of RIS elements grows large. Finally, numerical results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed design. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. We introduce a new value function estimation technique that leverages a natural language model to retrospectively reinterpret past experiences from alternative viewpoints. By employing a contrastive value function, we frame experience learning as a supervised task designed to differentiate between resampled transitions and their original versions. This approach, which we term Executive Ability (ExAb), is compatible with any standard value function estimator and can be integrated into any reinforcement learning algorithm. Our findings demonstrate that ExAb yields substantial performance gains over baseline methods when utilizing limited data, particularly in scenarios involving high-dimensional state spaces. Furthermore, we observe that the experience generated by ExAb enhances the expressiveness of the experience replay buffer, thereby improving the training of experience-based models. We also present an extension of ExAb that incorporates a lightweight, pretrained language model, which proves effective in high-data regimes. Finally, we show that our method can be combined with other techniques to construct a more robust experience representation. We have made the code for all our experiments publicly available. ExAb is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/executive_ability. Additional details regarding our experiments can be found in Appendix A.1.1. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has recently initiated its mission to study the Sun's outer atmosphere and the heliosphere by traversing the "solar breeze" near the heliospheric termination shock. This probe offers a novel perspective on solar wind dynamics, enabling the first detailed analysis of energy fluxes within the breeze. Utilizing data from the FIELDS suite of instruments aboard PSP, we examine the energy flow in the electric frame of reference. Our findings indicate that, on average, energy flux is directed toward the Sun across all measured energy densities. However, at the highest energy levels, the energy flow exhibits a slight outward component. Furthermore, we observed that the magnitude of energy flux increases as the solar zenith angle grows. These results align with prior studies conducted by the In-Space Situational Awareness (ISSA) mission. Additionally, our analysis of energy flux in the spacecraft's rest frame reveals that, on average, it is directed away from the Sun, with a more pronounced outward flow at higher energies. Finally, when comparing energy flow in both electric and magnetic frames, we determined that the cross-poynting vector is the primary driver of energy flux in the electric frame. These insights provide valuable context for understanding energy transport in the heliosphere and may inform future research on solar wind dynamics. Ultimately, the data from Parker Solar Probe will significantly enhance our comprehension of energy flow within the heliosphere. This study represents the inaugural analysis of its kind. Future investigations will expand upon these initial findings. The PSP dataset is accessible at https://www.parc.nasa.gov/parker. This paper introduces a generalized framework for constructing a noncommutative analog of a countable principal bundle with a compact structure group using a continuous action on a C*-algebra. This method encompasses the C*-algebraic characterization of a countable principal bundle with a compact group as a specific type of crossed product. We demonstrate that a local action by a compact Lie group on a commutative C*-algebra corresponds to a smooth action by a Lie group of automorphisms on a commutative C*-algebra. Furthermore, we establish that a locally free action by a compact Lie group on a commutative C*-algebra yields an equivalent action by a Lie group of automorphisms that preserves a continuous Riemannian metric. Finally, we extend these findings to actions by compact Lie groups on general C*-algebras. In each scenario, we construct canonical canonical connections, calculate their curvature, and derive a formula for the associated connection one-form. These findings provide a noncommutative generalization of recent work by J. L. Cortes and J. M. Gracia. Additionally, we offer a geometric interpretation of the curvature and discuss applications to the noncommutative geometric formulation of gauge theories. In the final section, we explore the relationship between our approach and the generalization of the Atiyah-Singer index theorem to the setting of a differentiable bundle of C*-algebras. We also present a geometric interpretation of the noncommutative gauge theory derived from this formulation. Finally, we illustrate the application of our framework to the quantum double copy, a recent development in theoretical physics. This application involves actions by noncommutative groups on noncommutative algebras, which can be viewed as a generalization of our work to the case of a free action by a noncommutative Lie group on a noncommutative C*-algebra. In this context, we derive expressions for the noncommutative curvature and the associated connection one-form. We also provide a noncommutative generalization of the Atiyah-Singer index theorem within the setting of a free action by a noncommutative Lie group on a noncommutative C*-algebra. This study introduces a cell-mean-based neural network approach designed to solve both hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. Unlike traditional finite difference or finite volume methods that rely on discrete grids, this technique avoids discretizing the domain into cells. Instead, it employs a meshless framework where a neural network approximates the solution, with weights adjusted through a modified back-propagation algorithm. The cell-mean flux is computed by averaging the input data from the immediate neighborhood of each node. This domain-discretization-free method is applied to resolve the linear advection equation, linear advection-diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, heat equation, and wave equation. Results demonstrate that the proposed cell-mean neural network method yields accurate solutions and exhibits superior performance compared to the residual-based neural network method. Furthermore, the study confirms that this neural network approach maintains high accuracy even when dealing with discontinuous solutions. Numerical experiments indicate that the cell-mean neural network method achieves greater accuracy with fewer nodes than residual-based techniques, offering a more efficient solution for both hyperbolic and parabolic problems. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness in handling problems with sharp gradients and discontinuities. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing potential extensions of this cell-mean neural network approach to address other types of partial differential equations. The ALICE experiment at CERN's LHC operates in a high-occupancy environment, necessitating a robust data filtering process to manage the vast data volumes generated by heavy-ion collisions. The current ALICE Online Trigger and Data Acquisition System (TDAQ) is engineered to handle up to 400 kHz of processed data, a capacity that is fully utilized during the LHC's Run 3. To prepare for future Runs 4 and beyond, a substantial upgrade of the ALICE TDAQ system is essential. This paper outlines the proposed ALICE TDAQ evolution and its integration with the CERN Wide Area Data Distribution System (WADDS) for the post-Run 3 era. Furthermore, we describe a new data processing framework designed to achieve the necessary performance levels. This solution incorporates a novel data format and a distributed processing architecture, which are critical for sustaining data rates exceeding 100 kHz. Additionally, the ALICE offline software is being updated to support data rates above 400 kHz, thereby ensuring a seamless transition from online to offline analysis. These advancements will facilitate the full utilization of the LHC's 400 kHz data processing capability during Run 3 and position ALICE to operate at data rates exceeding 100 kHz in Run 4 and subsequent runs. Event extraction remains a difficult area within natural language processing, primarily due to the vast diversity of event types and their varying structures. To address this, we introduce a novel multilingual dataset designed to enhance performance across multiple languages. Our data acquisition strategy involves two key steps: first, generating a broad set of event mentions from a large volume of text using a pre-trained language model; second, annotating this broad set with a standardized schema to facilitate cross-language analysis. We validate the efficacy of our dataset by training a model on it and testing its performance against existing monolingual datasets. The resulting model demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline approaches. We anticipate this dataset will prove valuable for event extraction tasks. The dataset and code can be accessed at: https://github.com/Deepanshu-123/Multilingual-Event Extraction. This paper investigates the positivity of characteristic forms associated with the direct image of line bundles on complex manifolds. We establish the global algebraic structure of these forms by defining a canonical family of vector bundles, termed "positive vector bundles," which are constructed through algebraic operations applied to vector bundles possessing a natural flat connection. This framework enables a systematic approach to analyzing global differential forms linked to positive line bundles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new structure is essential for deriving a general Hodge-Riemann relation applicable to positive line bundles. This finding resolves a question posed by Siu and confirms the Siu vanishing conjecture within this specific context. Additionally, we provide an explicit geometric characterization of positive vector bundles in terms of curvature properties and identify a class of positive vector bundles arising from arithmetic geometry. These contributions collectively address several open problems, including those formulated by Siu and by Nakamaye and Peter. Finally, this work serves as a foundational step toward establishing the general structure of positive vector bundles. To achieve this, we introduce a novel category of positive vector bundles, designated as "rational positive vector bundles," and demonstrate that they constitute an abelian category. This result serves as the geometric analogue to the recent algebraic result by Nakamaye and Peter. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions. This study examines the tidal flux fraction and merger rates of large early-type galaxies (LETGs) within the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). We identified 1,000 LETGs with redshifts of 0.02 < z < 0.1 and effective radii exceeding 10 kpc. Using HSC-SSP imaging data, we measured the ellipticity of tidal features in both positive and negative tranches, calculating the tidal flux proportion for each galaxy. We then correlated these proportions with merger rates, estimated via the formula $\tau^{-1} = 1.5 \times 10^{-11} \sigma v n$, where $\tau$ represents the merger timescale. Our results indicate that galaxies with prominent tidal features exhibit higher merger rates than those with faint features. Furthermore, we observed that galaxies possessing strong features in both the positive and negative tranches have significantly elevated merger rates compared to those with strong features in only one tranche. These findings suggest that the most significant mergers are those that generate extended tidal features in both directions. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between tidal flux proportions and galaxy properties, including effective radius, stellar mass, and velocity dispersion. The analysis reveals that galaxies with strong features in both tranches are more likely to be massive and have large effective radii, yet they do not necessarily possess high velocity dispersions. Finally, we compared our tidal flux proportions with those derived from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Field Survey and the Hyper Suprime-Cam Strategic Program for Cosmology, finding that the tidal flux proportions in the HSC-SSP are approximately 1.5 times greater than those in the other surveys. This discrepancy may stem from the HSC-SSP's deeper imaging data, which allows for the detection of fainter tidal features. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the tidal features of LETGs and their associated merger rates, contributing to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution. The tidal flux proportions identified here can be utilized to investigate the impact of mergers on the evolution of large early-type galaxies. This work extends the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), previously introduced in Part I, by incorporating the azimuthal component of the gravitational potential. This extension enables the derivation of the bipolar ejection phenomenon as a result of azimuthally symmetric gravitational fields. The bipolar ejection is characterized by a negative radial velocity ($v_r < 0$) alongside a positive azimuthal velocity ($v_\varphi > 0$). The phenomenon is modeled as a repellent gravitational effect driven by the azimuthal component of the gravitational field, which generates a centrifugal force. This centrifugal force is defined as the product of radial acceleration and the inverse of the azimuthal mass current density. The azimuthal mass current density is determined by the cross product of the radial velocity and the azimuthal unit vector with the mass density. The ASTG framework posits that the azimuthal component of the gravitational field is a direct consequence of the azimuthal component of the gravitational source, meaning the bipolar ejection is an inherent feature of ASTG. The theory's validity is substantiated by its successful application to the dynamics of the Earth's atmosphere, the solar wind, and the formation of spiral nebulae. Furthermore, the ASTG's capacity to explain the bipolar ejection phenomenon is demonstrated through its analysis of the 2011 eruption of Mount Sinabung in Indonesia. The resulting numerical simulations accurately reproduce the observed dynamics of the eruption, including the ejection of lava, smoke, and ash. Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are characterized by their high dispersion measure, rapid duration, and rapid rise times. While the latter two properties are often attributed to the optical depth of the emitting region, the spatial constraints imposed by these assumptions remain unexplored. This study demonstrates that the volume of an FRB emitting at a specific frequency is limited by the region's optical depth. Consequently, the total energy output is bounded by the product of this volume and the scattering time, which is proportional to the square of the electron density. Furthermore, we establish that the total energy emitted across all frequencies cannot exceed the product of the FRB's duration and the thermal energy of the emitting region. These findings suggest that FRBs originate from a scattering medium that is either highly ionized or possesses a low electron density. Additionally, we propose that FRBs are unlikely to be produced by a population of numerous, small, and short-lived regions. Finally, we examine the implications of these results for the neutron star binary system PSR B1937+21, which has been suggested as a potential FRB source. We conclude that an FRB resulting from this system would need to be either concurrent with the pulsar's emission or deferred by a substantial scattering time. If the emission is concurrent, the region must be larger than the pulsar's light-crossing time; if deferred, the region must be larger than the mean free path of the emission. In both scenarios, the region would be marginally larger than the binary separation, implying that the electron density is lower than the number density of the pulsar wind. These constraints are consistent with the FRB being a magnetar flare or a pulsar wind nebula. However, they rule out the FRB arising from a scattering region within the pulsar wind nebula, as such a region would need to be larger than the entire system. This result also excludes the possibility of the FRB originating from a scattering region in the pulsar wind nebula of a magnetar binary system. These findings further suggest that the FRB is not caused by a population of small, short-lived scattering regions within the pulsar wind nebula. Instead, the FRB is likely caused by a single, large, and long-lived scattering region, such as a pulsar wind nebula. This conclusion is supported by the observed rise time of the FRB, which is comparable to the age of the binary system. These results are also consistent with the FRB being a magnetar flare or a pulsar wind

The proposed system is designed to measure the relative longitudinal and transverse emittance of particle beams. It functions by scanning a beta-beat across both planes to transfer beam envelope information onto a beta-function discriminator, which is then recorded by a fast scaler. This scaling process is repeated at various betatron phases to determine the beam envelope at each phase. Theoretical analysis and simulations indicate that ensembles of as few as 10 phases are sufficient to accurately represent the beam envelope. Furthermore, the paper outlines the system's design and provides an overview of its current development status. Additionally, a prototype has been successfully installed and tested on the CERN PS Booster. Simulation results are presented, and comparisons with actual experimental data confirm the validity of the theoretical approach. The paper concludes with a discussion of the system's potential applications. Keywords: Emittance measurement, brightness scan, beam envelope. Corresponding author: Dr. Wei Li, Email: wei.li@cern.ch. 1. Introduction. Particle beam analysis is a crucial component of the accelerator physics research and development process. Beam envelopes serve as a key metric for characterizing beam quality. The transverse beam envelope is defined as the beam size, while the longitudinal beam envelope is defined as the bunch length. The emittance of a particle beam is defined as the area of the phase space occupied by the beam. Emittance serves as a critical indicator of beam quality. In general, the emittance of a particle beam is determined by the beam size and bunch length. Consequently, beam envelopes are widely used to assess beam quality. The brightness scan system is designed to measure the relative longitudinal and transverse emittances of particle beams. This paper presents a new measurement technique called the brightness scan. The brightness scan is implemented using a fast beam current transformer (BCT) and a beta-beat induced by an orbit bump. The brightness scan system is configured with one BCT and a single orbit bump. The bump is created by applying a single kick to the beam. The beam envelope is scanned by adjusting the bump amplitude and phase. The beam size is measured by the BCT. Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a synergistic approach that integrates data-driven and modeling-based techniques to enhance the performance of individual components. This survey examines recent advancements in DIM, with a specific focus on reinforcement learning (RL) and control. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles of DIM, followed by a review of its applications within model-based RL and control contexts. Our objective is to facilitate the adoption of DIM across diverse domains by synthesizing insights from recent literature. Given the rapid evolution of DIM, we anticipate that this area will continue to expand and hold significant promise for the future. By employing a non-standard weight initialization method, AskewSGD enhances the model's representational capacity, thereby facilitating the optimization of more expressive models. Additionally, we show that AskewSGD can be seamlessly integrated with existing optimization techniques for quantized networks without requiring modifications to those methods. Finally, we explore the application of AskewSGD in training large language models, where it successfully mitigates catastrophic forgetting during continual learning. These robots are typically engineered using one of two primary approaches: either by applying physical principles to mimic the mechanics of soft materials, or by utilizing experimental methods to derive data-driven control strategies. This paper reviews the current landscape of model-driven control for soft robots, examining both physical-based control techniques and the open challenges that remain. We introduce a template-driven decomposition approach that leverages large language models to create sub-goals based on a predefined template. Lengat and Roberts (2009) demonstrated that for a broad category of distributions, the log-concave sampler outperforms the Cauchy sampler. In this paper, we extend this finding to multi-modal distributions by demonstrating that the distributed step sampler surpasses the location-diffuse step sampler across all step distributions, regardless of their tail behavior. This work investigates two-particle correlations in a driven dissipative Bose-Hubbard model by analyzing the expectation values of two-boson density operators. The study compares two-particle correlation functions derived from chronological averages with those obtained from frequency-domain averages. Results indicate that two-particle correlations remain robust in the frequency domain, even when decoupling schemes are applied to eliminate higher-order terms. Furthermore, the frequency-domain correlation functions are observed to be analytic with respect to time. These findings are supported by extensive numerical simulations. Additionally, the two-boson density operator is evaluated using both exact diagonalization and the cluster expansion method. The latter proves highly accurate for two-particle correlations, even when truncating the expansion at the three-particle level. Finally, the study examines the impact of dissipation on two-particle correlations and their associated correlation times. In the absence of dissipation, the system exhibits strong two-boson correlations, which diminish as dissipation is introduced. However, these correlations are significantly enhanced when dissipation is modeled via a generalized quantum master equation. This enhancement is attributed to the non-Markovian nature of the dissipation, which is further corroborated by the behavior of frequency-domain correlation times. Overall, the results demonstrate that frequency-domain correlations offer a valuable tool for characterizing the dynamics of driven dissipative Bose-Hubbard models. The methodology employed is broadly applicable to other quantum systems, facilitating the analysis of two-particle correlations in both time and frequency domains. This approach holds particular promise for investigating the effects of dissipation on multi-particle correlations. Additionally, the two-particle correlation times are found to be substantially shorter than those of one-particle correlations, suggesting that frequency-domain correlations can be approximated using low-order cluster expansions. These outcomes provide a foundation for developing efficient and accurate methods to compute frequency-domain two-particle correlations in driven dissipative Bose-Hubbard models. Such methods could facilitate the design of experiments to observe two-boson correlations in these systems. Finally, the findings may have broader implications for quantum information processing, where two-particle correlations play a crucial role in quantum state engineering and quantum gate operations. The ability to control and manipulate these correlations in the frequency domain could enable the creation of novel quantum states and operations, thereby advancing quantum information processing capabilities. In summary, this study presents a comprehensive analysis of two-particle correlations in a driven dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, offering significant insights into the underlying physics and establishing a robust framework for future research in this area. The primary objective is to establish the existence of weak solutions within the space $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solvability can be ensured by imposing a quadratic growth condition on the drift. The proof methodology employs a compactness argument grounded in the theory of quadratic forms and utilizes a novel technique termed the "drift trick." This approach involves iteratively solving a sequence of elliptic problems with progressively stronger drifts, thereby enabling the drift to be treated as a coefficient. We also provide an alternative proof for the solvability of elliptic equations with coefficients independent of $\varepsilon$, a result originally due to Murat and Tardieu. Additionally, we explore the connection between the quadratic growth condition and the concept of quadratic forms. Specifically, we prove that the sequence of weak solutions converges weakly in $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$ to the weak solution of the limiting equation, which features a constant coefficient matrix. Specifically, we examine a two-component driven optical lattice coupled to an environment, where a scar-like pattern emerges in the open system's steady state. We show that a specific steady-state condensation of bosons arises from the interplay between a driving-induced scar-like pattern and Floquet heating. Furthermore, we identify the parameter regime where this heating-induced Bose condensation occurs and clarify its physical mechanism. Our findings indicate that heating-induced Bose condensation is a novel phenomenon exclusive to open systems, offering a new pathway for creating and investigating nonequilibrium long-range order in open quantum systems. Additionally, our work provides a new method for achieving Bose condensation in optical-lattice systems. Finally, we suggest that this phenomenon can be experimentally realized and examined using current technology. Specifically, the driven optical-lattice system under study can be implemented using Rubidium atoms within a two-component optical lattice coupled to a reservoir. This feasibility is supported by the fact that the system's dynamics can be accurately simulated using the quantum trajectories method. Consequently, our results pave the way for a new class of experiments aimed at exploring nonequilibrium long-range order in open quantum systems. Furthermore, our findings offer a novel approach to achieving Bose condensation in optical-lattice systems. Finally, our work establishes a new avenue for investigating the nature of order in open quantum systems. This work establishes the uniform Hölder continuity of viscosity solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, thereby confirming a conjecture originally proposed by Evans and Gariepy. Furthermore, these solutions constitute a weak minimizer for a specific variational problem. The proof leverages recent advancements in the Alexandrov maximum principle, which are also applicable to the solution of the corresponding variational problem. This finding offers a streamlined demonstration of the uniform Hölder continuity previously demonstrated by Giacone and Marini. Additionally, the methodology extends to the uniformly elliptic Monge–Ampère equation, yielding an optimal Hölder exponent of 1/2. Finally, the paper presents a novel Alexandrov maximum principle that generalizes the result found in Evans and Gariepy. The proof relies on a newly developed covering lemma, which may have broader applications. Specifically, this lemma provides an alternative demonstration of the John–Nirenberg lemma. The John–Nirenberg lemma is essential for establishing the uniform Hölder continuity of viscosity solutions to certain fully nonlinear elliptic equations, such as those involving the Monge–Ampère operator, where the right-hand side exhibits constrained behavior. This approach also facilitates the proof of the Alexandrov maximum principle in a more general setting. The paper concludes with a discussion of several open questions. The authors extend their gratitude to Professor Luca Giacomoni for sharing a preprint of his thesis, which contained a preliminary version of the Alexandrov maximum principle. Optical clocks represent the most precise timekeeping instruments available. While current research predominantly focuses on their repetitive operation, non-repetitive optical clocks offer a distinct alternative. This study presents the initial statistical analysis of such non-repetitive optical clocks. We examine the characteristics of the underlying stochastic processes, specifically the phase and frequency, by analyzing their power spectral density and correlation functions. Furthermore, we propose a novel statistical model for these stochastic processes and develop a corresponding stochastic differential equation. This work establishes a foundation for the future development of non-repetitive optical clocks. The methodologies employed are broadly applicable to other frequency metrology systems. This study addresses the dynamic restoration of Service Function Chains (SFCs) and fault mitigation within a Software Defined Network (SDN) utilizing Service-Aware Fog Computing. The primary goal is to restore failed SFCs while minimizing faulty flow mitigation costs and achieving energy-efficient resource allocation. To this end, we introduce a novel joint optimization framework that simultaneously performs SFC restoration, fault mitigation, and energy-efficient resource management in real-time. This approach leverages service information from the Fog Layer to make immediate, local restoration decisions, while the Control Layer dynamically adjusts the network to ensure energy efficiency. Furthermore, we develop a low-complexity algorithm based on the Lagrangian Dual Decomposition (LDD) method to solve the joint optimization problem. Simulation results demonstrate that our LDD algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to existing solutions. Additionally, we evaluate the effectiveness of service information in facilitating SFC restoration, showing that our LDD solution outperforms baseline algorithms. Specifically, it reduces SFC restoration time by 20% and 30% compared to the Fog Layer and Control Layer algorithms, respectively, while also lowering the failure restoration cost by 10% and 20% compared to the Fog Layer and Control Layer approaches. Finally, the LDD algorithm improves energy efficiency by 20% and 30% relative to the Fog Layer and Control Layer methods, respectively. These outcomes confirm that the proposed LDD algorithm effectively and efficiently restores failed SFCs, mitigates faults, and ensures energy-efficient resource allocation. Notably, the integration of service information from the service-aware Fog Layer significantly enhances the performance of the proposed LDD algorithm. Consequently, this work offers a promising framework for SFC restoration, fault mitigation, and energy-efficient resource allocation in SDN environments supported by service-aware Fog Computing. The proposed LDD algorithm can be readily deployed in SDN networks to optimize SFC restoration, mitigate faults, and manage resources efficiently. Ultimately, this research provides a promising framework for next-generation networks, with the LDD algorithm serving as a key component for SFC restoration, fault mitigation, and energy-efficient resource allocation in SDN networks supported by service-aware Fog Computing. The choice of loss function is a critical component of any machine learning model. While extensive research has been conducted on various loss functions, particularly in classification tasks, there remains a lack of understanding regarding their individual impacts on model parameters. This study employs an interpretable gradient analysis technique, termed "gradient surgery," to isolate the effects of different loss functions. By applying this method to a simple linear model, we demonstrate that gradient surgery can successfully identify the influence of loss functions on individual parameters. Furthermore, we illustrate how these losses affect the optimization landscape and the resulting optimization trajectory. Our findings indicate that although all loss functions aim to minimize prediction errors, their specific influences on model parameters vary significantly. We also present a unified framework for regularization that leverages the distinct characteristics of loss functions. Finally, we validate the efficacy of gradient surgery on more complex models, including logistic regression, linear regression, and convolutional neural networks. This study introduces and analyzes a novel class of holographic quantum error correction (HQC) codes, built upon a hyper-Invariant MERA (hIMERA) tensor network structure. These codes are defined by power-law correlations and achieve a new record for the best-known holographic ratio, reaching up to 1000. The codes are approximately holographic, with their geometric properties derived from the $L$-$S$ relation of the network's bulk. The tensor network is constructed by iteratively merging two qubits into a larger degree of freedom, resulting in bulk geometries that are hyperbolic and fractal. We demonstrate that these codes can be efficiently simulated on a quantum computer, enabling the calculation of their holographic ratio and the verification of their approximate holographic nature. Furthermore, we establish that these codes possess holographic error correction capabilities, meaning the network functions as a quantum error correction code. Finally, we examine the relationship between the code's parameters and its error correction performance, showing that while these codes are not holographic in the strict sense, they exhibit a form of "holography in disguise." This suggests that the physical principles underlying these codes may offer a pathway to developing fully holographic error correction codes. Additionally, we explore the potential of hIMERA as a framework for constructing a holographic theory of quantum gravity. Specifically, we outline how to derive the theory's action from the tensor network and demonstrate that the resulting theory is a variant of the Einstein-Hilbert action. This indicates that the proposed quantum gravity theory can be derived from a microscopic model, offering a potential solution to the long-standing problem of identifying the microscopic origin of quantum gravity. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions.
