Although regional attention mechanisms have enhanced the robustness of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) against adversarial attacks, they are susceptible to adversarial examples generated by disrupting these regions. This paper investigates the interaction between regional queries and coordinate queries within a regional attention framework. We demonstrate that while coordinate queries are essential for establishing a global perspective, they are insufficient on their own to guarantee resilience. Consequently, we introduce a novel dual-query approach that integrates both regional and coordinate queries. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks reveal that this dual-query method significantly outperforms existing techniques for global attention-based adversarial defense. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that regional queries are most effective in models with a high number of parameters, offering substantial improvements in such architectures. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/Regional-Query-Attention.

The Quick Sinkhorn algorithm serves as a practical alternative to classic Sinkhorn methods for solving optimal transport problems, offering a significant reduction in the number of iterations needed for convergence. However, it lacks precise convergence guarantees. This paper introduces a variant of Quick Sinkhorn designed to achieve precise and efficient computation of optimal transport plans. The proposed algorithm addresses the optimal transport problem between two $n$-dimensional spaces by utilizing two $n \times n$ collinear triangular matrices, where the $i$-th row of each matrix corresponds to the $i$-th dimension. By applying the algorithm row-by-row, it ensures that the resulting transport matrix remains low-rank. This collinear structure enables the algorithm to compute the optimal transport matrix in $O(n)$ time, with a convergence guarantee requiring $O(n)$ iterations. Furthermore, the method is robust against the common issue of ill-posedness in optimal transport problems. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach is both precise and efficient, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both speed and accuracy. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/leeyang1995/QuickSinkhornII}. This work serves as the successor to our previous study, Quick Sinkhorn I, which also addressed the optimal transport problem between two $n$-dimensional spaces but employed two $n \times n$ matrices rather than two collinear triangular matrices. In that earlier version, the $i$-th row of each matrix was not specifically linked to the $i$-th dimension. The primary distinction between the two versions lies in the utilization of the collinear structure of the triangular matrices. In the first version, this collinear structure was not leveraged, resulting in a computational complexity of $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n^2)$ iterations. In contrast, the second version exploits this collinear structure to reduce the complexity to $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ iterations. This paper focuses on the second version. The detailed comparison between these two approaches will be presented in a separate publication. Additionally, a comprehensive tutorial on the collinear structure of triangular matrices will be provided in another paper. This research was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the University of Washington. The AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system serves as a critical benchmark for understanding the evolution of planetary systems around active stars. This study investigates the behavior of AU Mic's active disk and its two known planets, AU Mic b and c, by analyzing 12 years of far-ultraviolet (FUV) photometry from the Swift UVOT and the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS). The research identifies 12 significant FUV eruptions, with the largest reaching a factor of 100 above the baseline flux. These events are attributed to magnetic reconnection within the disk, a process that also drives the steady accretion of material onto the star. The study further examines the correlation between these eruptions and the positions of the planets, as well as the potential impact of FUV irradiation on the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c. Finally, the temporal evolution of the FUV flux is modeled to determine the star's impact on the habitability of any potential planets in the system. The data indicate that AU Mic's FUV flux was approximately 10 times higher in its youth than it is today, a condition that would have been detrimental to life as we know it. Additionally, the FUV flux is projected to decline by a factor of 10 over the next 100 million years, a rate of change that is significantly more rapid than what is expected for the Sun. These findings have profound implications for the habitability of planets orbiting active stars. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between the FUV flux and the X-ray luminosity of AU Mic, revealing a strong correlation that supports the hypothesis that FUV and X-ray emissions share a common origin. This relationship is also observed in other young, active stars, such as HD 179949 and HD 142666. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the habitability of exoplanets. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the behavior of AU Mic and its planets, offering valuable insights into the evolution of planetary systems around active stars. The findings underscore the need for further research to better understand the impact of FUV irradiation on the habitability of exoplanets and the evolution of planetary systems around active stars. The data presented in this study will be invaluable for future studies of the AU Mic system and will contribute to our understanding of the broader population of active stars and their planetary systems. A novel form of radiation response drag, termed "RRD," is introduced. It is demonstrated that the emergence of RRD relies on the interplay between radiative and non-radiative energy fluxes, as well as between radiative energy flux and entropy production. Specifically, the work posits that RRD manifests when radiative and non-radiative energy fluxes oppose each other; while the former is defined by the medium's radiative properties, the latter is contingent upon the gradient of thermodynamic variables. Furthermore, the presence of an active medium is essential for RRD, as entropy production within the system is required to sustain a non-radiative energy flux. The paper illustrates that RRD arises in various scenarios, including the movement of a body through a resistive substance medium, the interaction between a body and a resistive substance medium, and the flow of a resistive substance medium itself. Additionally, the concept of radiative energy flux is extended to encompass non-radiative fluxes, such as those occurring in resistive substance media. The validity of this approach is confirmed by the recovery of the Darcy law for porous media and the Navier-Stokes equation for Newtonian fluids. The discussion also addresses the conditions under which the first law of thermodynamics is satisfied. Finally, the paper examines the characteristics of RRD, its relationship with the Joule effect, and the implications of these phenomena for the principle of energy conservation. The study concludes by exploring potential applications of RRD in engineering and technology. The paper is structured into the following sections: Section 2 introduces the concept of RRD; Section 3 applies this concept to the motion of a body within a resistive substance medium; Section 4 addresses the interaction between a body and a resistive substance medium; Section 5 considers the flow of a resistive substance medium; and Section 6 offers a discussion. The concluding section summarizes the key findings. The authors anticipate that this work will contribute to the advancement of radiative transfer theory and facilitate the application of RRD in engineering and technology. Keywords: radiative energy flux, entropy production, Joule effect, energy conservation, resistive substance medium.

This paper introduces a statistical approach to C-N nearest neighbor classification that leverages the distributional properties of classes within neighborhoods. The core concept involves assigning a weight to each class based on the inverse of its variance in a specific neighborhood, thereby favoring classes with more uniform distributions. A neighborhood is defined as the collection of neighbors surrounding a query point, determined by a specific radius. The optimal radius is selected by maximizing the weighted sum of class indicators across all neighborhoods. The study provides a statistical analysis of the estimator and establishes its strong consistency. Furthermore, the authors propose a data-driven method to estimate the radius of the neighborhood. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the standard C-N algorithm. Additionally, the paper offers a theoretical comparison between C-N and the proposed neighborhood-based variant, proving that the new method achieves the same minimax rate of risk as the original C-N algorithm. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of potential future research directions. The proposed method is implemented in the R programming language and is available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/NN. Utilizing SkyMapper Deep Sky Surveys, we have identified 1,000 new quasars, including 100 with redshifts greater than 3.5, thereby significantly expanding the known population of the most luminous quasars at high redshift. This study focuses on the 100 quasars with $z>3.5$, which are exceptionally bright, exhibiting a median absolute bolometric luminosity of $L_{\rm bol} = 10^{46.4}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and a median black hole mass of $M_{\rm BH} = 10^{9.1}$ M$_{\odot}$. We demonstrate that the bright-end slope of the luminosity function for quasars with $z>3$ is steeper than previously thought, with a slope of $\alpha = 2.6 \pm 0.2$ (where $dN/dL \propto L^{-\alpha}$). Furthermore, we show that the quasar luminosity function at $z>3$ can be described by a single Schechter-like function, implying that the bright-end slope of the quasar mass function is likely steeper than the black hole mass function. Additionally, we find that the quasar luminosity function at $z>3$ is well-fitted by a Schechter-like function with a characteristic luminosity of $L^* = 10^{46.0}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and a characteristic slope of $\alpha^* = 2.0 \pm 0.1$. Finally, we present the first evidence that the quasar luminosity function at $z>3$ is independent of redshift. These findings suggest that the most luminous quasars at $z>3$ are more massive and more luminous than their lower-redshift counterparts, and that the bright-end slope of the quasar luminosity function remains constant at $z>3$. These results indicate that the most luminous quasars at $z>3$ are extremely rare, with a comoving number density of $n \sim 10^{-9}$ Mpc$^{-3}$, and that their black hole accretion rates are comparable to the star formation rates of their host galaxies. These extreme properties may be linked to the early formation of supermassive black holes. The Ultra-bright high-redshift quasars from SkyMapper dataset will be made publicly available. This study investigates the charge transfer dynamics between a quantum dot and a superconducting reservoir using a charge sensor. By analyzing the time-dependent evolution of the sensor's backaction noise, we identify two distinct tunneling mechanisms: a transient event occurring immediately after the switch-on of a superconducting terminal, and a steady-state process driven by the co-tunneling of a Cooper pair. Furthermore, we examine how these mechanisms are influenced by variations in tunnel coupling and dot capacitance. Our findings offer valuable insights into the quantum charge-tunneling properties between a quantum dot and a superconducting terminal, which can be applied to various quantum information processing tasks. Additionally, the detailed examination of gate sensing and its dependence on dot capacitance may assist in the development of more efficient quantum dot capacitance sensors. Finally, our results could aid in the design of more precise quantum dot-based charge sensors. This research was conducted within the framework of the Quantum Engineering Technology and Application National Key Research and Development Program (Grant No. 2020YFB0504600). The corresponding authors are J. Q. You and H. Q. Xu. This work introduces contraction conditions applicable to all admissible entropy/supply pairs for frameworks of conservation laws, specifically addressing the entropic discontinuous solutions encountered in systems like conservation laws and Hamilton-Jacobi equations. We demonstrate that these conditions are naturally fulfilled by the relative entropy contraction, the Entropy/Contraction/Holmgren (ECH) condition, and the Contradiction condition. Furthermore, we establish that these three conditions are equivalent within the framework of conservation laws. Finally, we analyze the relationship between these conditions and the concept of contractivity found in Hamilton-Jacobi equations. The proposed conditions are notably advantageous because they rely solely on the structure of the conservation law's right-hand side, thereby eliminating the necessity to compute the characteristic matrix, a step that is often impractical in the context of Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Additionally, the paper includes illustrative examples of frameworks where these conditions hold or fail. Notably, the ECH condition was previously characterized as necessary and sufficient for the well-posedness of Hamilton-Jacobi equations; this study extends that result by proving its sufficiency for frameworks of conservation laws as well. The methodology is applicable to both scalar and multi-dimensional problems, as well as finite-dimensional systems. The paper also features an appendix dedicated to the theory of generalized differentials and subdifferentials. This appendix refines the findings of Bardi and Da Prato regarding the equivalence between the contractivity of value functions and the contractivity of their subdifferentials, and it offers an alternative proof of the latter's sufficiency. The appendix also presents novel results concerning the relationship between these conditions and the concept of strict differentiability. These findings are essential for the subsequent analysis of the sufficiency of the ECH condition regarding the well-posedness of Hamilton-Jacobi equations. The appendix is structured into three sections: the first covers the differential of the value function, the second addresses the subdifferential of the value function, and the third explores the connection between these two concepts. The proofs for these relationships are notably more concise than those found in the original work by Bardi and Da Prato. The appendix is written to be largely self-contained, though it assumes familiarity with the foundational concepts of viscosity solutions. Single-view 3D dreaming aims to create novel, perpetual views from a limited set of 3D assets based on a specific camera prompt. Although recent approaches utilizing 3D diffusion models have shown promise, they often suffer from unreliable rendering, particularly in handling lighting and geometry. To address this, we introduce DiffDreamer, a straightforward yet robust framework that leverages conditional 3D diffusion to generate novel perpetual views. Our method first refines the 3D scene to better accommodate high-resolution image synthesis, followed by a conditional 2D diffusion model that incorporates both the 3D scene and camera parameters to produce high-quality, high-resolution images. To further enhance image realism, we employ a 2D control system that integrates 3D geometry and lighting cues. We demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on both 3D and 2D benchmarks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashley-chen/DiffDreamer. This paper introduces a new, purely data-driven approach to the prediction, simulation, and control of dynamics on networks. Specifically, we develop a data-driven framework capable of modeling networked processes without requiring knowledge of their underlying structure or dynamics. We demonstrate that this method can be applied to various network dynamics, including the well-known Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model. Furthermore, we prove that the proposed framework enables the prediction and control of network dynamics with accuracy comparable to structure-based methods. Our approach relies on a graph neural network that learns network dynamics from data, utilizing a novel loss function designed to ensure the learned dynamics adhere to the conservation laws inherent in network processes. We validate the effectiveness of this framework through numerical experiments on the SIS epidemic model, comparing its performance against other structure-based methods. The results indicate that the proposed data-driven framework achieves accuracy on par with existing structure-based techniques. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this framework for controlling network dynamics by applying it to limit the spread of epidemics. Numerical experiments confirm that the framework can successfully control epidemic dynamics, achieving results similar to those of structure-based approaches. The source code for our method is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/GraphNeuralNetworks}.

Keywords: data-driven, prediction, enhancement, control, networked processes, SIS epidemic model.

This paper investigates the stability of the Hunter-Saxton equation, expressed in its Lagrangian formulation as a transport equation accompanied by a transport formula. We demonstrate that solutions remain uniformly Lipschitz stable, provided the initial velocity field possesses sufficient regularity. This finding strengthens a previous result by Bressan and Shen, who required Lipschitz regularity for the velocity. Furthermore, our proof technique is more streamlined than the one previously employed. As an additional contribution, we extend Hunter and Saxton's result to establish the optimal $L^p$ bound for the solution's blow-up rate when $p > 1$. Our approach to proving Lipschitz stability relies on a novel technique for deriving a priori estimates within transport equations. Specifically, we introduce a new class of function spaces that are closed under the operation of transporting a Lipschitz function by another. These spaces are strictly larger than those previously utilized in stability analyses for the Hunter-Saxton transport formula. Consequently, this advancement facilitates the extension of Hunter and Saxton's optimal blow-up rate estimate to a broader range of $p$. Notably, this enhancement is achieved without relying on the recently developed optimal blow-up rate formula for the Hunter-Saxton equation. To ensure self-containment, we have included a detailed review of that formula. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research. Our methodology is applicable to a wide array of hyperbolic conservation laws, and we anticipate that this work will stimulate further investigation into the Hunter-Saxton equation. In particular, we propose that our findings may contribute to the longstanding open question regarding the equivalence between $L^1$-stability and the existence of a dual variational principle. Additionally, we suggest that our results could aid in clarifying the relationship between the critical Hunter-Saxton norm and the dual variational framework. Finally, we demonstrate that the recently discovered second Hunter-Saxton type equation also exhibits Lipschitz stability. This equation arises from a dual variational principle and is anticipated to generate the same type of blow-up scenario as the original Hunter-Saxton equation. To ensure accessibility, we have provided a comprehensive review of the dual variational principle. Finally, we have incorporated a detailed discussion of the original Hunter-Saxton blow-up rate formula into our analysis. **Background:** Ultrasound (US) imaging is increasingly utilized to assess spinal curvature in scoliosis patients. However, the reliability of this technique remains uncertain. **Objectives:** This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of scoliosis measurement via US compared to the gold standard, fluoroscopy. **Methods:** The study involved 20 scoliosis patients. Spinal curvature was measured using the Ultrasound Scoliosis Measurement System (USMS), which employs a robotic arm to automatically scan the spine. Two independent radiologists performed the assessments. **Results:** Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) indicated strong reliability for both manual (ICC = 0.91) and robotic (ICC = 0.90) US methods. The robotic approach demonstrated high agreement with fluoroscopy (ICC = 0.92). Furthermore, no statistically significant differences were found between the mean Cobb angles of manual, robotic, and fluoroscopy methods (P > 0.05). **Conclusion:** The findings suggest that scoliosis evaluation using ultrasound is a reliable and reproducible modality. Additionally, the use of a robotic arm enhances the consistency of ultrasound scans, yielding results comparable to those of fluoroscopy. **Limitations:** The study's sample size was relatively small. **Future Directions:** Larger-scale studies are necessary to validate these findings. **Implications:** These results may influence clinical practice by supporting the adoption of ultrasound for scoliosis assessment. **Study Design:** Clinical trial. **Keywords:** Scoliosis, Ultrasound, Robotic Arm, Reliability. **Source:** *Ultrasound in Medicine & Biology*, 2021, Vol. 47, No. 10, pp. 2701-2708. **DOI:** 10.1016/j.ultrasmedbio.2021.05.021. **Funding:** Supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 81871770). **Conflict of Interest:** The authors declare no conflicts of interest. **Correspondence:** Dr. Jie Chen, Department of Ultrasound, The First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University, Hefei, Anhui, China. This study introduces a novel, non-statistical approach designed to generate a collection of speech utterances with varying lengths based on a single median-length input. The proposed method operates by repeatedly applying a neural network to mediate between an existing utterance and a reference null-utteraction, thereby creating speech-like outputs of multiple shorter durations. We assessed this median length creation (MLC) system using both perceptual and automatic metrics. Automatic evaluation revealed that the generated utterances maintain semantic integrity and demonstrate natural prosodic characteristics. Conversely, a noiserating-based perceptual evaluation indicated that these synthetic utterances are perceived as resembling speech. The research also examined the impact of speaker and median operations on the quality of the synthesized results. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the proposed non-statistical method is effective for producing synthetic speech with diverse lengths. Furthermore, the study explores potential applications of the MLC system within speech enhancement and synthesis frameworks. Specifically, we demonstrate that incorporating the MLC system into a recently developed speech enhancement method yields superior performance compared to a statistical-based alternative. Additionally, we illustrate that integrating the MLC system with a recently introduced speech synthesis technique allows for the generation of utterances of arbitrary lengths. These results confirm the utility of the proposed non-statistical MLC system for producing synthetic speech of multiple lengths. Finally, the method's efficacy is validated through its application in creating synthetic data for training a speaker adaptation model. Experimental outcomes indicate that the synthetic data generated via the non-statistical MLC approach enhances speaker adaptation performance more effectively than data produced by a statistical-based method. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tae-hwan-goh/MLC. The term "null-utteraction" is a neologism derived from combining "null" and "utterance" to describe an empty utterance that serves as a reference for mediating with other speech signals. This paper investigates the application of a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture to deep neural networks for speech enhancement. Within this framework, multiple neural networks operate in parallel, receiving distinct feature inputs from an acoustic model to produce speech enhancement estimates. The primary objective is to determine the optimal number of networks and feature dimensions required to maximize performance. We demonstrate that, contrary to the typical trend of increasing parameters for improved accuracy, effective feature sharing can be achieved with a minimal parameter count, thereby yielding substantial computational savings. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to a asymmetric structure, which is particularly suited for real-time applications. Experimental results indicate that both the symmetric and asymmetric configurations utilizing shared features outperform a standard feedforward network in terms of speech enhancement quality. Additionally, the shared-structure models achieve these results with significantly fewer parameters and computational cost compared to the feedforward approach. The optimal configuration identified requires only 12.5% of the parameters and 16.7% of the computational cost of the feedforward model, while delivering a 1.5 dB higher Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepSpeechEnhancement/. This study introduces a smoothness-based control (SBC) approach for the smooth tracking control of a direct-drive robot joint. The method utilizes auxiliary encoders to measure the angular velocity of the joint, enabling the design of a smooth closed-loop system. By employing a smooth activation function, the resulting controller eliminates the discontinuous switching typically found in sliding mode control (SMC), thereby mitigating chattering. Furthermore, the designed SBC system inherits the robustness against disturbances and modeling uncertainties inherent to SMC. Simulation and experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed SBC system. Additionally, a comparison between the proposed SBC and SMC demonstrates that the SBC achieves superior smoothness. The findings indicate that the SBC not only outperforms SMC in terms of smoothness but also matches its tracking performance. This result is achieved through the use of auxiliary encoders to measure angular velocity, facilitating the design of a smooth closed-loop system. Consequently, this research offers a viable solution for addressing the trade-off between smoothness and tracking performance. The proposed SBC is particularly advantageous for robot joints equipped with auxiliary encoders, which are commonly found in commercially available robots. The study is supported by simulation and experimental results, and the proposed approach is expected to be applicable to other smooth control systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the problem formulation; Section 3 details the SBC design; Section 4 provides stability analysis; Section 5 offers simulation and experimental results; and Section 6 concludes the paper. This study introduces a multiple state examination (MSE) model designed to analyze multiple time-to-occur data points within a life course health trajectory framework. We demonstrate that the MSE model is mathematically equivalent to a multi-state model featuring a specific absorbing state. The model is evaluated using two datasets: a retrospective study of myocardial infarction patients and a prospective study of a healthy population. In the infarction dataset, time-to-occur variables include the age at diagnosis, age at reinfarction, age at death, age at hospitalization, and age at discharge, with hospitalization and discharge treated as time-dependent covariates. In the healthy population dataset, these variables correspond to the age at first pregnancy, age at second pregnancy, age at miscarriage, age at death, and age at diagnosis of depression. The MSE model is formulated as a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and solved via a novel method that avoids the need to estimate a large number of transition rates. We show that the model can be fitted to both type-I censored and type-II censored data, with the latter utilizing a simulation-based approach. Furthermore, the model allows for the estimation of the joint distribution of time-to-occur variables, which is applied to investigate the correlation between time-to-occur events in the healthy population. Finally, the paper discusses the construction of life course health paths, a visualization tool for life course data. This approach was applied to the infarction dataset to illustrate how the MSE model can be used to identify distinct health trajectories among patients. The findings suggest that the proposed MSE model is a versatile tool for life course data analysis, applicable to both retrospective and prospective studies. It enables the investigation of multiple time-to-occur variables and the identification of health trajectories, offering a novel method for analyzing complex life course data. The model is implemented in R, with code available at https://github.com/JulieBourhis/MSE. This paper introduces a quadrature approach designed to address the issue of molecular energy repulsion. By utilizing the electronic wave function, we construct a quadrature set of points and weights that enable the evaluation of potential energy at arbitrary spatial locations. This technique is particularly valuable for simulations involving multiple potential energy surfaces, such as those modeling non-adiabatic dynamics. We have developed a code capable of computing potential energy derivatives up to the third order at any site within the quadrature framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the accuracy of our quadrature method scales with the size of the basis set. Finally, we outline a computational strategy to minimize the number of gradient evaluations required during potential energy surface scans, thereby enhancing the efficiency of our approach. Our findings indicate that this quadrature-based scheme offers significant computational advantages over traditional methods for evaluating molecular potential energy surfaces. This paper investigates the decision problem for determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving set of size at most $k$, under the constraint that $k$ is parameterized by various graph parameters, including the size of a feedback vertex set, the treewidth, the pathwidth, and the branchwidth of $G$. We demonstrate that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set, as well as by the minimum of the treewidth, pathwidth, and branchwidth, provided the parameters are raised to the power of a logarithmic factor. The approach for the latter scenario extends the technique proposed by Marx and Schiermeyer (2011). Furthermore, we establish that the problem is linearly kernelizable with respect to the pathwidth parameter and conditionally fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the edge clique cover number. Finally, we prove that the problem is NP-complete for chordal bipartite graphs, even in instances where every resolving set is weakly dominating. Additionally, we examine how the problem behaves when the number of resolving sets is bounded. In this context, we show that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable for graphs with a bounded path covering number, and we extend the technique by Marx and Schiermeyer to demonstrate fixed-parameter tractability for graphs with a bounded tree depth. The findings are supported by a comprehensive set of examples and counterexamples. The paper concludes with an outline of the techniques employed and an explanation of the challenges encountered in the analysis. We introduce the concept of an $S$-fractured space, where $S$ denotes a directed space, and establish a functor that maps these spaces into categories enriched over the poset of subspaces. This functor is demonstrated to be monadic over the category of directed spaces. Furthermore, we examine specific examples, including $\cat{B}$-fractured spaces, to illustrate the applicability and structure of this framework. Additionally, we establish a correspondence between $\cat{B}$-fractured spaces and monads defined on the category of reflexive graphs. Finally, we outline a method for converting $S$-fractured spaces into $S$-directed spaces. This paper extends the research presented in [1].

This study examines the potential for recurring floods in simulated greenhouse climates, utilizing the coupled General Circulation Model (GCM) and ocean model developed by Valcke et al. (2007). The atmosphere-ocean system is subjected to a gradual increase in greenhouse gas concentrations, resulting in a rise in surface temperature and a corresponding decrease in the water vapor mixing ratio at the tropopause. Concurrently, the total water inventory within the model increases. The research investigates the evolution of the hydrological cycle, specifically focusing on precipitation and surface temperature, to determine if the system can transition from a stable climate to a recurrent flood state. The atmosphere is represented as a single layer with a fixed surface pressure, while the ocean is modeled as a single layer with a heat capacity that scales with the surface temperature. The system's response to a gradual rise in atmospheric composition is analyzed using both linear and nonlinear stability methods. Results indicate that the system can shift from a stable climate to a recurrent flood state if the rate of atmospheric composition change exceeds a specific threshold. This critical transition rate is determined by the rate at which the tropopause temperature increases. The evolution of the system is characterized by a linear growth of perturbations, with the growth rate and spatial pattern dictated by the rate of atmospheric composition change. Furthermore, the transition to recurrent floods is shown to be hysteretic, meaning the threshold for returning to a stable climate is higher than the threshold for the initial transition. Finally, the paper explores the implications of these findings for the simulated transition between stable and greenhouse climates. Key references include Valcke et al. We introduce the concept of higher-spin extensions for (self-dual) Yang-Mills theories, termed "twistor creations," which arise from the factorization of monodromy matrices associated with higher-spin Riemann surfaces. This framework encompasses both Yang-Mills theories at various spins and Abelian higher-spin fields. The resulting extensions maintain a strong resemblance to the Yang-Mills description of gravity and M-theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cohomology of these twistor creations encodes the cohomology of the corresponding higher-spin Yang-Mills theory. Finally, we propose that these twistor creations serve as a foundation for developing a higher-spin version of topological field theory. Additionally, we elucidate how to construct such theories using the factorization of monodromy matrices within higher-spin Riemann surfaces. Deep learning has achieved remarkable success across various image processing tasks, including segmentation, classification, and object detection. However, the necessity for large volumes of labeled data remains a significant barrier to the widespread adoption of these methods in medical imaging. To address this, semi-supervised learning has emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging unlabeled samples. Despite this, the presence of label noise in medical datasets continues to pose a critical challenge. This study introduces a framework designed to mitigate noisy labels during training. The proposed approach utilizes Bayesian statistics to reassign training labels, thereby reducing noise impact. Additionally, a consistency regularization mechanism is employed to further refine the model's predictions on unlabeled data. Experiments conducted on the ISIC 2018 skin lesion dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/BS-LRM. This work is partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 61976048). This paper aims to reestablish a well-known inequality concerning the Lebesgue constant for polynomial interpolation at scattered nodes within bounded domains, utilizing the commutative diagram method. We employ this approach to demonstrate that, under the assumption of continuity, the constant $C$ in the estimate $\|I_n\| \leq Cn^\alpha$ for the sequence $\{f_n=P_n(f)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ must satisfy $\alpha \geq 1/2$. Furthermore, in the context of polynomial interpolation at equidistant nodes on the interval $I=[-1,1]$, we derive the sharper estimate $\|I_n\| \leq Cn$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, where $C$ denotes the growth rate of the Hilbert matrix. Additionally, we present several novel inequalities related to polynomial interpolation. Specifically, for any $f\in C^1(I)$, the following holds:
$$\|I_n\| \leq C\left(1+\frac{n}{\|f''\|}\right), \quad \forall n\in\mathbb{N}.$$
This result improves upon a recent finding by S. Rautenbach, who had previously established the estimate $\|I_n\| \leq C\left(1+\frac{n^2}{\|f''\|}\right)$ for the same scenario. We also provide several remarks and examples to illustrate the applicability of our new estimates. Finally, we outline several open problems for future research.
**Keywords:** Polynomial interpolation; Lebesgue constant; Commutative diagram; Hilbert matrix.

Let $G=(V,E)$ represent an undirected graph where $V$ denotes the set of vertices and $E$ the set of edges. A symmetric transition matrix $P$ is defined for the random walk on $G$, with $p_{ij}$ indicating the probability of moving from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$. The transition probability distribution associated with this matrix is defined as $f_p(t)=\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}p^t$, where $p$ is a vertex in $V$. This document introduces a distinctive polynomial $f_{p,i}(t)$ for the transition probability matrix of the random walk on $G$, which encodes the size of the set $\{t \in \mathbb{N} | f_p(t)=p_i\}$. We demonstrate that $f_{p,i}(t)$ can be derived from the minimal polynomial of the adjacency matrix of $G$ and the degree polynomial of vertex $i$. Furthermore, we establish that the polynomial $f_{p,i}(t)$ is unique for a given graph $G$ and vertex $i$. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the transition probability distribution and the eigenvalues of $P$. Specifically, we prove that the transition probability distribution $f_p(t)$ is uniquely determined by the eigenvalues of $P$. Consequently, we show that the transition probability distribution $f_p(t)$ can be recovered from the characteristic polynomial of $P$. Finally, we illustrate these findings with examples of random walk transition probability distributions for specific graphs. These results offer a novel approach to analyzing random walks on graphs. The paper concludes with several open problems. We introduce a theoretical framework for Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals, which emerge when Hofstadler superlattices are overlaid on materials hosting Weyl semimetal phases. These states exhibit unique topological characteristics, including nontrivial Chern numbers and quantized anomalous Hall conductance. Furthermore, their energy dispersion relations display a distinctive pinning effect at zero Landau level energies. By applying the low-energy effective theory of time-reversal-violated Weyl semimetals within the Hofstadler regime, we demonstrate that their momentum-resolved spectral features can be characterized by a set of topological invariants known as Weyl charges. Finally, we illustrate how these momentum-resolved properties can be observed experimentally through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Additionally, we identify a novel topological phase featuring a single isolated zero Landau level, which represents a new member of the family of noncontractible topological states. This phase is distinguished by a non-zero, quantized anomalous Hall conductance and a non-zero first Stiefel-Whitney class. Our findings provide a comprehensive topological description of Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals, offering a robust foundation for future experimental investigations. Specifically, our results suggest the existence of topologically nontrivial states in honeycomb lattices with time-reversal violation, a prediction that contrasts with the conventional understanding of Hofstadler models on honeycomb lattices. Our work establishes a new class of topological states in Hofstadler lattices, which are characterized by non-zero, quantized anomalous Hall conductance and a non-zero first Stiefel-Whitney class. These states are topologically equivalent to quantum Hall states with a single quantum Hall Landau level. We anticipate that these findings will inspire experimental efforts to realize Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals and will facilitate the development of novel topological quantum technologies. Finally, we note that our theoretical framework can be extended to other lattice structures, such as kagome and triangular lattices. Anomalous screening, a phenomenon where larger particles settle between smaller ones in a mixture, is examined through both experiments and simulations. This model is corroborated by simulation outcomes and data from a ratchet experiment. Furthermore, the framework is extended to a one-dimensional setup involving particles with a continuous size distribution. The resulting theoretical predictions align well with simulation results and are consistent with existing literature. The one-dimensional model is also utilized to forecast the behavior of granular mixtures containing a mixture of two types of monodisperse particles. These forecasts are supported by simulations and validated against available experimental data. This discrepancy underscores the necessity of a more comprehensive theoretical approach to explain the mechanics of anomalous segregation. The current work represents a significant advancement toward achieving such a theory. The proposed framework is versatile and applicable to diverse granular systems, including those involving polydisperse particles, fluid interactions, and external forces. This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) through first-principles calculations. Specifically, we examine how Mn adatoms alter these characteristics. Our results indicate that Mn atoms bind to the Si atoms at the second-highest and second-lowest sites, forming structures that are energetically favorable and dynamically stable. The undoped system exhibits a direct band gap of 0.14 eV, which increases to 0.22 eV upon Mn adsorption. Spin-polarized calculations reveal that the magnetic moment of the Mn adatom is 4.95 $\mu_B$, aligning well with the expected value of 5 $\mu_B$. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that Mn adatoms induce strong ferromagnetic coupling between them. Finally, we show that silicene adorned with Mn adatoms can serve as an effective spin filter. These findings suggest that Mn-decorated silicene has significant potential for applications in spintronics. Additionally, this research offers a viable method for engineering the electronic and magnetic properties of silicene via the adsorption of transition metal atoms. The data presented can facilitate the design of advanced silicene-based electronic and spintronic devices. All calculations were performed using the VASP code. The structural model was constructed with help from Avogadro, and the figures were generated using Gnuplot. The VASP input files are available upon request. Sgr A East is a supernova remnant situated near the Galactic center, with its progenitor identified as a massive star that exploded approximately 2.5 million years ago. The remnant's morphology is highly asymmetric, featuring a compact region measuring 0.3 pc by 0.1 pc adjacent to the Galactic center and a large, diffuse area extending 1.5 pc toward the Galactic anticenter. This study employs a three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation to investigate the interaction between the supernova and the surrounding interstellar medium, aiming to replicate the remnant's current structure. We demonstrate that a supernova occurring within 0.1 pc of the Galactic center can reproduce the overall shape of Sgr A East, provided the explosion energy falls between 10^50 and 10^51 ergs. Our findings indicate that the compact region is a direct result of the supernova's asymmetric expansion, whereas the diffuse region was shaped by the interaction between the ejecta and the ambient medium. Furthermore, we show that a supernova within 0.5 pc of the Galactic center can account for the 13-microsecond radio delay observed between the Galactic center and Sgr A East. Our results suggest that the dense gas cloud S28, located 0.2 pc from the Galactic center, serves as an ideal site for the supernova explosion. Additionally, we propose that supernovae occurring within 0.5 pc of the Galactic center are likely to produce asymmetric remnants, a hypothesis supported by the observed asymmetry of the S147 remnant. Finally, we demonstrate that supernovae occurring within 0.3 pc of the Galactic center can trigger star formation in nearby dense gas clouds, such as S28, S106, and S110. These findings underscore the critical role of the Galactic center's environment in determining the supernova's explosion site and the subsequent evolution of the remnant. Our research highlights the necessity of conducting high-resolution simulations to accurately model the complex dynamics of supernova explosions in this region. Multi-class text categorization is a fundamental NLP task that has garnered significant research interest, particularly due to the advent of large-scale datasets like Wikipedia. Although most existing studies assume a balanced distribution of classes, real-world scenarios often involve numerous categories with highly imbalanced sample sizes. This imbalance complicates classification, as models tend to favor larger classes, resulting in reduced accuracy for smaller ones. To address this, various oversampling techniques have been developed. This paper evaluates the efficacy of three specific methods—random, nearest neighbor, and nearest sub-space oversampling—applied to text categorization. The results indicate that nearest sub-space oversampling is the most effective, yielding an average accuracy improvement of 1.2% over nearest neighbor and 2.1% over random oversampling. Furthermore, experiments using different sub-space dimensions reveal that a dimension of 1000 produces the optimal results. Finally, the study demonstrates that nearest sub-space oversampling is the most efficient approach for training large-scale models. The accompanying code and data are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/Multi-class-Text-Categorization. The authors can be contacted at abhishekkumar123@gmail.com. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06095. The title for the paper is "A Comparison of Artificial Oversampling Techniques for Multi-class Text Categorization."
Keywords: multi-class text categorization, imbalanced data, oversampling, sub-space, text categorization.

This study examines the interrelationships between regional news online (RNO) outlets and COVID-19 within the United States. Utilizing a dataset of 1.1 million RNO articles from 125 domains across 12 regions, alongside daily U.S. COVID-19 data from Johns Hopkins University, the research employs a Bayesian network approach. These results offer valuable insights for journalists, RNO publishers, and public health officials. Additionally, the research underscores the need for RNOs to adapt their coverage to the evolving phases of the pandemic. Finally, the study recommends that RNOs prioritize serving communities with lower levels of existing coverage. The data utilized in this research is accessible at https://osf.io/5742a/. The preservation of physical quantities is a fundamental requirement for any computational method. The Rapid Multipole Method (RMM) is a widely used algorithm designed to efficiently calculate multipole interactions in quantum chemistry. However, previous implementations have demonstrated notable inaccuracies when handling angular momentum greater than 2. This study introduces a novel approach to constructing RMM basis functions that guarantees the exact preservation of angular momentum up to any desired level. The efficacy of this technique is validated through applications to hydrogen and neon atoms. Furthermore, the method is extended to represent angular momentum in the presence of magnetic fields, with accuracy confirmed by comparing results against analytical solutions. These findings demonstrate that the proposed RMM algorithm maintains high accuracy across a broad spectrum of multipole interactions. Consequently, this work establishes a new standard for RMM basis function construction, offering a significant advancement for quantum chemistry computations. Additionally, the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekbisht/RMM. Parametric authorities, including Bayesian, variational, and neural likelihood-free inference methods, are increasingly popular for probabilistic reasoning with limited data. However, these approaches often struggle to generalize when data is scarce or when the authority's parameters are poorly specified. This paper investigates the relationship between an authority's sensitivity to its parameters and the amount of data required for robust learning. We demonstrate that data amplification—repeatedly applying a stochastic forward model to a single data point—can significantly decrease the information needed to train an effective parametric authority. Furthermore, we show that data amplification can be seamlessly integrated with both Markov chain Monte Carlo and stochastic gradient descent. Our method is validated across a diverse range of problems, from simple to complex, using both synthetic and real-world datasets. We find that data amplification consistently yields substantial performance gains, particularly in low-data regimes. Additionally, we observe that data amplification acts as a regularizer, enabling the training of more complex models that generalize better to unseen data. Finally, we demonstrate that data amplification is compatible with various likelihood-free inference techniques, including approximate Bayesian computation, neural variational inference, and neural posterior estimation. This suggests that data amplification is a broadly applicable strategy for enhancing learning from restricted datasets when utilizing parametric authorities. This study investigates the non-resonant double production of Higgs bosons in association with a vector boson (WW, WZ, or ZZ) at the LHC. The analysis utilizes 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV. A search is conducted for events featuring two Higgs bosons decaying into $\mathrm{b\overline{b}}$ pairs and a vector boson decaying into leptons, with the vector boson mass constrained to be off-shell. No significant excess above the predicted background is observed. The resulting 95% confidence level upper limits on the Higgs boson coupling to bottom quarks and the gauge boson self-coupling are determined to be 1.9 and 2.1 times, respectively, the Standard Model predictions. These findings represent the first observation of Higgs pair production with a vector boson and the most stringent constraints to date on the Higgs self-coupling. Additionally, the study examines the production of Higgs pairs through the $\mathrm{b\overline{b}}$ and $\tau\tau$ channels, as well as the associated production of two Higgs bosons with a Z boson. The analysis further explores the production of two Z bosons and sets the first direct limits on the trilinear Z coupling. Finally, the results are compared with predictions from various theoretical models. This search will be expanded in the future using the complete dataset from the LHC's Run 2 and Run 3. The accompanying paper details a similar investigation for Higgs pair production with a WW or WZ configuration. We introduce a theoretical framework for an electronic spin laser utilizing an alkali-metal vapor illuminated by an electronic dipole transition laser. This system features an active medium consisting of the alkali vapor and an optical pumping laser that drives spin excitations via non-resonant dipole transitions between the electron spin-up and spin-down hyperfine sublevels. We demonstrate that these non-resonant spin excitations can achieve population inversion between the sublevels, enabling lasing at the dipole transition frequency. Furthermore, we show that this lasing action is driven by spin excitations and can be regulated via the electron spin. Our findings indicate that the proposed electronic spin laser is feasible using standard materials, such as those currently employed in atomic vapor quantum information experiments. This device offers significant potential for applications in atomic vapor-based quantum technologies, including quantum information processing and communication. Additionally, our theoretical model is broadly applicable to any alkali-metal vapor system. We anticipate that this theoretical proposal will inspire experimental efforts to realize an electronic spin laser. This paper introduces a randomized Newton approach designed for high-dimensional distributed convex optimization. In this framework, a master node coordinates a collection of worker nodes, each trained on a subset of data. The proposed method leverages the fact that, under specific conditions, the Hessian of the objective function can be approximated using only the Hessians of individual local objectives. Consequently, the master node is not required to exchange gradients with workers, a step that typically creates a bottleneck in existing distributed Newton techniques. We demonstrate that this method achieves a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log(K) \log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\epsilon})$ to reach an $\epsilon$-accurate solution, where $K$ represents the number of workers and $\epsilon$ denotes the target accuracy. This complexity is superior to the $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log(K^2) \log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\epsilon})$ sample complexity of prior distributed Newton methods. Furthermore, we extend this approach to stochastic distributed convex optimization, proving a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log(K) \log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\epsilon^2 B^2})$, where $B$ reflects the stochasticity of the problem. Experimental results confirm the method's efficacy. To our knowledge, this work presents the first application of Newton methods to distributed stochastic convex optimization. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive analysis of the impact of master-worker communication costs on the overall computational complexity. Finally, we examine the influence of worker computation time on total complexity and explore strategies to mitigate this factor. High-resolution gas time projection chambers (TPCs) utilizing gas proportional detection are capable of measuring the position, energy, and timing of charged particles with sub-millimeter accuracy. These instruments are increasingly vital for dark matter searches, neutron physics, fundamental symmetry studies, and nuclear astrophysics. However, the detection of nuclear recoils from dark matter candidates or neutrinos presents significant challenges due to their low ionization yields and the need to distinguish them from electron recoils caused by background sources. This study introduces novel TPC observables that enhance the discrimination between nuclear and electron recoils. By analyzing the spatial distribution of charges on individual wires within each pixel, we derive new variables that improve the analysis of 3D point clouds. We demonstrate that these new observables achieve superior performance compared to the traditional summed charge signal, with a 20% gain in signal significance observed in a 100 cm$^3$ prototype. Furthermore, we outline a rigorous framework for evaluating the potential of these methods across various TPC designs and provide a toolkit for their implementation. This research is conducted within the NUCLEON collaboration, a global initiative dedicated to advancing gas TPC technology for dark matter research. This study introduces a sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral method designed to reconstruct the linear Koopman operator within state-space models. By applying sparse-grid quadrature to the linear Koopman equation, the approach efficiently addresses the curse of dimensionality inherent in high-dimensional systems. The technique utilizes a spectral basis function to represent the operator and adaptively refines a sparse-grid quadrature rule to enhance approximation accuracy. These results demonstrate that the approach yields a low-rank approximate representation of the Koopman operator that effectively captures the essential dynamics of the system. Additionally, the method exhibits superior performance in high-dimensional scenarios compared to existing techniques. Finally, the study confirms the method's utility in estimating the system's spectral abscissa. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a powerful iterative technique employed to solve the Schr\"odingri problem, which facilitates independent component analysis (ICA) and maximum entropy modeling in image analysis. This method iteratively normalizes the rows and columns of a matrix $A$ to approximate a matrix $B$ that is element-wise proportional to $A$ ($B\propto A$) while satisfying specified row and column marginals. Although the existence of such a matrix $B$ is not guaranteed for every matrix $A$, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn iterates converge to a matrix $B$ that maximizes the geometric mean of the discrepancies between the row and column marginals of $A$. This limiting matrix $B$ uniquely maximizes the same metric under the constraint of row marginals, or equivalently, under the constraint of a specific power of the marginals. These findings extend previous work by Carmon and Shamir (2019), which addressed the case where the problem always admits a solution. Furthermore, we establish that the Sinkhorn iterates converge linearly when the problem is solvable, a result that follows from Carmon and Shamir's (2019) findings. Our approach is less restrictive, as it accommodates matrices $A$ that prevent the existence of a matrix $B$ with equal marginals. Finally, we validate these theoretical results through experiments on various matrices, including those with zero entries. These numerical experiments confirm that the Sinkhorn method effectively solves the ICA problem, even when $A$ contains zero values. Specifically, we observe that the method successfully identifies the true mixing matrix, provided that the product of the counts of zero entries in each row and column of $A$ is sufficiently small. Additionally, we show that the convergence of Sinkhorn is significantly slower when the number of zero entries in $A$ is large. This behavior is attributed to the presence of submatrices within $A$ that are entirely zero, a phenomenon that can be mitigated by modifying $A$ to eliminate these zero submatrices. This modification strategy is also applicable to other scenarios where zero entries in $A$ hinder the existence of a matrix $B$ with equal marginals. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed modification can also address cases where a solution exists but leads to extremely slow convergence. This study examines the localization dynamics of a central site within a ring of $N$ sites connected to it. The ring is governed by a localized Anderson model, while the central site follows either a localized or delocalized Anderson model. We demonstrate that although the central site can be localized even when the entire system is delocalized, its localization dynamics are significantly slower than those of the global system. Furthermore, we establish that the localization length of the central site scales with the global localization length as $l_{\rm center}\sim l_{\rm global}^{0.5}$. These findings were validated through numerical simulations of the full system. Additionally, we present an analytical framework that captures the primary qualitative aspects of these results. Finally, we outline several potential applications of the central site's localization behavior in central-satellite systems. The approaches compared are the Black-Oil with Fixed Point (BOFP) method and the Black-Oil with Fixed Point with Newton Linearization (BOFNL) method. Both techniques employ a Schur complement-based nested solver, where the inner system is solved using a standard iterative multigrid method. The research details the construction of each preconditioner and presents a comprehensive performance comparison across various benchmark test cases. Furthermore, the study assesses both methods against additional benchmarks featuring complex 3D geological structures, observing consistent performance trends. Finally, a novel benchmark involving a heterogeneous fault zone is introduced, and its performance is analyzed in detail. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that BOFNL is more efficient than BOFP for the tested benchmarks, with the BOFNL multigrid preconditioner proving particularly advantageous in heterogeneous fault zones. We introduce a novel design for chiral optical cavities featuring unilateral coupling between the two orthogonal transverse modes. This mechanism stems from the intrinsic properties of the transverse magnetic modes within a circularly symmetric cavity, specifically their non-orthogonality and the direction-dependent (chiral) nature of their mutual overlap integral. This novel approach offers a pathway to enhanced chiral light-matter interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these mode characteristics can be exploited to generate a non-thermal, single-photon state with directional probability flow. This state is produced by injecting a weak coherent pulse into the cavity, where the resulting thermo-optic shift in the resonant frequency causes the cavity to operate off-resonance in a self-biased manner. Our findings are validated through full-wave simulations of both a practical and a simplified cavity model. Additionally, we outline potential applications, including the creation of chiral photonic crystals and the development of chiral lasers. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our work for the design of photonic devices. The accompanying supplementary material provides further details on the proposed applications and explores the underlying physics of the transverse modes. This paper investigates the relationship between the matrix model and Liouville CFT within the framework of 2D JT gravity. We demonstrate that the partition function of Liouville CFT on a sphere with two insertions can be derived from the large-$N$ limit of the matrix model partition function in the semi-classical regime. This finding offers a novel method for calculating the partition function of Liouville CFT on a sphere with two operator insertions. Furthermore, we compute the connected 4-point correlation function involving holomorphic scalar operator insertions in the semi-classical limit and compare these results with those predicted by JT gravity. Our analysis indicates that the semi-classical limit of the matrix model successfully captures the connected 4-point function in the semi-classical limit of Liouville CFT. Additionally, we show that in the semi-classical limit, the connected 4-point function in Liouville CFT is entirely determined by the spectrum of the Virasoro algebra. Finally, we extend our discussion to the sphere three-point function and the two-point function in the presence of a scalar operator insertion. We find that the semi-classical limit of the matrix model accurately reproduces the sphere three-point function in Liouville CFT, as well as the two-point function with a scalar operator insertion. However, regarding the two-point function with an operator insertion, we observe that the spectrum of the Virasoro algebra is no longer necessary. We also examine the sphere two-point function in Liouville CFT when a scalar operator is inserted, noting that it is not fully reproduced by the semi-classical limit of the matrix model. This discrepancy is attributed to the presence of a non-trivial conformal block in Liouville CFT, which arises from the interaction between the bulk and boundary degrees of freedom. Consequently, this suggests that a quantum correction to the matrix model may be required to fully reproduce the sphere two-point function in Liouville CFT with an operator insertion. Finally, we briefly discuss the implications of these findings for the holographic duality between Liouville CFT and 2D JT gravity. The warping of spacetime to generate ideal fluid warp drive solutions is achieved through a specific tensor decomposition of the Ricci tensor. This method relies on the cosmological constant and the Ricci curvature tensor, which is derived from the Riemann curvature tensor. The study examines two scenarios: one where the Ricci tensor depends on the four-velocity of an observer, and another where it does not. In the first scenario, the analysis identifies two novel ideal fluid warp drive solutions, while the second scenario yields a single solution. For both cases, the warp field metric is derived from the Riemann curvature tensor. Furthermore, the paper explores the physical implications of these new solutions, noting that they possess non-zero energy density, pressure, and the cosmological constant. The discussion concludes by addressing the nature of the energy density and whether it satisfies the weak energy condition. Finally, the study examines the equation of state for the ideal warp field fluid, specifically analyzing the parameter $w$ to determine if it falls within the range $-1 < w < 1$. The analysis indicates that the value of $w$ is not fixed but can vary depending on the specific spacetime geometry. Additionally, the paper investigates the influence of the cosmological constant on the equation of state and the parameter $w$. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the cosmological constant exerts a significant impact on the warp field fluid's equation of state. These results provide a foundation for future research into warp field physics and the development of more efficient warp drive technologies. The paper also includes several new results and theorems. This strategy focuses on four core pillars: establishing a unified data model, enhancing data quality, ensuring open data availability, and developing a robust data infrastructure. To support this initiative, the city has formed a dedicated team dedicated to designing and constructing a scalable data infrastructure. This paper outlines the team's methodology, emphasizing the critical role of data modeling and the adoption of a data lake architecture. Additionally, we introduce GUIDES, an open-source Python framework that facilitates data engineering for both batch and streaming processes. GUIDES is specifically tailored to support Helsinki's data strategy and is fully compatible with the city's existing data infrastructure. The framework is built upon four foundational components: a data model, a data lake, a data warehouse, and a data pipeline. GUIDES is designed to be modular, enabling the city to integrate it with existing tools and systems. Furthermore, the framework is highly extensible, allowing the team to continuously refine the infrastructure and adapt to the evolving needs of the data strategy. We provide an overview of GUIDES and demonstrate its application through a case study involving the processing of mobile network data. This demonstration includes the development of a data pipeline for both batch and streaming scenarios, as well as the integration of mobile data into the city's data lake. We introduce and implement a two-step spectroscopy method to investigate heating rates, non-thermal motional state distributions, and energy transfer within a two-dimensional ion crystal. This approach utilizes a spectroscopic mode filter to dephase the collective spin of $N$ ions by driving a single mode with a specific frequency $\omega_c$. By adjusting $\omega_c$ to match the spacing between motional sidebands of a fundamental mode, we can determine its heating rate. Furthermore, this technique offers a versatile tool for examining the dynamics of ion crystals. We validate these findings by comparing them with a stochastic Schrödinger equation model. Our results indicate that the ion crystal remains in close proximity to a coherent state throughout the experiment. Finally, we demonstrate the method's utility in probing crystal dynamics by observing the transfer of excitation from a fundamental to a shear mode. This observation confirms that the shear mode is not fully isolated from the fundamental mode, as the two are weakly coupled through anharmonicity. The demonstrated capability to measure heating rates and non-thermal state populations establishes this approach as a valuable tool for characterizing the performance of large-scale trapped-ion quantum processors. Additionally, the method's adaptability suggests it can be extended to more complex systems, such as chains of multiple ions. This study introduces a fully quantum mechanical approach grounded in time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) to investigate the nonlinear enhancement mechanisms of tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS). The method explicitly accounts for the complex electronic and light-matter interactions occurring at the junction between a silver nanoparticle and a semiconducting tip, as well as between the tip and a monolayer of 4-mercaptopyridine. By employing a realistic illumination geometry, we demonstrate that TERS enhancement arises from a combination of electromagnetic and chemical effects. Specifically, we observe a nonlinear amplification of the illumination field at the molecule-tip junction, alongside a significant increase in both charge transfer and depolarization factors within the molecule-surface junction. These findings underscore the critical role of the atomically defined tip structure in achieving the observed enhancement. Furthermore, our results indicate that the tip's electronic structure is pivotal in determining the chemical enhancement of TERS. Finally, the proposed methodology is shown to be broadly applicable to a wide range of molecules and tip geometries. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/mauricio-fernandez/TERS.

This study investigates the entropy changes occurring during the phase transitions of ammonium sulfate ($(NH_4)_2SO_4$), a well-established molecular ferroelectric. By analyzing the entropy alterations at both the paraelectric-ferroelectric and ferroelectric-superionic transitions, we demonstrate that entropy changes in molecular ferroelectrics are primarily driven by the entropy of reorienting dipoles. This conclusion is supported by a comparison with other molecular ferroelectrics, as well as intrinsic evidence derived from the temperature dependence of the entropy change across both transitions. Our findings indicate that the entropy change at the ferroelectric transition is predominantly determined by the entropy of dipoles in their high-temperature state, a concept that can be readily applied to other molecular and solid-state ferroelectrics. Furthermore, we show that the entropy change at the paraelectric-ferroelectric transition is largely independent of the specific crystallographic phase, a result that can be utilized to predict the entropy change at this transition for other materials. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the development of molecular caloric materials. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of entropy changes at molecular caloric transitions, offering a pathway to enhance the performance of molecular caloric materials. Additionally, they offer a new perspective on the nature of molecular ferroelectrics and their potential applications. The methodology employed in this work is broadly applicable to caloric materials and can be used to investigate entropy changes at various phase transitions. Artificial intelligence, particularly reinforcement learning (RL), has achieved remarkable success across various domains, including games, by emulating decision-making processes. However, the cognitive subtypes reflected in these algorithms remain poorly understood. This study investigates the relationship between subtypes of RL strategies and human brain activity during a probabilistic learning task. We developed a computational model of human behavior utilizing a novel, unsupervised classification method that identifies distinct subtypes of RL strategies based on their reinforcement learning profiles. This new approach categorizes participants into subtypes and demonstrates that, compared to the traditional model, it better accounts for behavioral data. Furthermore, we find that individuals employing suboptimal or characteristic RL strategies exhibit distinct patterns of activity in the midbrain, specifically in how the midbrain encodes prediction errors. These findings suggest that RL subtypes may reflect distinct neurobiological mechanisms. Additionally, we introduce a new, unsupervised RL clustering method that offers a flexible framework for analyzing RL models and can be applied to diverse scenarios. The lattice $E_8$ is defined over a commutative ring $R$. When $R$ is the complex numbers, the resulting system is designated as the $E_8(\mathbb{C})$ lattice. This study examines quantum entanglement and contextuality within a quantum system built upon the Hilbert space of the $E_8(\mathbb{C})$ lattice. Furthermore, this work explores the potential of the $E_8(\mathbb{C})$ lattice system for simulating both high-energy and condensed matter systems. The $E_8$ lattice was first identified in 1887 by Felix Klein. In 1980, John Conway and Simon Plesset demonstrated that the lattice can be constructed using the 240 norm-one vectors of the octonions. Building on this, in 1988, Conway and Norton conjectured a link between the $E_8$ lattice and a specific exceptional Lie algebra. This hypothesis was later confirmed by affine Kac in 1989. The $E_8$ lattice has since become a cornerstone in numerous areas of mathematics and physics. In 1993, Vafa and Affleck introduced the concept of a 4-dimensional topological quantum code based on the $E_8$ lattice, which exhibits a ground state degeneracy of 256. Additionally, the $E_8$ lattice plays a crucial role in the Leech lattice and the Monster group. Notably, the Leech lattice is significant in string theory, while the Monster group is essential for the theory of superstring. This paper focuses specifically on the quantum entanglement and contextuality aspects of the $E_8(\mathbb{C})$ lattice. The remainder of this work is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the foundational concepts of quantum entanglement and contextuality. Section 3 introduces the $E_8$ lattice and its associated quantum system. Section 4 investigates the quantum entanglement of this system. Section 5 explores the contextuality of the system using the formalism of non-contextual hidden variables. Finally, Section 6 outlines potential future research directions concerning the $E_8$ lattice. The $E_8$ lattice is an example of a root lattice, which are fundamental to the classification of simple Lie algebras. This work establishes strict limits for the Close Neighbor Searching (CNS) problem within the Discrete Fréchet distance model. Given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of $n$ time series, each of length $k$, the task involves computing a user-defined threshold $\tau$ and identifying all pairs $(p, q)$ where $p \in \mathcal{D}$ and $q \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ such that the distance $d(p,q) \leq \tau$. We introduce a novel approach that achieves a worst-case running time of $\tilde{O}(k^{1.5}n + k n^{1+1/(\lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1)})$. This method surpasses the best existing solution, which operates in $\tilde{O}(k^{2.5}n)$ time, by a factor of $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(\lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1)})$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm is nearly optimal by proving a lower bound of $\Omega(k n^{1+\lfloor 1/(k-1) \rfloor})$ on the PAM model. Our findings are supported by experimental results that validate the practical efficiency of the proposed algorithm. Qubit measurement errors are a primary factor restricting the scalability of near-term quantum computing. To address this, we introduce a new algorithm designed to mitigate such errors by executing quantum circuits multiple times with varying measurement bases. This approach, termed expandable measurement error reduction (eMER), is grounded in the iterative Bayesian Unraveling (iBEU) method originally developed for quantum state tomography. We demonstrate that eMER achieves superior performance compared to existing correction techniques, including the repeat before measure (RBM) strategy and recent methods utilizing additional quantum circuits. Furthermore, we illustrate that eMER can be applied to characterize measurement errors in multiqubit systems. Finally, we show that combining eMER with postprocessing enhances the fidelity of estimating expectation values for quantum circuits. These findings indicate that implementing a simple, adaptable measurement error correction scheme can significantly boost the utility of near-term quantum hardware. Our research is detailed in the paper "Expandable measurement error reduction via iterative Bayesian Unraveling" (Phys. Rev. Research 3, 023060, 2021).
